title: Subject
definition: The nominative case denotes the subject of the verb.

examples.greek: ταῦτα οἱ αἱρετοὶ ἀγγέλλουσι τοῖς στρατιώταις
examples.translation: The delegates report these things to the soldiers
Proxenus was present

title: Predicate
definition: The predicate noun in agreement of the subject of verbs such as εἰμί and γίγνομαι is in the nominative.

examples.translation: Clearchus was an exile
Man is entirely (a victim of) chance.

title: Independent
definition:
The nominative may be used independently in citing the names of persons and things.
Independent nominatives are also used in incomplete sentences:

smyth.text:
Independent Nominative.—The nominative may be used independently in citing the names of persons and things: prosei/lhfe th\n tw=n ponhrw=n koinh\n e)pwnumi/a_n su_kofa/nths he received the common appellation of the vile, i.e. ‘informer’
Aes. 2.99, to\ d' u(_mei=s o(/tan le/gw, le/gw th\n po/lin when I say You, I mean the State
D. 18.88. Cp. 908. (The accus. is also possible.) So in lists (cp. 904 c):

ti/qhmi du/o poihtikh=s ei)/dh: qei/a_ me\n kai\ a)nqrwpi/nh I assume two kinds of poetry: the divine and the human
P. Soph. 266d.

A sentence may begin with the nominative as the subject of the thought in place of an oblique case: oi( de\ fi/loi, a)/_n tis e)pi/sthtai au)toi=s xrh=sqai, ti/ fh/somen au)tou\s ei)=nai; but as for friends, if one knows how to treat them, what shall we call them?
X. O. 1.14 (for tou\s de\ fi/lous . . . ti/ fh/somen ei)=nai).
a. On the nominative in suspense see under Anacoluthon (Index).

In referring to himself in letters a man may use his own name in the nominative, either in apposition to the first person contained in the verb (976), or as subject of a verb in the third person: *qemistoklh=s h(/kw para\ se/ I, Themistocles, have come to you
T. 1.137,

*)artace/rchs nomi/zei Artaxerxes thinks
X. H. 5.1.31.
a. A speaker referring to himself in the third person usually soon reverts to the first person (
D. 18.79).

Incomplete sentences consist of a single member only. Such sentences stand outside the structure of the sentence. The chief classes of incomplete sentences are
a. Interjections, such as w)=, feu=, ai)ai=, oi)/moi.
b. Asseverations which serve as a predicate to a sentence spoken by another: nai/ yes, surely, ou)/ no, ma/lista certainly, kalw=s very well!
c. Headings, titles: *ku/_rou *)ana/basis the Expedition of Cyrus, *)antigo/nh the Antigone,

summaxi/a_ *)aqhnai/wn kai\ *qettalw=n the Alliance of the Athenians and Thessalians
C.I.A. /lref>b.
d. Vocatives (1283), and nominatives used in exclamation (1288).
e. Exclamations without a verb: deu=ro hither!
N.—Examples of such incomplete sentences in English are oh, assuredly, no wonder, right about face, away, fire!

examples.greek: προσείληφε τὴν τῶν πονηρῶν κοινὴν ἐπωνυμίαν συκοφάντης
examples.translation: he received the common appellation of the vile, i.e. ‘informer’

examples.greek: τὸ δ᾽ ὑμεῖς ὅταν λέγω, λέγω τὴν πόλιν
examples.translation: when I say You, I mean the State

examples.greek: τίθημι δύο ποιητικῆς εἴδη: θεία μὲν καὶ ἀνθρωπίνη
examples.translation: I assume two kinds of poetry: the divine and the human

title: As Vocative
definition: In a few cases, the nominative is used instead of a vocative for addressing or invoking.

examples.translation: O city, city\!

examples.greek: ὁ παῖς ἀκολούθει δεῦρο τὰ σκεύη φέρων
examples.translation: Follow, slave, and bring my baggage.

title: Possessor
definition:
The genitive denotes ownership, possession, or belonging. The genitive of possessor marks a person or thing that possesses someone or something else (and not the possessed). When referring to people, the genitive can denote the relationship of child to parent, wife to husband, or inferior to superior.
The possessive genitive is used with the neuter article (singular or plural) denoting affairs, conditions, power, and the like:

smyth.text:
The genitive denotes ownership, possession, or belonging:

h( oi)ki/a_ h( *si/mwnos the house of Simon
L. 3.32,

o( *ku/_rou sto/los the expedition of Cyrus
X. A. 1.2.5. Cp. the dative of possession (1476).

Here may be classed the genitive of origin:

oi( *so/lwnos no/moi the laws of Solon
D. 20.103, h( e)pistolh\ tou= *fili/ppou the letter of Philip 18. 37, ku/_mata pantoi/wn a)ne/mwn waves caused by all kinds of winds B 396.

The possessive genitive is used with the neuter article (singular or plural) denoting affairs, conditions, power, and the like:

to\ tw=n e)fo/rwn the power of the ephors
P. L. 712d,

to\ th=s te/xnhs the function of the art
P. G. 450c,

to\ tou= *so/lwnos the maxim of Solon
P. Lach. 188b,

a)/dhla ta\ tw=n pole/mwn the chances of war are uncertain
T. 2.11,

ta\ th=s po/lews the interests of the State
P. A. 36c,

ta\ tou= dh/mou fronei= is on the side of the people
Ar. Eq. 1216. Sometimes this is almost a mere periphrasis for the thing itself:

to\ th=s tu/xhs chance
D. 4.12 ta\ th=s swthri/a_s safety 23. 163, to\ th=s o(si/a_s, o(tidh/pot' e)sti/ the quality of holiness, whatever it is 21. 126,

to\ tw=n presbute/rwn h(mw=n we elders
P. L. 657d. So to\ tou/tou
S. Aj. 124 is almost = ou(=tos, as tou)mo/n is = e)gw/ or e)me/. Cp.
L. 8.19.

The genitive of possession may be used after a demonstrative or relative pronoun:

tou=to/ mou diaba/llei he attacks this action of mine
D. 18.28.

With persons the genitive may denote the relation of child to parent, wife to husband, and of inferior to superior: *qouku_di/dhs o( *)olo/rou Thucydides, the son of Olorus
T. 4.104 (and so uio/s is regularly omitted in Attic official documents), *dio\s *)/artemis Artemis, daughter of Zeus
S. Aj. 172,

h( *smi_kuqi/wnos *melisti/xh Melistiche wife of Smicythion
Ar. Eccl. 46, *au_do\s o( *ferekle/ous Lydus, the slave of Pherecles
And. 1.17,

oi( *me/nwnos the troops of Menon
X. A. 1.5.13 (oi( tou= *me/nwnos stratiw=tai 1. 5. 11).
a. In poetry we may have an attributive adjective: *telamw/nios *ai)/a_s ( = *ai)/a_s o( *telamw=nos) B 528. Cp. 846 f.

The word on which the possessive genitive depends may be represented by the article: a)po\ th=s e(autw=n from their own country (gh=s)
T. 1.15 (cp. 1027 b). A word for dwelling (oi)ki/a_, do/mos, and also i(ero/n) is perhaps omitted after e)n, ei)s, and sometimes after e)c. Thus,

e)n *)ari/fronos at Ariphron's
P. Pr. 320a, e)n *dionu/_sou (scil. i(erw=|) at the shrine of Dionysus
D. 5.7,

ei)s didaska/lou foita=n to go to school
X. C. 2.3.9,

e)k *patrokle/ous e)/rxomai I come from Patroclus's
Ar. Plut. 84. So, in Homer, ei)n（ei)s) *)ai/da_o.

examples.translation: the expedition of Cyrus
the house of Simon
Thucydides, the son of Olorus
Artemis, daughter of Zeus
Melistiche wife of Smicythion
Lydus, the slave of Pherecles
(the function) of the art
(the maxim) of Solon
(the chances) of war are uncertain
(the interests) of the State

title: Partitive
definition: The genitive may express the general class to which a specific noun belongs. The partitive genitive or the genitive of the divided whole may be used with any word that expresses or implies a part.

smyth.text: The genitive may denote a whole, a part of which is denoted by the noun it limits. The genitive of the divided whole may be used with any word that expresses or implies a part.

Position.—The genitive of the whole stands before or after the word denoting the part:

tw=n *qra|kw=n peltastai/ targeteers of the Thracians
T. 7.27,

oi( a)/poroi tw=n poli_tw=n the needy among the citizens
D. 18.104; rarely between the limited noun and its article:

oi( tw=n a)di/kwn a)fiknou/menoi those of the unrighteous who come here
P. G. 525c. Cp. 1161 N. 1.

When all are included there is no partition: so in ou(=toi pa/ntes all of these, all these, te/ttares h(mei=s h)=men there were four of us,

to\ pa=n plh=qos tw=n o(pli_tw=n the entire body of the hoplites
T. 8.93, o(/soi e)ste\ tw=n o(moi/wn as many of you as belong to the ‘peers’
X. A. 4.6.14.
The idea of division is often not explicitly stated. See third example in 1310.

(I) The genitive of the divided whole is used with substantives.

me/ros ti tw=n barba/rwn some part of the barbarians
T. 1.1, oi( *dwrih=s h(mw=n those of us who are Dorians 4. 61. The governing word may be omitted: *)arxi/a_s tw=n *(hra_kleidw=n Archias (one) of the Heraclidae
T. 6.3. To an indefinite substantive without the article may be added a genitive denoting the special sort: *ferau/la_s *pe/rshs tw=n dhmotw=n Pheraulas, a Persian, one of the common people
X. C. 2.3.7.

Chorographic Genitive.—

th=s *)attikh=s e)s *oi)no/hn to Oenoë in Attica
T. 2.18 (or e)s *oi)no/hn th=s *)attikh=s, not e)s th=s *)attikh=s *oi)no/hn), th=s *)itali/a_s *aokroi/ the Locrians in Italy 3. 86. The article, which is always used with the genitive of the country (as a place well known), is rarely added to the governing substantive (

to\ *kh/naion th=s *eu)boi/a_s Cenaeum in Euboea
T. 3.93).

(II) With substantive adjectives and participles.

oi( a)/dikoi tw=n a)nqrw/pwn the unjust among men
D. 27.68 (but always oi( qnhtoi\ a)/nqrwpoi),

mo/nos tw=n pruta/newn alone of the prytans
P. A. 32b,

o)li/goi au)tw=n few of them
X. A. 3.1.3,

tw=n a)/llwn *(ellh/nwn o( boulo/menos whoever of the rest of the Greeks so desires
T. 3.92. So

to\ katantikru\ au)tw=n tou= sphlai/ou the part of the cavern facing them
P. R. 515a. For nihil novi the Greek says ou)de\n kaino/n.

Adjectives denoting magnitude, and some others, may conform in gender to the genitive, instead of appearing in the neuter:

e)/temon th=s gh=s th\n pollh/n they ravaged most of the land
T. 2.56, th=s gh=s h( a)ri/sth the best of the land 1. 2. This construction occurs more frequently in prose than in poetry.

examples.translation: the needy among the citizens
targeteers of the Thracians
few of them
whoever of the rest of the Greeks so desires

examples.greek: οἱ μὲν αὐτῶν, οἱ δ᾽ οὔ
examples.translation: some of them and not others
those of the enemy who were taken later
no one in the world
a part of the wall
one of the many things

title: Quality
definition:
The genitive of quality denotes the quality of a person or thing and often is used as a predicate.
The attributive use occurs in poetry:

smyth.text:
The genitive to denote quality occurs chiefly as a predicate.

e)w\n tro/pou h(suxi/ou being of a peaceful disposition
Hdt. 1.107,

oi( de/ tines th=s au)th=s gnw/mhs o)li/goi kate/fugon but some few of the same opinion fled
T. 3.70,

tau=ta pampo/llwn e)sti\ lo/gwn this calls for a thorough discussion
P. L. 642a, qewrh/sat' au)to/n, mh\ o(pote/rou tou= lo/gou, a)ll' o(pote/rou tou= bi/ou e)sti/n consider, not the manner of his speech, but the manner of his life
Aes. 3.168,

ei) dokei= tau=ta kai\ dapa/nhs mega/lhs kai\ po/nwn pollw=n kai\ pra_gmatei/a_s ei)=nai if these matters seem to involve great expense and much toil and trouble
D. 8.48.
a. The attributive use occurs in poetry:

xo/rtwn eu)de/ndrwn *eu)rw/pa_s Europe with its pastures amid fair trees
E. I. T. 134, leukh=s xio/nos pte/ruc a wing white as snow (of white snow)
S. Ant. 114.

The use of the genitive to express quality, corresponding to the Latin genitive, occurs in the non-predicate position, only when age or size is exactly expressed by the addition of a numeral (genitive of measure, 1325). The Latin genitive of quality in mulier mirae pulchritudinis is expressed by gunh\ qaumasi/a_ ka/llos (or tou= ka/llous), gunh\ qaumasi/a_ i)dei=n, gunh\ e)/xousa qauma/sion sxh=ma, etc.

## GENITIVE OF EXPLANATION (APPOSITIVE GENITIVE)

examples.translation: being of a peaceful disposition

examples.greek: οἱ δέ τινες τῆς αὐτῆς γνώμης ὀλίγοι κατέφυγον
examples.translation: but some few of the same opinion fled
this calls for a thorough discussion

examples.greek: θεωρήσατ᾽ αὐτόν, μὴ ὁποτέρου τοῦ λόγου, ἀλλ᾽ ὁποτέρου τοῦ βίου ἐστίν
examples.translation: consider, not the manner of his speech, but the manner of his life

examples.greek: εἰ δοκεῖ ταῦτα καὶ δαπάνης μεγάλης καὶ πόνων πολλῶν καὶ πραγματείας εἶναι
examples.translation: if these matters seem to involve great expense and much toil and trouble
Europe with its pastures amid fair trees
a wing white as snow (of white snow)

title: Explanation
definition: The genitive of explanation, also called appositive genitive, adds specification or explanation to the meaning of a more general word. This construction is mostly used in poetry, but it can also be found in prose.

smyth.text:
The genitive of an explicit word may explain the meaning of a more general word.
*)i_li/ou po/lis E 642, as urbs Romae,

a)/ellai pantoi/wn a)ne/mwn blasts formed of winds of every sort
e 292. This construction is chiefly poetic, but in prose we find u(o\s me/ga xrh=ma a monster (great affair, 1294) of a boar
Hdt. 1.36,

to\ o)/ros th=s *)istw/nhs Mt. Istone
T. 4.46 (very rare, 1142 c). An articular infinitive in the genitive often defines the application of a substantive:

a)maqi/a_ h( tou= oi)/esqai ei)de/nai a:\ ou)k oi)=den the ignorance of thinking one knows what one does not know
P. A. 29b.
a. But with o)/noma the person or thing named is usually in apposition to o)/noma:

tw=| de\ newta/tw| e)qe/mhn o)/noma *kalli/straton I gave the youngest the name Callistratus
D. 43.74.

## GENITIVE OF MATERIAL OR CONTENTS

examples.translation: blasts of wind of every sort
a monster of a boar
the hill Istone

title: Material
definition: The genitive of material expresses the composition or contents of a noun or specifies the material out of which something is made.

smyth.text:
The genitive expresses material or contents.
e(/rkos o)do/ntwn the fence (consisting) of the teeth
*d 350,

krh/nh h(de/os u(/datos a spring of sweet water
X. A. 6.4.4, swroi\ si/_tou, cu/lwn, li/qwn heaps of corn, wood, stones
X. H. 4.4.12,

e(cako/sia ta/lanta fo/rou six hundred talents in taxes
T. 2.13 (cp. 1296).

Predicate Use:

stefa/nous r(o/dwn o)/ntas, a)ll' ou' xru_si/ou crowns that were of roses, not of gold
D. 22.70,

e)strwme/nh e)sti\ o(do\s li/qou a road was paved with stone
Hdt. 2.138, and often with verbs of making, which admit also the instrumental dative. Hdt. has poiei=sqai a)po/ and e)/k tinos.

## GENITIVE OF MEASURE

examples.translation: the fence (consisting) of the teeth
a spring of sweet water
heaps of corn, wood, stones

examples.greek: στεφάνους ῥόδων ὄντας, ἀλλ᾽ ου᾽ χρυσίου
examples.translation: crowns that were of roses, not of gold
a road was paved with stone

title: Measure
definition: The genitive of measure denotes the extent in space, time or degree of a noun or its amount.

smyth.text:
The genitive denotes measure of space, time, or degree.

o)ktw\ stadi/wn tei=xos a wall eight stades long
T. 7.2, pe/nte h(merw=n si_ti/a provisions for five days 7. 43 (cp. fossa pedum quindecim, exilium decem annorum Less commonly with a neuter adjective or pronoun: e)pi\ me/ga e)xw/rhsan duna/<*> they advanced to a great pitch of power
T. 1.118, ti\ do/chs some honour (aliq<*> famae) 1. 5, a)mh/xanon eu)daimoni/a_s (something infinite in the way of happiness) infinite happiness
P. A. 41c (with emphasis on the adj.). But the phrases ei)s tou=to, ei)s tosou=to a)fike/sqai (h)/kein, e)lqei=n, prosbai/nein, usually with a personal subject) followed by the genitive of abstracts are common:

ei)s tou=to qra/sous a)fi/_keto he reached such a pitch of boldness
D. 21.194,

e)n panti\ a)qu_mi/a_s in utter despondency
T. 7.55, e)n tou/tw| paraskeuh=s in this stage of preparation 2. 17, kata\ tou=to kairou= at that critical moment 7. 2. The article with this genitive is unusual in classical Greek:

ei)s tou=to th=s h(liki/a_s to this stage of life
L. 5.3. Some of these genitives may also be explained by 1306.

Under the head of measure belongs amount:

duoi=n mnai=n pro/sodos an income of two minae
X. Vect. 3.10. Cp. 1296, 1323.

Predicate Use.—

e)peida\n e)tw=n h)=| tis tria/_konta when a man is thirty years old
P. L. 721a,

ta\ tei/xh h)=n stadi/wn o)ktw/ the walls were eight stades long
T. 4.66.

## SUBJECTIVE AND OBJECTIVE GENITIVE

examples.translation: a wall eight stades long
provisions for five days
when a man is thirty years old
the walls were eight stades long
an income of two minae

title: Subjective
definition: With nouns derived from verbs, the genitive may denote the subject of the action expressed in the noun. The subjective genitive is active in sense.

smyth.text:
The Subjective Genitive is active in sense: tw=n barba/rwn fo/bos the fear of the barbarians (which they feel: oi( ba/rbaroi fobou=ntai)
X. A. 1.2.17, h( basile/ws e)piorki/a_ the perjury of the king (basileu\s e)piorkei=) 3. 2. 4,

to\ o)rgizo/menon th=s gnw/mhs their angry feelings
T. 2.59 (such genitives with substantive participles are common in Thucydides; cp. 1153 b, N. 2).

examples.translation: the fear of the barbarians (which they feel: οἱ βάρβαροι φοβοῦνται)
the perjury of the king (βασιλεὺς ἐπιορκεῖ)
Sing, o goddess, the anger of Achilles son of Peleus

title: Objective
definition: The objective genitive denotes the object in a passive sense with nouns derived from verbs, and it is very common with nouns indicating a state of mind or an emotion:

smyth.text:
The Objective Genitive is passive in sense, and is very common with substantives denoting a frame of mind or an emotion: fo/bos tw=n *ei(lw/twn the fear of the Helots (felt towards them: fobou=ntai tou\s *ei(/lwtas)
T. 3.54, h( tw=n *(ellh/nwn eu)/noia good-will towards the Greeks (eu)noei= toi=s *(/ellhsi)
X. A. 4.7.20, h( tw=n kalw=n sunousi/a_ intercourse with the good (su/neisi toi=s kaloi=s)
P. L. 838a.
a. The objective genitive often precedes another genitive on which it depends:

meta\ th=s cummaxi/a_s th=s ai)th/sews with the request for an alliance
T. 1.32.

Various prepositions are used in translating the objective genitive:

o( qew=n po/lemos war with the gods
X. A. 2.5.7,

o(/rkoi qew=n oaths by the gods
E. Hipp. 657,

qew=n eu)xai/ prayers to the gods
P. Phae. 244e,

a)dikhma/twn o)rgh/ anger at injustice
L. 12.20,

e)gkra/teia h(donh=s moderation in pleasure
I. 1.21,

h( tw=n h(donw=n ni/_kh victory over pleasures
P. L. 840c,

tro/paia barba/rwn memorials of victory over barbarians
X. A. 7.6.36,

paraine/seis tw=n cunallagw=n exhortations to reconciliation
T. 4.59,

mu=qos fi/lwn tidings about friends
S. Ant. 11,

sou= mu=qos speech with thee
S. O. C. 1161. In

qana/tou lu/sis release from death
i 421, metapauswlh\ pole/moio respite from war T 201, it is uncertain whether the genitive is objective or ablatival (1392).

The objective genitive is often used when a prepositional expression, giving greater precision, is more usual: to\ *megare/wn yh/fisma the decree relating to (peri/) the Megarians
T. 1.140, a)po/basis th=s gh=s a descent upon the land (e)s th\n gh=n) 1. 108, a)po/stasis tw=n *)aqhnai/wn revolt from the Athenians (a)po\ tw=n *)aqhnai/wn) 8. 5.

For the objective genitive a possessive pronoun is sometimes used:

sh\n xa/rin for thy sake
P. Soph. 242a,

diabolh\ h( e)mh/ calumniation of me
P. A. 20e. o( e)mo\s fo/bos is usually objective: the fear which I inspire. (But

sou= mu=qos speech with thee
S. O. C. 1161.)

Predicate Use.—ou) tw=n kakou/rgwn oi)=ktos, a)lla\ th=s di/khs compassion is not for wrong-doers, but for justice E. fr. 270.

## GENITIVE OF VALUE

examples.translation: the fear of the Helots (felt towards them: φοβοῦνται τοὺς Εἵλωτας）

examples.greek: ἡ **τῶν** **Ἑλλήνων** εὔνοια **X. A. 4.7.20**; ⇾ good-will towards the Greeks (εὐνοεῖ τοῖς Ἕλλησι)
examples.translation: good-will towards the Greeks (εὐνοεῖ τοῖς Ἕλλησι)
intercourse with the good (σύνεισι τοῖς καλοῖς)
war with the gods
oaths by the gods
anger at injustice
moderation in pleasure
speech with thee

title: Value
definition: The genitive of value denotes the value of a noun, such as price of an object. With verbs of buying, selling, costing or exchanging, the price given is in the genitive.

smyth.text:
The genitive expresses value.

i(era\ triw=n tala/ntwn offerings worth three talents
L. 30.20,

xi_li/wn draxmw=n di/khn feu/gw I am defendant in an action involving a thousand drachmas
D. 55.25.

Predicate Use:

tou\s ai)xmalw/tous tosou/twn xrhma/twn lu/_esqai to ransom the captives at so high a price
D. 19.222, triw=n draxmw=n ponhro\s w)/n a threepenny rogue 19. 200.

## TWO GENITIVES WITH ONE NOUN

examples.translation: offerings worth three talents
I am defendant in an action involving a thousand drachmas
to buy or sell a horse for money
they deemed Themistocles worthy of the greatest gifts

examples.greek: οὐκ ἀνταλλακτέον μοι τὴν φιλοτιμίαν οὐδενὸς κέρδους
examples.translation: I must not barter my public spirit for any price

title: Complement of the Verb
definition: Some verbs use the genitive as the object, such as verbs of sharing, beginning, aiming, attaining, remembering, smelling, touching, hearing, perceiving, filing, ruling, separating, releasing, depriving, commanding, etc. Many of these verbs can also take an accusative or dative object, with slight differences in meaning. Object of certain compound verbs (particularly those beginning with ἀπο-, ἐκ-, κατα-, προ- etc.) is in genitive. Furthermore, the objects in genitive could often be regarded as the genitive of source, cause, comparison, etc.

smyth.text:
A verb may be followed by the partitive genitive if the action affects the object only in part. If the entire object is affected, the verb in question takes the accusative.
*)adrh/stoio d' e)/ghme qugatrw=n he married one of Adrastus' daughters
*c 121, tw=n pw/lwn lamba/nei he takes some of the colts
X. A. 4.5.35, labo/ntes tou= barbarikou= stratou= taking part of the barbarian force 1. 5. 7, kle/ptontes tou= o)/rous seizing part of the mountain secretly 4. 6. 15 (cp. tou= o)/rous kle/yai ti 4. 6. 11), th=s gh=s e)/temon they ravaged part of the land
T. 2.56 (cp. th\n gh=n pa=san e)/temon 2. 57 and e)/temon th=s gh=s th\n pollh/n 2. 56), katea/_gh th=s kefalh=s he had a hole knocked somewhere in his head
Ar. Vesp. 1428 (

th\n kefalh\n katea_ge/nai to have one's head broken
D. 54.35).

With impersonals a partitive genitive does duty as the subject:

pole/mou ou) meth=n au)th=| she had no share in war
X. C. 7.2.28,

e)moi\ ou)damo/qen prosh/kei tou/tou tou= pra/_gmatos I have no part whatever in this affair
And. 4.34. Cp. 1318.

The genitive is used with verbs of sharing.

pa/ntes metei=xon th=s e(orth=s all took part in the festival
X. A. 5.3.9, metedi/dosan a)llh/lois w(=n (= tou/twn a(\) ei)=xon e(/kastoi they shared with each other what each had 4. 5. 6,

to\ a)nqrw/pinon ge/nos metei/lhfen a)qanasi/a_s the human race has received a portion of immortality
P. L. 721b,

si/_tou koinwnei=n to take a share of food
X. M. 2.6.22,

dikaiosu/nhs ou)de\n u(_mi=n prosh/kei you have no concern in righteous dealing
X. H. 2.4.40,

poli_tei/a_, e)n h(=| pe/nhsin ou) me/testin a)rxh=s a form of government in which the poor have no part in the management of affairs
P. R. 550c. So with metalagxa/nein get a share (along with somebody else), sunai/resqai and koinou=sqai take part in, metaitei=n and metapoiei=sqai demand a share in.

The part received or taken, if expressed, stands in the accusative. oi( tu/rannoi tw=n megi/stwn a)gaqw=n e)la/xista mete/xousi tyrants have the smallest por- tion in the greatest blessings
X. Hi. 2.6,

tou/twn metaitei_ to\ me/ros he demands his share of this
Ar. Vesp. 972.
a. With me/testi the part may be added in the nominative:

me/testi xu)_mi=n tw=n pepra_gme/nwn me/ros ye too have had a share in these doings
E. I. T. 1299.

The genitive is used with verbs signifying to touch, take hold of, make trial of.
（h( no/sos)

h(/yato tw=n a)nqrw/pwn the plague laid hold of the men
T. 2.48, th=s gnw/mhs th=s au)th=s e)/xomai I hold to the same opinion 1. 140,

e)n th=| e)xome/nh| e)mou= kli/_nh| on the couch next to me
P. S. 217d,

a)ntila/besqe tw=n pra_gma/twn take our public policy in hand
D. 1.20, o(/pws peirw=|nto tou= tei/xous to make an attempt on (a part of) the wall
T. 2.81. So with yau/ein touch (rare in prose), a)nte/xesqai cling to, e)pilamba/nesqai and sullamba/nesqai lay hold of.

The genitive of the part, with the accusative of the person (the whole) who has been touched, is chiefly poetical:

to\n de\ peso/nta podw=n e)/labe but him as he fell, he seized by his feet
*d 463,

e)/labon th=s zw/nhs to\n *)oro/nta_n they took hold of Orontas by the girdle
X. A. 1.6.10 (but

mou= labo/menos th=s xeiro/s taking me by the hand
P. Charm. 153b),

a)/gein th=s h(ni/a_s to\n i(/ppon to lead the horse by the bridle
X. Eq. 6.9 (cp.

bou=n d' a)ge/thn kera/wn they led the cow by the horns
g 439).

Verbs of beseeching take the genitive by analogy to verbs of touching: e)me\ lisse/sketo gou/nwn she besought me by (clasping) my knees I 451 (cp. genei/ou a(ya/menos li/ssesqai beseech by touching his chin K 454).

The genitive is used with verbs of beginning.
a. Partitive:

e)/fh *ku=ron a)/rxein tou= lo/gou w(=de he said that Cyrus began the discussion as follows
X. A. 1.6.5, tou= lo/gou h)/rxeto w(=de he began his speech as follows 3. 2. 7. On a)/rxein as distinguished from a)/rxesqai see 1734. 5.
b. Ablatival (1391) denoting the point of departure: se/o d' a)/rcomai I will make a beginning with thee I 97. In this sense a)po/ or e)c is usually added: a)rca/menoi a)po\ sou=
D. 18.297,

a)/rcomai a)po\ th=s i)_a_trikh=s le/gwn I will make a beginning by speaking of medicine
P. S. 186b.

With verbs signifying to cease, release, remove, restrain, give up, fail, be distant from, etc., the genitive denotes separation.

lh/gein tw=n po/nwn to cease from toil
I. 1.14,

e)pisth/mh xwrizome/nh dikaiosu/nhs knowledge divorced from justice
P. Menex. 246e,

metasta\_s th=s *)aqhnai/wn cummaxi/a_s withdrawing from the alliance with the Athenians
T. 2.67,

pau/santes au)to\n th=s strathgi/a_s removing him from his office of general
X. H. 6.2.13,

ei)/rgesqai th=s a)gora=s to be excluded from the forum
L. 6.24,

sw=sai kakou= to save from evil
S. Ph. 919,

e)kw/lu_on th=s porei/a_s au)to/n they prevented him from passing
X. Ages. 2.2,

pa=s a)sko\s du/o a)/ndras e(/cei tou= mh\ katadu=nai each skin will keep two men from sinking
X. A. 3.5.11,

lo/gou teleuta=n to end a speech
T. 3.59,

th=s e)leuqeri/a_s paraxwrh=sai *fili/ppw| to surrender their freedom to Philip
D. 18.68, ou) po/nwn u(fi/_eto, ou) kindu/_nwn a)fi/_stato, ou) xrhma/twn e)fei/deto he did not relax his toil, stand aloof from dangers, or spare his money
X. Ages. 7.1,

yeusqe/ntes tw=n e)lpi/dwn disappointed of their expectations
I. 4.58 (but cp. 1352),

h( nh=sos ou) polu\ die/xousa th=s h)pei/rou the island being not far distant from the mainland
T. 3.51.
Several verbs of separation, such as e)leuqerou=n (especially with a personal subject), may take a)po/ or e)c when the local idea is prominent. Many take also the accusative.

The genitive, instead of the accusative (1628), may be used with verbs of depriving:

a)posterei= me tw=n xrhma/twn he deprives me of my property
I. 17.35,

tw=n a)/llwn a)fairou/menoi xrh/mata taking away property from others
X. M. 1.5.3.

The genitive of the place whence is employed in poetry where a compound verb would be used in prose:

ba/qrwn i(/stasqe rise from the steps
S. O. T. 142 (cp.

u(pani/stantai qa/_kwn they rise from their seats
X. S. 4. 31),

xqono\s a)ei/ra_s raising from the ground
S. Ant. 417.

The genitive with verbs signifying to want, lack, empty, etc. may be classed with the genitive of separation.

tw=n e)pithdei/wn ou)k a)porh/somen we shall not want provisions
X. A. 2.2.11,

e)pai/nou ou)/pote spani/zete you never lack praise
X. Hi. 1.14,

a)ndrw=n ta/_nde po/lin kenw=sai to empty this city of its men
A. Supp. 660. So with e)llei/pein and ste/resqai lack, e)rhmou=n deliver from.

de/w I lack (the personal construction) usually takes the genitive of quantity:

pollou= ge de/w nothing of the sort
P. Phae. 228a,

mi_krou= e)/deon e)n xersi\ tw=n o(pli_tw=n ei)=nai they were nearly at close quarters with the hoplites
X. H. 4.6.11,

tosou/tou de/w zhlou=n I am so far from admiring
D. 8.70 (also tosou=ton de/w).

de/omai I want, request may take the genitive, or the accusative (regularly of neuter pronouns and adjectives), of the thing wanted; and the genitive of the person: e)rwtw/menos o(/tou de/oito, *)askw=n, e)/fh, disxi_li/wn deh/somai being asked what he needed, he said ‘I shall have need of two thousand skins’
X. A. 3.5.9,

tou=to u(_mw=n de/omai I ask this of you
P. A. 17c. The genitive of the thing and of the person is unusual:

deo/menoi *ku/_rou a)/llhs a)/llhs pra/_cews petitioning Cyrus about different matters
X. C. 8.3.19.

dei= (impersonal) is frequently used with genitives of quantity:

pollou= dei= ou(/tws e)/xein far from that being the case
P. A. 35d, ou)de\ pollou= dei=
D. 8.42 (only in D.) and ou)d' o)li/gou dei= no, far from it
D. 19.184. dei=n may be omitted (but not with pollou=), leaving o)li/gou and mi_krou= in the sense of almost, all but; <*>li/gou pa/ntes almost all
P. R. 552d,

o)li/gou ei(=lon th\n po/lin they all but. took the city
T. 8.35. On dei=n used absolutely, see 2012 d; on de/wn with numerals, 350 c.

title: Source and Separation
definition: The genitive may indicate the place or point from which something is separated, particularly with words denoting motion or separation. Here may be classed the genitive of origin, indicating origin, source or offspring.

smyth.text:
The genitive may denote the source.

pi/qwn h)fu/sseto oi)=nos wine was broached from the casks
y 305,

*da_rei/ou kai\ *parusa/tidos gi/gnontai pai=des du/o of Darius and Parysatis are born two sons
X. A. 1.1.1, tau=ta de/ sou tuxo/ntes obtaining this of you 6. 6. 32,

ma/qe mou kai\ ta/de learn this also from me
X. C. 1.6.44.

With verbs of hearing from and the like the genitive is probably ablatival rather than partitive (1364):

e)mou= a)kou/sesqe pa=san th\n a)lh/qeian from me you shall hear the whole truth
P. A. 17b,

tou/twn punqa/nomai o(/ti ou)k a)/bato/n e)sti to\ o)/ros I learn from these men that the mountain is not impassable
X. A. 4.6.17, toiau=ta/

tou paro/ntos e)/kluon such a tale I heard from some one who was present
S. El. 424,

ei)de/nai de/ sou xrh/|zw I desire to know of thee
S. El. 668.
a. Usually (except with punqa/nesqai) we have para/ (a)po/ rarely), e)c or pro/s (in poetry and Hdt.) with verbs of hearing from.
b. The genitive with ei)=nai in

patro\s d' ei)/m' a)gaqoi=o I am of a good father
*f 109,

toiou/twn me/n e)ste progo/nwn of such ancestors are you
X. A. 3.2.13 is often regarded as a genitive of source, but is probably possessive.

## GENITIVE WITH ADJECTIVES

With verbs signifying to cease, release, remove, restrain, give up, fail, be distant from, etc., the genitive denotes separation.

lh/gein tw=n po/nwn to cease from toil
I. 1.14,

e)pisth/mh xwrizome/nh dikaiosu/nhs knowledge divorced from justice
P. Menex. 246e,

metasta\_s th=s *)aqhnai/wn cummaxi/a_s withdrawing from the alliance with the Athenians
T. 2.67,

pau/santes au)to\n th=s strathgi/a_s removing him from his office of general
X. H. 6.2.13,

ei)/rgesqai th=s a)gora=s to be excluded from the forum
L. 6.24,

sw=sai kakou= to save from evil
S. Ph. 919,

e)kw/lu_on th=s porei/a_s au)to/n they prevented him from passing
X. Ages. 2.2,

pa=s a)sko\s du/o a)/ndras e(/cei tou= mh\ katadu=nai each skin will keep two men from sinking
X. A. 3.5.11,

lo/gou teleuta=n to end a speech
T. 3.59,

th=s e)leuqeri/a_s paraxwrh=sai *fili/ppw| to surrender their freedom to Philip
D. 18.68, ou) po/nwn u(fi/_eto, ou) kindu/_nwn a)fi/_stato, ou) xrhma/twn e)fei/deto he did not relax his toil, stand aloof from dangers, or spare his money
X. Ages. 7.1,

yeusqe/ntes tw=n e)lpi/dwn disappointed of their expectations
I. 4.58 (but cp. 1352),

h( nh=sos ou) polu\ die/xousa th=s h)pei/rou the island being not far distant from the mainland
T. 3.51.

Here may be classed the genitive of origin:

oi( *so/lwnos no/moi the laws of Solon
D. 20.103, h( e)pistolh\ tou= *fili/ppou the letter of Philip 18. 37, ku/_mata pantoi/wn a)ne/mwn waves caused by all kinds of winds B 396.

title: Time
definition:
The genitive denotes the time *within which*, or at a certain point *of which*, an action takes place. As contrasted with the accusative of time, the genitive signals a time frame for an action.
The genitive may denote the time *since* an action has happened or the time *until* an action will happen:

smyth.text:
Time.—The genitive denotes the time within which, or at a certain point of which, an action takes place. As contrasted with the accusative of time (1582), the genitive denotes a portion of time. Hence the genitive of time is partitive. Cp. to\n me\n xeimw=na u(/_ei o( qeo/s, tou= de\ qe/reos xrhi/skontai tw=| u(/dati during the (entire) winter the goo<*>rains, but in (a part of) summer they need the water
Hdt. 3.117.
h(me/ra_s by day, nukto/s at or by night, meshmbri/a_s at midday, dei/lhs in the afternoon, e(spe/ra_s in the evening, qe/rous in summer, xeimw=nos in winter, h)=ros in spring, o)pw/ra_s in autumn, tou= loipou= in the future. The addition of article or attributive usually defines the time more exactly. Thus, ou)kou=n h(du\ me\n qe/rous yu_xeinh\n e)/xein, h(du\ de\ xeimw=nos a)leeinh/n; is it not pleasant to have (a house) cool in summer, and warm in winter?
X. M. 3.8.9,

w)/|xeto th=s nukto/s he departed during the night
X. A. 7.2.17, kai\ h(me/ra_s kai\ nukto\s a)/gwn e)pi\ tou\s polemi/ous both by day and by night leading against the enemy 2. 6. 7, e)/legon tou= loipou= mhke/ti e)cei=nai a)nomi/a_s a)/rcai they said that for the future (at any time in the future) it should no longer be permitted to set an example of lawlessness 5. 7. 34. (Distinguish to\ loipo/n for the (entire) future 3. 2. 8.) e)nto/s within is sometimes added to the genitive.

The addition of the article may have a distributive sense:

draxmh\n e)la/mbane th=s h(me/ra_s he received a drachm a day
T. 3.17.

The genitive may denote the time since an action has happened or the time until an action will happen:

ou)dei/s me/ pw h)rw/thke kaino\n ou)de\n pollw=n e)tw=n for many years nobody has put a new question to me
P. G. 448a,

basileu\s ou) maxei=tai de/ka h(merw=n the king will not fight for ten days
X. A. 1.7.18.

The genitive may or may not denote a definite part of the time during which anything takes place; the dative fixes the time explicitly either by specifying a definite point in a given period or by contracting the whole period to a definite point; the accusative expresses the whole extent of time from beginning to end: cp.

th=| de\ u(sterai/a| oi( me\n *)aqhnai=oi to/ te proa/steion ei(=lon kai\ th\n h(me/ra_n a(/pa_san e)dh/|oun th\n gh=n, oi(/ te tria_ko/sioi tw=n *skiwnai/wn th=s e)piou/shs nukto\s a)pexw/rhsan on the next day the Athenians captured the suburb and laid waste the land for that entire day, while the three hundred Scionaeans departed in the course of the following night
T. 4.130; h(me/ra| de\ a)rca/menoi tri/th| w(s oi)/koqen w(/rmhsan, tau/thn te ei)rga/zonto kai\ th\n teta/rthn kai\ th=s pe/mpths me/xri a)_ri/stou beginning on the third day after their departure, they continued their work (all) this day and the fourth, and on the fifth until the mid-day meal 4. 90.
a. The genitive of time is less common than the dative of time (1539) with ordinals, or with o(/de, ou(=tos, e)kei=nos; as tau/ths th=s nukto/s
T. 6.97,
P. Cr. 44a,

e)kei/nou tou= mhno/s in the course of that month
X. M. 4.8.2. For qe/rous we find e)n qe/rei rarely and, in poetry, qe/rei.
T. 4.133 has both tou= au)tou= qe/rous and e)n tw=| au)tw=| qe/rei in the course of the same summer; cp. i)=sos r(e/ei e)/n te qe/rei+ kai\ xeimw=ni o( *)/istros
Hdt. 4.50 and *)/istros i)=sos r(e/ei qe/reos kai\ xeimw=nos 4. 48 (the Ister flows with the same volume in summer and winter).

examples.translation: during the (entire) *winter the god rains*, *but in* (a part of) summer they need the water

examples.translation: for many years nobody has put a new question to me

title: Comparison
definition:
The genitive of comparison complements comparatives and superlatives as a standard of comparison.
It is also used with a superlative adverb:

smyth.text:
(III) With comparatives and superlatives.

h(mw=n o( gerai/teros the elder of us
X. C. 5.1.6 (1066 b),

oi( presbu/tatoi tw=n strathgw=n the oldest of the generals
X. A. 3.3.11,

si/_tw| pa/ntwn a)nqrw/pwn plei/stw| xrw/meq' e)peisa/ktw| we make use of imported grain more than all other people
D. 18.87. So with a superlative adverb:

h( nau=s a)/rista/ moi e)/plei panto\s tou= stratope/dou my ship was the best sailer of the whole squadron
L. 21.6.

In poetry this use is extended to positive adjectives: a)ridei/ketos a)ndrw=n conspicuous among men A 248,

w)= fi/la_ gunaikw=n oh dear among women
E. Alc. 460. In tragedy an adjective may be emphasized by the addition of the same adjective in the genitive:

a)/rrht' a)rrh/twn horrors unspeakable
S. O. T. 465. Cp. 1064.

examples.translation: the elder of us
the oldest of the generals

examples.greek: σίτῳ πάντων ἀνθρώπων πλείστῳ χρώμεθ᾽ ἐπεισάκτῳ
examples.translation: we make use of imported grain more than all other people

examples.greek: ἡ ναῦς ἄριστά μοι ἔπλει παντὸς τοῦ στρατοπέδου
examples.translation: my ship was the best sailer of the whole squadron

title: Place
definition: The genitive denotes the place *within which* or *at which* an action happens. This is more frequent in poetry than in prose.

smyth.text:
Place.—The genitive denotes the place within which or at which an action happens. This is more frequent in poetry than in prose.
pedi/oio diwke/men to chase over the plain E 222, i(=zen toi/xou tou= e(te/roio he was sitting by the other wall (lit. in a place of the wall) I 219, leloume/nos *)wkeanoi=o having bathed in Oceanus E 6,

ou)/te *pu/lou i(erh=s ou)/t' *)/argeos ou)/te *mukh/nhs neither in sacred Pylos nor in Argos nor in Mycenae
f 108,

to/nd' ei)sede/cw teixe/wn thou didst admit this man within the walls
E. Phoen. 451,

i)e/nai tou= pro/sw to go forward
X. A. 1.3.1,

e)peta/xu_non th=s o(dou= tou\s sxolai/teron prosio/ntas they hastened on their way those who came up more slowly
T. 4.47;

laia=s xeiro\s oi)kou=si they dwell on the left hand
A. Pr. 714 (possibly ablatival).

examples.greek: **πεδίοιο** διωκέμεν **Hom. Il. 5.202**; ⇾ to chase over the plain
examples.translation: to chase over the plain

examples.greek: λελουμένος **Ὠκεανοῖο** **Hom. Il. 5.6**; ⇾ having bathed in Oceanus
examples.translation: having bathed in Oceanus

examples.greek: οὔτε Πύλου ἱερῆς οὔτ᾽ Ἄργεος οὔτε Μυκήνης
examples.translation: neither in sacred Pylos nor in Argos nor in Mycenae
thou didst admit this man within the walls
they dwell on the left hand (possibly ablatival).

title: In Genitive Absolute
definition: A circumstantial participle agreeing with a genitive noun or pronoun which is not in the main construction of the sentence stands in the genitive absolute. The noun or pronoun accompanying the participle expresses the subject:

smyth.text:
Genitive Absolute.—A circumstantial participle agreeing with a genitive noun or pronoun which is not in the main construction of the sentence, stands in the genitive absolute. Like other circumstantial participles, the genitive absolute expresses time, cause, condition, concession, or simply any attendant circumstance.
a. Time:

tau=t' e)pra/_xqh *ko/nwnos strathgou=ntos these things were effected while Conon was in command
I. 9.56,

tou/twn lexqe/ntwn a)ne/sthsan this said, they rose
X. A. 3.3.1,

*)hi+o/na . . . *mh/dwn e)xo/ntwn poliorki/a| ei(=lon they blockaded and captured Eïon which was held by the Medes
T. 1.98.
b. Cause:

tw=n swma/twn qhlu_nome/nwn kai\ ai( yu_xai\ a)rrwsto/terai gi/gnontai by the enfeebling of the body, the spirit too is made weaker
X. O. 4.2.
c. Opposition or Concession: kai\ metapempome/nou au)tou= ou)k e)qe/lw e)lqei=n even though he is sending for me, I am unwilling to go
X. A. 1.3.10. kai/per is usually added (2083).
d. Condition: oi)/omai kai\ nu=n e)/ti e)panorqwqh=nai a)\n ta\ pra/_gmata tou/twn gignome/- nwn if these measures should be taken, I am of the opinion that even now our situation might be rectified
D. 9.76.
e. Attendant Circumstance: *ku=ros a)ne/bh e)pi\ ta\ o)/rh ou)deno\s kwlu/_ontos Cyrus ascended the mountains without opposition (lit. no one hindering)
X. A. 1.2.22 (or since no one opposed him).

e(kw/n willing, a)/_kwn unwilling are properly participles and are treated as such (cp. 2117 c). Thus,

e)mou= ou)x e(ko/ntos without my consent
S. Aj. 455.
a. a)/_kwn, a)ekaco/menos, a)frone/wn, a)elpte/wn, a)na/rmenos, a)nomologou/menos, a)ti/cwn are the only cases in Greek showing the earlier method of negativing the participle with alpha privative. Elsewhere ou) or mh/ is used.

The genitive of the participle may stand without its noun or pronoun
a. When the noun or pronoun may easily be supplied from the context. Thus, oi( de\ pole/mioi, prosio/ntwn (tw=n *(ellh/nwn, previously mentioned),

te/ws me\n h(suxi/azon the enemy, as they were approaching, for a while remained quiet
X. A. 5.4.16, e)rw/ta_, e)/fh, w)= *ku=re, . . . w(s (e)mou=) ta)_lhqh= e)rou=ntos put your question (said he), Cyrus, on the supposition that I will speak the truth
X. C. 3.1.9.
b. When the noun or pronoun may easily be supplied otherwise; here, e.g., a)nqrw/pwn or pra_gma/twn is said to be supplied grammatically. Thus, i)o/ntwn ei)s ma/xhn when (men) are going into battle
X. C. 3.3.54, tou=ton to\n tro/pon pra_xqe/ntwn th=s po/lews gi/gnetai ta\ xrh/mata when (things) have happened in this way, the property belongs to the State
D. 24.12; and in u(/_ontos (*dio/s, 934 a)

pollw=| when it was raining hard
X. H. 1.1.16. Quasi-impersonal verbs (933) thus take the genitive rather than the accusative absolute:

ou(/tws e)/xontos in this state of things
P. R. 381c, influenced by ou(/tws e)xo/ntwn
X. A. 3.1.40.
c. When a subordinate clause with o(/ti follows upon the participle in the passive. Thus,

e)saggelqe/ntwn o(/ti *foi/nissai nh=es e)p' au)tou\s ple/ousin it having been announced that Phoenician ships were sailing against them
T. 1.116, dhlwqe/ntos o(/ti e)n tai=s nausi\ tw=n *(ellh/nwn ta\ pra/_gmata e)ge/neto it having been shown that the salvation of the Greeks depended on their navy 1. 74. The plural is used when the subject of the subordinate clause is plural, or when several circumstances are mentioned.

Exceptionally, the subject of the genitive absolute is the same as that of the main clause. The effect of this irregular construction is to emphasize the idea contained in the genitive absolute. Thus,

bohqhsa/ntwn u(_mw=n proqu/_mws po/lin proslh/yesqe nautiko\n e)/xousan me/ga if you assist us heartily, you will gain to your cause a State having a large navy
T. 3.13. The genitive absolute usually precedes the main verb.
a. The genitive absolute may be used where the grammatical construction demands the dative. Thus,

diabebhko/tos *perikle/ous . . . h)gge/lqh au)tw=| o(/ti *me/gara a)fe/sthke when Pericles had already crossed over, news was brought to him that Megara had revolted
T. 1.114 (in Latin: Pericli iam transgresso nuntiatum est).
b. The subject of the genitive absolute may be identical with the object of the leading verb:

h(=lqon e)pi\ th\n *)epi/dauron w(s e)rh/mou ou)/shs . . . ai(rh/sontes they came against Epidaurus expecting to capture it undefended
T. 5.56.

Observe that the genitive absolute differs from the Latin ablative abso lute herein: 1. The subject need not be expressed (2072). 2. The subject may appear in the leading clause (2073 a). 3. With a substantive the participle w)/n is always added in prose, whereas Latin has to omit the participle. Thus,

pai/dwn o)/ntwn h(mw=n nobis pueris
P. S. 173a. On e)mou= a)/_kontos me invito, see 2071. 4. Because it has a present participle passive and an aorist and perfect participle active, Greek can use the genitive absolute where Latin, through lack of a past participle active, has to use a clause with dum, cum, etc. Thus,

o(/lhs th=s po/lews e)n toi=s polemikoi=s kindu/_nois e)pitrepome/nhs tw=| strathgw=| cum bellicis in periculis universa respublica imperatori committatur
X. M. 3.1.3, tou= paido\s gela/santos cum puer risisset. Latin uses the absolute case more frequently than Greek because it employs the perfect participle passive where Greek uses the aorist participle active. Thus, *ku=ros sugkale/sa_s tou\s strathgou\s ei)=pen Cyrus, convocatis ducibus, dixit
X. A. 1.4.8.

The genitive absolute took its rise from such cases as *sarph/donti d' a)/xos ge/neto *glau/kou a)pio/ntos but sorrow came on Sarpedon for Glaucus—departing M 392. The genitive, here properly dependent on a)/xos ge/neto, ceased to be felt as dependent on the governing expression, and was extended, as a distinct construction, to cases in which the governing expression did not take the genitive. Cp. the development of the accusative with the infinitive (1981).

title: Reference
definition: The genitive of reference is used with verbs of saying or thinking to state the subject and expresses a more or less close connection or relation to a subject.

smyth.text:
The genitive may express a more or less close connection or relation, where peri/ is sometimes added.
With verbs of saying or thinking: ti/ de\ i(/ppwn oi)/ei; but what do you think of horses?
P. R. 459b. Often in poetry:

ei)pe\ de/ moi patro/s but tell me about my father
l 174, tou= kasignh/tou ti/ fh/|s; what dost thou say of thy brother?
S. El. 317.

The genitive is often used loosely, especially at the beginning of a construction, to state the subject of a remark: i(/ppos h)\n kakourgh=|, to\n i(ppe/a_ kaki/zomen: th=s de\ gunaiko/s, ei) kakopoiei= ktl. if a horse is vicious, we lay the fault to the groom; but as regards a wife, if she conducts herself ill, etc.
X. O. 3.11,

w(sau/tws de\ kai\ tw=n a)/llwn texnw=n and so in the case of the other arts too
P. Charm. 165d, ti/ de\ tw=n pollw=n kalw=n; what about the many beautiful things?
P. Ph. 78d.

title: Cause
definition: With verbs of emotion and dispute, the genitive denotes the cause. Such verbs are *to wonder at, admire*, *envy*, *praise*, *blame, hate*, *pity*, *grieve for*, *be angry at, take vengeance on*, and the like. The genitive of cause is closely connected with the genitive with verbs of disputing and verbs of judicial action.

smyth.text:
With verbs of judicial action the genitive denotes the crime, the accusative denotes the person accused.

ai)tia=sqai a)llh/lous tou= gegenhme/nou to accuse one another of what had happened
X. Ages. 1.33,

diw/kw me\n kakhgori/a_s, th=| d' au)th=| yh/fw| fo/nou feu/gw I bring an accusation for defamation and at the same trial am prosecuted for murder
L. 11.12,

e)me\ o( *me/lhtos a)sebei/a_s e)gra/yato Meletus prosecuted me for impiety
P. Euth. 5c,

dw/rwn e)kri/qhsan they were tried for bribery
L. 27.3. On verbs of accusing and condemning compounded with kata/, see 1385.

With verbs of emotion the genitive denotes the cause. Such verbs are to wonder at, admire, envy, praise, blame. hate, pity, grieve for, be angry at, take vengeance on, and the like.

e)qau/masa th=s to/lmhs tw=n lego/ntwn I wondered at the hardihood of the speakers
L. 12.41,

tou=ton a)gasqei\s th=s pra|o/thtos admiring him for his mildness
X. C. 2.3.21, zhlw= se tou= nou=, th=s de\ deili/a_s stugw= I envy thee for thy prudence, I hate thee for thy cowardice
S. El. 1027, se\ hu)daimo/nisa tou= tro/pou I thought you happy because of your disposition
P. Cr. 43b,

sugxai/rw tw=n gegenhme/nwn I share the joy at what has happened
D. 15.15,

a)ne/xesqai tw=n oi)kei/wn a)meloume/nwn to put up with the neglect of my household affairs
P. A. 31b,

to\n ce/non di/kaion ai)ne/sai proqu_mi/a_s it is right to praise the stranger for his zeal
E. I. A. 1371,

ou)/pot' a)ndri\ tw=|de khru_keuma/twn me/myh| never wilt thou blame me for my tidings
A. Sept. 651,

tou= pa/qous w)/|kti_ren au)to/n he pitied him for his misery
X. C. 5.4.32,

ou)d' ei)ko\s xalepw=s fe/rein au)tw/n nor is it reasonable to grieve about them
T. 2.62, ou)ke/ti w(=n ou(=toi kle/ptousin o)rgi/zesqe, a)ll' w(=n au)toi\ lamba/nete xa/rin i)/ste you are no longer angry at their thefts, but you are grateful for what you get yourselves
L. 27.11,

ti_mwrh/sasqai au)tou\s th=s e)piqe/sews to take revenge on them for their attack
X. A. 7.4.23. Here belongs, by analogy,

suggignw/skein au)toi=s xrh\ th=s e)piqu_mi/a_s it is necessary to forgive them for their desire
P. Eu. 306c (usually suggignw/skein th\n e)piqu_mi/a_n tini/ or th=| e)piqu_mi/a| tino/s).
a. The genitive of cause is partly a true genitive, partly ablatival.

title: Complement of the verb
definition:
Dative expresses the indirect object of a verb, while the direct object is usually in accusative. The dative may be used as the object of many verbs, such as to benefit, help, injure, please, displease, be friendly or hostile, blame, be angry, threaten, envy, trust, believe, meet, obey, etc.
Object of certain compound verbs (in particular with σύν, ἐν, ἐπί, and with some compounded with παρά, περί, πρός, and ὑπό, etc.) is in dative, because the preposition keeps a sense that requires the dative. The objects in dative often could also be regarded as the dative of advantage, accompaniment, etc.

smyth.text: The dative may be used as the sole complement of many verbs that are usually transitive in English. Such are

(I) To benefit, help, injure, please, displease, be friendly or hostile, blame, be angry, threaten, envy.

bohqei=n toi=sin h)dikhme/nois to help the wronged
E. I. A. 79,

ou)k a)\n h)nw/xlei nu=n h(mi=n he would not now be troubling us
D. 3.5, <*>nti\ tou= sunergei=n e(autoi=s ta\ sumfe/ronta e)phrea/zousin a)llh/lois instead of coöperating for their mutual interests, they revile one another
X. M. 3.5.16,

ei) toi=s ple/otin a)re/skonte/s e)smen, toi=sd' a)\n mo/nois ou)k o)rqw=s a)pare/skoimen if we are pleasing to the majority, it would not be right if we should displease them alone
T. 1.38,

eu)noei=n toi=s kako/nois to be friendly to the ill-intentioned
X. C. 8.2.1,

e)moi\ o)rgi/zontai they are angry at me
P. A. 23c,

tw=| *qhra_me/nei h)pei/loun they threatened Theramenes
T. 8.92,

ou) fqonw=n toi=s ploutou=sin not cherishing envy against the rich
X. A. 1.9.19.
Some verbs of benefiting and injuring take the accusative (w)felei=n, bla/ptein, 1591 a); mi_sei=n tina hate some one. lu_sitelei=n, sumfe/rein be of advantage take the dative.

(II) To meet, approach, yield.

e)pei\ de\ a)ph/nthsan au)toi=s oi( strathgoi/ but when the generals met them
X. A. 2.3.17,

peritugxa/nei *filokra/tei he meets Philocrates
X. H. 4.8.24,

poi/ois ou) xrh\ qhri/ois pela/zein what wild beasts one must not approach
X. C. 1.4.7, su\ d' ei)=k' a)na/gkh| kai\ qeoi=si mh\ ma/xou yield to necessity and war not with heaven E. fr. 716. On the genitive with verbs of approaching, see 1353.

(III) To obey, serve, pardon, trust, advise, command, etc.

toi=s no/mois pei/qou obey the laws
I. 1.16,

tw=| u(_mete/rw| cumfo/rw| u(pakou/ein to be subservient to your interests
T. 5.98,

a)\_n mhdemia=| douleu/h|s tw=n h(donw=n if you are the slave of no pleasure
I. 2.29,

e)pi/steuon au)tw=| ai( po/leis the cities trusted him
X. A. 1.9.8, strathgw=| stratiw/tais parainou=nti a general advising his men P. Ion 540 d,

tw=| *mu_sw=| e)sh/mhne feu/gein he ordered the Mysian to flee
X. A. 5.2.30,

tw=| *klea/rxw| e)bo/a_ a)/gein he shouted to Clearchus to lead
X. A. 1.8.12.

keleu/ein command (strictly impel) may be followed in Attic by the accusative and (usually) the infinitive; in Hom. by the dative either alone or with the infinitive. Many verbs of commanding (paragge/llein, diakeleu/esqai) take in Attic the accusative, not the dative, when used with the infinitive (1996 N.). u(pakou/ein (and a)kou/ein = obey) may take the genitive (1366).

(IV) To be like or unlike, compare, befit.

e)oike/nai toi=s toiou/tois to be like such men
P. R. 349d, ti/ ou)=n pre/pei a)ndri\ pe/nhti; what then befits a poor man?
P. A. 36d.

The dative of the person and the genitive of the thing are used with the impersonals dei= (1400), me/testi, me/lei, metame/lei, prosh/kei. Thus,

misqofo/rwn a)ndri\ tura/nnw| dei= a tyrant needs mercenaries
X. Hi. 8.10,

w(s ou) meto\n au)toi=s *)epida/mnou inasmuch as they had nothing to do with Epidamnus
T. 1.28,

ou)x w(=n e)bia/_sato mete/melen au)tw=| he did not repent of his acts of violence
And. 4.17,

tou/tw| th=s *boiwti/a_s prosh/kei ou)de/n he has nothing to do with Boeotia
X. A. 3.1.31. e)/cesti/ moi it is in my power does not take the genitive. For the accusative instead of the dative, see 1400. Cp. 1344.
a. For dokei= moi it seems to me (mihi videtur), dokw= moi (mihi videor) may be used. b. For other cases of the dative as direct complement see 1476, 1481.
Many compound verbs take the dative because of their meaning as a whole. So a)nte/xein hold out against, a)mfisbhtei=n dispute with (1523 b).

The dative is used with verbs compounded with su/n (regularly), with many compounded with e)n, e)pi/, and with some compounded with para/, peri/, pro/s, and u(po/, because the preposition keeps a sense that requires the dative.

e)mble/ya_s au)tw=| looking at him
P. Charm. 162d,

e)lpi/das e)mpoiei=n a)nqrw/pois to create expectations in men
X. C. 1.6.19,

au)toi=s e)pe/pese to\ *(ellhniko/n the Greek force fell upon them
X. A. 4.1.10, e)pe/keinto au)toi=s they pressed hard upon them 5. 2. 5, sunadikei=n au)toi=s to be their accomplice in wrong-doing 2. 6. 27, cuni/sa_si *melh/tw| yeudome/nw| they are conscious that Meletus is speaking falsely (i.e. they know it as well as he does)
P. A. 34b,

ou(=toi ou) parege/nonto basilei= these did not join the king
X. A. 5.6.8, pare/stw u(_mi=n o( kh=ruc let the herald come with us 3. 1. 46, *cenofw=nti prose/trexon du/o nea_ni/skw two youths ran up to Xenophon 4. 3. 10,

u(pokei=sqai tw=| a)/rxonti to be subject to the ruler
P. G. 510c.
a. So especially with verbs of motion and rest formed from i)e/nai, pi/_ptein, tiqe/nai, tre/xein, ei)=nai, gi/gnesqai, kei=sqai, etc.
Some verbs of motion compounded with para/, peri/, u(po/ take the accusative (1559).
Some verbs have an alternative construction, e.g. periba/llein: tini/ ti <*>nvest a person with something, ti/ tini surround something with something.
Compounds of su/n take the instrumental, compounds of e)n take the locative dative.

When the idea of place is emphatic, the preposition may be repeated:

e)mmei/nantes e)n th=| *)attikh=| remaining in Attica
T. 2.23; but it is generally not repeated when the idea is figurative:

toi=s o(/rkois e)mme/nwn abiding by one's oath
I. 1.13. meta/ may be used after compounds of su/n:

met' e)mou= sune/plei he sailed in company with me
L. 21.8.

The prepositions are more frequently repeated in prose than in poetry.

## ACCUSATIVE

title: Possessor
definition: Dative denotes possession, belonging, or interest with verbs such as γίγνομαι and εἰμί. The person for whom a thing exists is put in the dative.

smyth.text:
Dative of the Possessor.—The person for whom a thing exists is put in the dative with ei)=nai, gi/gnesqai, u(pa/rxein, fu=nai (poet.), etc., when he is regarded as interested in its possession.

a)/llois me\n xrh/mata/ e)sti, h(mi=n de\ cu/mmaxoi a)gaqoi/ others have riches, we have good allies
T. 1.86,

tw=| dikai/w| para\ qew=n dw=ra gi/gnetai gifts are bestowed upon the just man by the gods
P. R. 613e,

u(pa/rxei h(mi=n ou)de\n tw=n e)pithdei/wn we have no supply of provisions
X. A. 2.2.11,

pa=si qna_toi=s e)/fu_ mo/ros death is the natural lot of all men
S. El. 860.

So with verbs of thinking and perceiving: to\n a)gaqo\n a)/rxonta ble/ponta no/mon a)nqrw/pois e)no/misen Cyrus considered that a good ruler was a living law to man
X. C. 8.1.22,

qarrou=si ma/lista pole/mioi, o(/tan toi=s e)nanti/ois pra/_gmata punqa/nwntai the enemy are most courageous when they learn that the forces opposed to them are in trouble
X. Hipp. 5.8.

In the phrase o)/noma/ (e)sti/) tini the name is put in the same case as o)/noma. Thus,

e)/doca a)kou=sai o)/noma au)tw=| ei)=nai *)aga/qwna I thought I heard his name was Agathon
P. Pr. 315e. o)/noma/ moi/ e)sti and o)/noma (e)pwnumi/a_n) e)/xw are treated as the passives of o)noma/zw. Cp. 1322 a.

Here belong the phrases (1) ti/ (e)stin) e)moi\ kai\ soi/; what have I to do with thee?; cp. ti/ tw=| no/mw| kai\ th=| basa/nw|; what have the law and torture in common?
D. 29.36. (2) ti/ tau=t' e)moi/; what have I to do with this?
D. 54.17. (3) ti/ e)moi\ ple/on; what gain have I?
X. C. 5.5.34.

The dative of the possessor denotes that something is at the disposal of a person or has fallen to his share temporarily. The genitive of possession lays stress on the person who owns something. The dative answers the question what is it that he has?, the genitive answers the question who is it that has something? The uses of the two cases are often parallel, but not interchangeable. Thus, in *ku=ros, ou(= su\ e)/sei to\ a)po\ tou=de Cyrus, to whom you will henceforth belong
X. C. 5.1.6, w(=| would be inappropriate. With a noun in the genitive the dative of the possessor is used (tw=n e(kate/rois cumma/xwn
T. 2.1); with a noun in the dative, the genitive of the possessor (toi=s e(autw=n cumma/xois 1. 18).

title: Advantage (or Disadvantage)
definition: The person or thing for (or against) whom an action is done, is put in dative. With verbs which have no sense of advantage or disadvantage, the dative of advantage (or disadvantage) refers to the beneficiary or malefactive.

smyth.text:
Dative of Advantage or Disadvantage (dativus commodi et incommodi).—The person or thing for whose advantage or disadvantage, anything is or is done, is put in the dative. The dative often has to be translated as if the possessive genitive were used; but the meaning is different.
e)peidh\ au)toi=s oi( ba/rbaroi e)k th=s xw/ra_s a)ph=lqon after the barbarians had departed (for them, to their advantage) from their country
T. 1.89,

a)/llo stra/teuma au)tw=| sunele/geto another army was being raised for him
X. A. 1.1.9,

a)/llw| o( toiou=tos ploutei=, kai\ ou)x e(autw=| such a man is rich for another, and not for himself
P. Menex. 246e,

stefanou=sqai tw=| qew=| to be crowned in honour of the god
X. H. 4.3.21,

*filisti/dhs e)/pra_tte *fili/ppw| Philistides was working in the interest of Philip
D. 9.59, ta\ xrh/mat' ai)/ti' a)nqrwpoi=s kakw=n money is a cause of misery to mankind E. Fr. 632, oi( *qra=|kes oi( tw=| *dhmosqe/nei u(sterh/santes the Thracians who came too late (for, i.e.) to help Demosthenes
T. 7.29, h(/de h( h(me/ra_ toi=s *(/ellhsi mega/lwn kakw=n a)/rcei this day will be to the Greeks the beginning of great sorrows 2. 12,

a)/_n ti/s soi tw=n oi)ketw=n a)podra=| if any of your slaves runs away
X. M. 2.10.1.
a. For the middle denoting to do something for oneself, see 1719.
b. In the last example in 1481, as elsewhere, the dative of a personal pronoun is used where a possessive pronoun would explicitly denote the owner.

A dative, dependent on the sentence, may appear to depend on a substantive:

soi\ de\ dw/sw a)/ndra th=| qugatri/ to you I will give a husband for your daughter
X. C. 8.4.24. Common in Hdt.

With verbs of depriving, warding off, and the like, the dative of the person may be used: to\ sustrateu/ein a)felei=n sfi/sin e)deh/qhsan they asked him to relieve them (lit. take away for them) from serving in the war
X. C. 7.1.44, *danaoi=sin loigo\n a)/mu_non ward off ruin from (for) the Danai A 456. So a)le/cein tini/ ti (poet.). Cp. 1392, 1628.

With verbs of receiving and buying, the person who gives or sells may stand in the dative. In de/xesqai/ ti/ tini (chiefly poetic) the dative denotes the interest of the recipient in the donor: *qe/misti de/kto de/pas she took the cup from (for, i.e. to please) Themis O 87. So with po/sou pri/wmai/ soi ta\ xoiri/dia; at what price am I to buy the pigs of you?
Ar. Ach. 812.

With verbs of motion the dative of the person to whom is properly a dative of advantage or disadvantage: h)=lqe toi=s *)aqhnai/ois h( a)ggeli/a_ the message came to (for) the Athenians
T. 1.61. Cp. 1475.

Dative of Feeling (Ethical Dative).—The personal pro nouns of the first and second person are often used to denote the interest of the speaker, or to secure the interest of the person spoken to, in an action or statement.

me/mnhsqe/ moi mh\ qorubei=n pray remember not to make a disturbance
P. A. 27b,

a)mouso/teroi genh/sontai u(_mi=n oi( ne/oi your young men will grow less cultivated
P. R. 546d,

toiou=to u(_mi=n e)sti h( turanni/s such a thing, you know, is despotism
Hdt. 5.92 h, *)artafe/rnhs u(_mi=n *(usta/speo/s e)sti pai=s Artaphernes, you know, is Hystaspes' son 5. 30. The dative of feeling may denote surprise:

w)= mh=ter, w(s kalo/s moi o( pa/ppos oh mother, how handsome grandpa is
X. C. 1.3.2. With the dative of feeling cp. “knock me here” Shakesp. T. of Sh. 1. 2. 8, “study me how to please the eye” L. L. L. i. 1. 80. toi\ surely, often used to introduce general statements or maxims, is a petrified dative of feeling (= soi/).
a. This dative in the third person is very rare (au)th=| in
P. R. 343a).
b. This construction reproduces the familiar style of conversation and may often be translated by I beg you, please, you see, let me tell you, etc. Sometimes the idea cannot be given in translation. This dative is a form of 1481.
