title: Ethical Dative (or Dative of Feeling)
definition: A dative personal pronoun of the first and second person (μοι, ἡμῖν, σοι \[or τοί\], ὑμῖν) signals the interest of the speaker or the one being spoken to in the action of a statement and may also denote surprise. This dative is very rare in the third person. In many cases, ethical Dative (or Dative of Feeling) is left untranslated.

smyth.text:
Dative of Feeling (Ethical Dative).—The personal pro nouns of the first and second person are often used to denote the interest of the speaker, or to secure the interest of the person spoken to, in an action or statement.

me/mnhsqe/ moi mh\ qorubei=n pray remember not to make a disturbance
P. A. 27b,

a)mouso/teroi genh/sontai u(_mi=n oi( ne/oi your young men will grow less cultivated
P. R. 546d,

toiou=to u(_mi=n e)sti h( turanni/s such a thing, you know, is despotism
Hdt. 5.92 h, *)artafe/rnhs u(_mi=n *(usta/speo/s e)sti pai=s Artaphernes, you know, is Hystaspes' son 5. 30. The dative of feeling may denote surprise:

w)= mh=ter, w(s kalo/s moi o( pa/ppos oh mother, how handsome grandpa is
X. C. 1.3.2. With the dative of feeling cp. “knock me here” Shakesp. T. of Sh. 1. 2. 8, “study me how to please the eye” L. L. L. i. 1. 80. toi\ surely, often used to introduce general statements or maxims, is a petrified dative of feeling (= soi/).
a. This dative in the third person is very rare (au)th=| in
P. R. 343a).
b. This construction reproduces the familiar style of conversation and may often be translated by I beg you, please, you see, let me tell you, etc. Sometimes the idea cannot be given in translation. This dative is a form of 1481.

e)moi\ boulome/nw| e)sti/, etc.—Instead of a sentence with a finite verb, a participle usually denoting inclination or aversion is added to the dative of the person interested, which depends on a form of ei)=nai, g<*>gnesqai, etc.
tw=| plh/qei tw=n *plataiw=n ou) boulome/nw| h)=n tw=n *)aqhnai/wn a)fi/stasqai the Plataean democracy did not wish to revolt from the Athenians (= to\ plh=qos ou)k e)bou/leto a)fi/stasqai)
T. 2.3 (lit. it was not for them when wishing), a)\_n boulome/nois a)kou/ein h)=| toutoisi/_, mnhsqh/somai if these men (the jury) desire to hear it, I shall take the matter up later (= a)\_n ou(=toi a)kou/ein bou/lwntai)
D. 18.11,

e)pane/lqwmen, ei)/ soi h(dome/nw| e)sti/n let us go back if it is your pleasure to do so
P. Ph. 78b,

ei) mh\ a)sme/nois u(_mi=n a)fi=gmai if I have come against your will
T. 4.85, *ni_ki/a| prosdexome/nw| h)=n ta\ para\ tw=n *)egestai/wn Nicias was prepared for the news from the Egestaeans 6. 46,

h)=n de\ ou) tw=| *)a_ghsila/_w| a)xqome/nw| this was not displeasing to Agesilaus
X. H. 5.3.13. Cp. quibus bellum volentibus erat.

Attic h, a_.—Attic has h for original a_ of the earlier period, as fh/mh report (Lat. fāma). Ionic also has h for original a_. Doric and Aeolic retain original a_ (fa/_ma_).
a. This is true also of the a_ which is the result of early compensative lengthening, by which -ans-, -asl-, -asm-, and -asn- changed to -a_s-, -a_l-, -a_m-, and -a_n-. (See 37 b.) But in a few cases like ta/_s for ta/ns, and in pa=sa for pa/nsa (113) where the combination ans arose at a later period, a_ was not changed to h. u(fa=nai for u(fh=nai to weave follows tetra=nai to pierce.
b. Original a_ became h after u, as fuh/ growth. In some words, however, we find a_.

§30 D. 1
Doric and Aeolic retain original a_, as in ma=lon apple (cp. Lat. mālum, Att. mh=lon), ka=ruc herald (Att. kh=ruc). But Doric and Aeolic have original h when h interchanges with e, as in ti/qhmi I place, ti/qemen we place, ma/_thr ma_te/ra mother, poimh/n poime/ni shepherd.
2. Ionic has h after e, i, and r. Thus, geneh/, skih/, h(me/rh.

A vowel before a diphthong not beginning with the same sound generally contracts with the first vowel of the diphthong; the last vowel, if i, is subscript (5): ti_ma/ei = ti_ma=|, ti_ma/oimen = ti_mw=|men, lei/peai = lei/ph|, memnhoi/mhn = memnw/|mhn.
a. But e + oi becomes oi: file/oi = filoi=; o + ei, o + h| become oi: dhlo/ei = dhloi=, dhlo/h| = dhloi=.

examples.translation: such a thing, you know, is despotism
pray remember not to make a disturbance
your young men will grow less cultivated

examples.greek: ὦ μῆτερ, ὡς καλός μοι ὁ πάππος
examples.translation: oh mother, how handsome grandpa is\!

title: Agent
definition:
With either verbal adjectives ending in \-τός and \-τέος or passive verbs in the perfect or pluperfect tenses, the dative of agent indicates the person in whose interest an action is done.
The notion of agency does not belong to the dative, but it is a natural inference that the person interested is the agent. The usual restriction of the dative to tenses of completed action seems to be due to the fact that the agent is represented as placed in the position of viewing an already completed action in the light of its relation to himself (interest, advantage, possession).

examples.translation: let so much have been said by me
has been done by (for) me and these men
when they had got their preparations ready
envied by those at home

examples.greek: ἡμῖν γ᾽ ὑπὲρ τῆς ἐλευθερίας ἀγωνιστέον
examples.translation: we at least must struggle to defend our freedom

title: Manner and means
definition:
The dative, usually of an abstract noun, may indicate accompanying circumstance and manner or the means of an action. The datives of manner, means and attendant circumstances are sometimes similar to adverbs, for instance: βίᾳ by force, δίκῃ justly, δόλῳ by craft, (τῷ) ἔργῳ in fact, ἡσυχῇ quietly, σπουδῇ hastily, τῇ ἀληθείᾳ in truth, τῷ ὄντι in reality, ὀργῇ in anger.
The dative of price and the dative of material and constituent parts may fall under this category:

examples.translation: they attacked with loud shouts
with all one's might
They ate in silence.

examples.greek: κατὰ σπουδὴν καὶ πολλῷ θορύβῳ ταῖς μὲν ναυσὶν ἐπὶ τὴν Σαλαμῖνα ἔπλεον
examples.translation: Hastily and with much noise they sailed their ships to Salamis.
to die (by) a violent death.
to run at full speed

examples.greek: μέρει τῶν ἀδικημάτων τὸν κίνδυνον ἐξεπρίαντο
examples.translation: they freed themselves from the danger at the price of a part of their unjust gains
he made chariots with strong wheels
they punished him by a fine

title: Measure of Difference
definition: With comparative adjectives, the dative marks the degree by which one thing differs from another. The dative of measure of difference indicates the extent of the difference and is used with comparatives or superlatives and other expressions of comparison.

smyth.text:
Manner (see also 1527).—The dative of manner is used with comparative adjectives and other expressions of comparison to mark the degree by which one thing differs from another (Dative of Measure of Difference).
kefalh=| e)la/_ttwn a head shorter (lit. by the head)
P. Ph. 101a,

ou) pollai=s h(me/rais u(/steron h)=lqen he arrived not many days later
X. H. 1.1.1,

i)o/ntes de/ka h(me/rais pro\ *panaqhnai/wn coming ten days before the Panathenaic festival
T. 5.47,

tosou/tw| h(/di_on zw= o(/sw| plei/w ke/kthmai the more I possess the more pleasant is my life
X. C. 8.3.40,

pollw=| mei/zwn e)gi/gneto h( boh\ o(/sw| dh\ plei/ous e)gi/gnonto the shouting became much louder as the men increased in number
X. A. 4.7.23. So with pollw=| by much, o)li/gw| by little, tw=| panti/ in every respect (by all odds).
a. With the superlative:

makrw=| a)/rista by far the best
P. L. 858e.

With comparatives the accusatives (1586) ti/, ti\, ou)de/n, mhde/n without a substantive are always used:

ou)de\n h(=tton nihilo minus
X. A. 7.5.9. In Attic prose (except in Thuc.) polu/ and o)li/gon are more common than pollw=| and o)li/gw| with comparatives. Hom. has only polu\ mei/zwn.
Measure of difference may be expressed by e)/n tini; ei)/s ti, kata/ ti; or by e)pi/ tini.

examples.greek: “**κεφαλῇ** ἐλάττων **P. Ph. 101a**; ⇾ a head shorter (lit. by the head)
examples.translation: a head shorter (lit. by the head)
he arrived not many days later
coming ten days before the Panathenaic festival

examples.greek: πολλῷ μείζων ἐγίγνετο ἡ βοὴ ὅσῳ δὴ πλείους ἐγίγνοντο
examples.translation: the shouting became much louder as the men increased in number
by far the best

title: Instrument
definition: The dative of instrument expresses the instrument or tool by which or with which an action is done or accompanied. This use of the dative is the representative of the lost instrumental case.

examples.translation: he hit me with stone
he hurls his ax at him (hurls with his ax)

examples.greek: “**ταῖς** **μαχαίραις** κόπτοντες **X. A. 4\. 6\. 26**; ⇾ hacking them with their swords
examples.translation: hacking them with their swords
defending themselves by pickets

title: Cause or Purpose
definition:
For the dative of purpose (to what end?), a predicate noun is used:
“ἐκείνῳ ἡ χώρα **δῶρον** ἐδόθη” **X. H. 3.1.6**; ⇾ the country was given to him as a gift
The dative, especially with verbs of emotion, expresses the occasion (external cause) or the motive (internal cause). Sometimes the dative of cause may resemble the dative of purpose.
→ “Ἀθηναῖοι ἐφ᾽ ἡμᾶς ὥρμηνται Λεοντίνων **κατοικίσει**” **T. 6.33**; ⇾ the Athenians have set out against us (with a view to) to restore the Leontines

smyth.text:
For the dative of purpose (to what end?), common in Latin with a second dative (dono dare), Greek uses a predicate noun:

e)kei/nw| h( xw/ra_ dw=ron e)do/qh the country was given to him as a gift
X. H. 3.1.6. The usage in Attic inscriptions (

h(=loi tai=s qu/rais nails for the doors
C.I.A. /lref>, add. 834 b, 1, 38) is somewhat similar to the Latin usage. Cp. 1502.
a. The infinitive was originally, at least in part, a dative of an abstract substantive, and served to mark purpose: ti/s t' a)/r sfwe qew=n e)/ridi cune/hke ma/xesqai; who then of the gods brought the twain together (for) to contend in strife? A 8. Cp. “what went ye out for to see?” St. Matth. 11. 8.

## DATIVE AS A MODIFIER OF THE SENTENCE

## DATIVE OF INTEREST

Cause.—The dative, especially with verbs of emotion, expresses the occasion (external cause) or the motive (internal cause).
Occasion:

th=| tu/xh| e)lpi/sa_s confident by reason of his good fortune
T. 3.97, qauma/zw th=| a)poklh/|sei mou tw=n pulw=n I am astonished at being shut out of the gates 4. 85,

tou/tois h(/sqh he was pleased at this
X. A. 1.9.26, h)xqo/meqa toi=s gegenhme/nois we were troubled at what had occurred 5. 7. 20, xalepw=s fe/rw toi=s parou=si pra/_gmasin I am troubled at the present occurrences 1. 3. 3. Motive:

fili/a| kai\ eu)noi/a| e(po/menoi following out of friendship and good will
X. A. 2.6.13. Occasion and motive: oi( me\n a)pori/a| a)kolou/qwn, oi( de\ a)pisti/a| some (carried their own food) because they lacked servants, others through distrust of them
T. 7.75,

u(/brei kai\ ou)k oi)/nw| tou=to poiw=n doing this out of insolence and not because he was drunk
D. 21.74.

Some verbs of emotion take e)pi/ (with dat.) to denote the cause; so always me/ga fronei=n to plume oneself, and often xai/rein rejoice, lu_pei=sqai grieve, a)ganaktei=n be vexed, ai)sxu/_nesqai be ashamed. Many verbs take the genitive (1405).

The dative of cause sometimes approximates to a dative of purpose (1473): *)aqhnai=oi e)f' h(ma=s w(/rmhntai *leonti/_nwn katoiki/sei the Athenians have set out against us (with a view to) to restore the Leontines
T. 6.33. This construction is common with other verbal nouns in Thucydides.

examples.translation: confident by reason of his good fortune
he was pleased at this
we were troubled at what had occurred
following out of friendship and good will

examples.greek: ὕβρει καὶ οὐκ οἴνῳ τοῦτο ποιῶν
examples.translation: doing this out of insolence and not because he was drunk

title: Accompanimen
definition:
The dative of accompaniment is used with verbs signifying to accompany or follow, mainly in military terminology. This meaning of dative is often equivalent to a dative of means outside the context of military terms.
An extension of this usage occurs when the persons in the dative are essentially the same as the persons forming the subject (distributive use).

examples.translation: to follow the leader
I am willing to follow you
he marches out with all his army

examples.greek: ἡμῖν ἐφείποντο οἱ πολέμιοι καὶ ἱππικῷ καὶ πελταστικῷ
examples.translation: the enemy pursued us with their cavalry and peltasts

title: Time
definition: The dative without a preposition is commonly used to express an specific moment or period of time (chiefly *day*, *night*, *month*, *year*, season) at which an action occurred. The dative contrasts one point of time with another, and is usually accompanied by an attributive.

examples.greek: ταύτην μὲν τὴν ἡμέραν αὐτοῦ ἔμειναν, τῇ δὲ ὑστεραίᾳ κτλ.
examples.translation: throughout that day they waited there, but on the day following, etc.
in the third month
when summer was coming to an end
in the sixtieth year
in the winter season
at the Panathenaea
at the representations of the tragedies

title: Place
definition: In poetry the dative without a preposition is used to express the place where a person or thing is or where an action is taking place. In prose, the dative of place is limited to a few place names. This use of the dative is representative of the lost locative case.

examples.translation: taking his stand in the middle of the court
she lay on the ground
conspicuous among the Trojans
may be rose up among them (or for them).
fell on the ground
put thy sword into its sheath

title: Respect
definition: The dative of respect indicates a thing in respect to which the verb or adjective is limited and is often nearly equivalent to the accusative of respect. The dative expresses the particular point of view from which a statement is made.

smyth.text:
The dative of manner may denote the particular point of view from which a statement is made. This occurs chiefly with intransitive adjectives but also with intransitive verbs (Dative of Respect). (Cp. 1600.)

a)nh\r h(liki/a| e)/ti ne/os a man still young in years
T. 5.43, toi=s sw/masi to\ ple/on i)sxu/_ousa h)\ toi=s xrh/masin a power stronger in men than in money 1. 121,

a)sqenh\s tw=| sw/mati weak in body
D. 21.165,

th=| fwnh=| tra_xu/s harsh of voice
X. A. 2.6.9,

fronh/sei diafe/rwn distinguished in understanding
X. C. 2.3.5,

tw=n to/te duna/mei prou/xwn superior in power to the men of that time
T. 1.9, o)no/mati spondai/ a truce so far as the name goes 6. 10.
a. The accusative of respect (1600) is often nearly equivalent to the dative of respect.

examples.translation: weak in body
a man still young in years
harsh of voice
distinguished in understanding
superior in power to the men of that time
a truce so far as the name goes

title: Experiencer
definition:
The dative of a noun or pronoun can express the person in whose opinion a statement holds true or a situation or a direction is defined. The dative of experiencer is also common with impersonal verbs expressing emotions, necessity or need.
The dative participle, without a noun or pronoun, is frequently used in the singular or plural to denote indefinitely the person judging or observing. This construction is most common with participles of verbs of coming or going and with participles of verbs of considering.

smyth.text:
Dative of Reference.—The dative of a noun or pronoun often denotes the person in whose opinion a statement holds good.

ga/mous tou\s prw/tous e)ga/mei *pe/rsh|si o( *da_rei=os Darius contracted marriages most distinguished in the eyes of the Persians
Hdt. 3.88,

pa=si ni_ka=n toi=s kritai=s to be victorious in the judgment of all the judges
Ar. Av. 445,

polloi=sin oi)ktro/s pitiful in the eyes of many
S. Tr. 1071. para/ is often used, as in para\ *da_rei/w|

krith=| in the opinion of Darius
Hdt. 3.160.

examples.greek: γάμους τοὺς πρώτους ἐγάμει Πέρσῃσι ὁ Δαρεῖος
examples.translation: Darius contracted marriages most distinguished in the eyes of the Persians.
to be victorious in the judgment of all the judges
pitiful in the eyes of many

examples.greek: ἔδοξέ τῇ βουλῇ ἢ τῷ δήμῳ ἢ ἀμφοτέροις
examples.translation: The council or the people or both decided

examples.greek: ἡ Θρᾴκη ἐστὶν ἐπὶ δεξιὰ εἰς τὸν Πόντον εἰσπλέοντι
examples.translation: Thrace is on the right as you sail into the Pontus

examples.greek: ἔλεγον ὅτι ἡ ὁδὸς διαβάντι τὸν ποταμὸν ἐπὶ Λυδίαν φέροι
examples.translation: they said that, when you had crossed the river, the road led to Lydia

examples.greek: οὐκ οὖν ἄτοπον διαλογιζομένοις τὰς δωρεὰς νυνὶ πλείους εἶναι;
examples.translation: *is it not strange*, when we reflect, that gifts are more frequent now?

examples.greek: τὸ μὲν ἔξωθεν ἁπτομένῳ σῶμα οὐκ ἄγαν θερμὸν ἦν
examples.translation: if you touched the surface the body was not very hot

examples.greek: πρὸς ὠφέλειαν σκοπουμένῳ ὁ ἐπαινέτης τοῦ δικαίου ἀληθεύει
examples.translation: if you look at the matter from the point of view of advantage, the panegyrist of justice speaks the truth

title: Direct Object
definition: Accusative is used as the direct object with verbs which take an object.

smyth.text: The accusative is the case of the direct object (919). The accusative is used with all transitive verbs (and with some intransitive verbs used transitively), with some verbal nouns, and with adjectives.

The direct object is of two kinds:
a. The internal object (object effected): o( a)nh\r tu/ptei polla\_s plhga/_s the man strikes many blows.
N. 1.—Here the object is already contained (or implied) in the verb, and its addition is optional. The accusative of the internal object is sometimes called the accusative of content. The object stands in apposition to the result of the verbal action. The effect produced by the verb is either (1) transient, when the object is a nomen actionis, and disappears with the operation of the verb, as in ma/xhn ma/xesqai to fight a battle, or (2) permanent, and remains after the verbal action has ceased, as in tei=xos teixi/zein to build a wall. The latter form is the accusative of result (1578).
N. 2.—Almost any verb may take one of the varieties of the internal object.
b. The external object (object affected): o( a)nh\r tu/ptei to\n pai=da the man strikes the boy.
N.—Here the object is not contained in the verb, but is necessary to explain or define the character of the action in question. The external object stands outside the verbal action.

Many verbs may take an accusative either of the external or of the internal object: te/mnein u(/_lhn fell timber, te/mnein ta\_s tri/xas cut off the hair, te/mnein o(do/n open a road, but sponda\_s or o(/rkia te/mnein, with a specialized verbal idea, to make a treaty by slaying a victim (pass. o(/rkia e)tmh/qh), te/mnein o(do/n make one's way (poet.), teixi/zein xwri/on fortify a place, but teixi/zein tei=xos build a wall. Cp.
E. Supp. 1060: A. ni_kw=sa ni/_khn ti/na; maqei=n xrh/|zw se/qen. B. pa/_sa_s gunai=kas, ktl. A. Victorious in what victory? This I would learn of thee. B. Over all women. Here the construction shifts from the internal to the external object.

examples.translation: I see the man
Everyone praises the man
I am ashamed of my lowly descent.

title: Cognate
definition: The cognate accusatives are objects added to specify the nature of the action of the verb and are either etymologically or semantically related to the verb. They can be nouns in the accusative that are of the *same origin* as the verb (they contain the same stem), or of *kindred meaning* with the verb (they express the same meaning). In many cases, the cognate accusative is left untranslated to avoid redundancy.

smyth.text: The cognate accusative is of two kinds, of which the second is an extension of the first.

(I) The substantive in the accusative is of the same origin as the verb.

pollh\n flua_ri/a_n flua_rou=nta talking much nonsense
P. A. 19c, cune/fuge th\n fugh\n tau/thn he shared in the recent exile 21 a,

th\n e)n *salami=ni naumaxi/a_n naumaxh/santes victorious in the sea-fight at Salamis
D. 59.97, ta\_s u(posxe/seis a(\_s ou(=tos u(pi_sxnei=to the promises which he made 19. 47,

h( ai)ti/a_ h(\n ai)tiw=ntai the charge they bring
Ant. 6.27.
a. Sometimes the verb may be suppressed, as h(mi=n me\n eu)xa\_s ta/_sde (eu)/xomai) for us these prayers
A. Ch. 142.

The cognate accusative occurs even with adjectives of an intransitive character:

mh/te ti sofo\s w)\n th\n e)kei/nwn sofi/a_n mh/te a)maqh\s th\n a)maqi/a_n being neither at all wise after the fashion of their wisdom nor ignorant after the fashion of their ignorance
P. A. 22e, a)ti/_mous e)poi/hsan a)ti_mi/a_n toia/_nde w(/ste ktl. they disfranchised them in such a way that, etc.
T. 5.34 (a)ti/_mous e)poi/hsan = h)ti/_mhsan, cp. 1598).

Passive:

po/lemos e)polemei=to war was waged
X. H. 4.8.1.

(II) The substantive in the accusative is of kindred meaning with the verb.

e)ch=lqon a)/lla_s o(dou/s they went forth on other expeditions
X. H. 1.2.17,

to\n i(ero\n kalou/menon po/lemon e)stra/teusan they waged what is called the Sacred War
T. 1.112,

h)sqe/nhse tau/thn th\n no/son he fell ill of this disease
I. 19.24,

a)nqrw/pou fu/sin blastw/n born to man's estate
S. Aj. 760.

Passive:

po/lemos e)tara/xqh war was stirred up
D. 18.151.

An extension of the cognate accusative appears in poetry with kei=sqai, sth=nai, kaqi/zein and like verbs:

to/pon, o(/ntina kei=tai the place in which he is situated
S. Ph. 145, ti/ e(/sthke pe/tra_n; why stands she on the rock?
E. Supp. 987,

tri/poda kaqi/zwn sitting on the tripod
E. Or. 956.

An attributive word is usually necessary (but not in Hom.); otherwise the addition of the substantive to the verb would be tautologous. But the attribute is omitted:
a. When the nominal idea is specialized:

fulaka\_s fula/ttein to stand sentry
X. A. 2.6.10, fo/ron fe/rein to pay tribute 5. 5. 7.
b. When the substantive is restricted by the article:

to\n po/lemon polemei=n to wage the present war
T. 8.58, th\n pomph\n pe/mpein to conduct the procession 6. 56.
c. When a plural substantive denotes repeated occurrences:

e)trihra/rxhse trihrarxi/a_s he performed the duty of trierarch
D. 45.85.
d. In various expressions:

*)olu/mpia ni_ka=n to win an Olympian victory
T. 1.126,

th\n naumaxi/a_n ni_kh=sai to be victorious in the sea-fight
L. 19.28,

qu/_ein ta\ eu)agge/lia to offer a sacrifice in honour of good news
X. H. 1.6.37.
e. In poetry the use of a substantive to denote a special form of the action of the verb is much extended: sta/zein ai(=ma to drip (drops of) blood
S. Ph. 783,

*)/arhpnei=n to breathe war
A. Ag. 375, pu=r dedorkw/s looking (a look of) fire
t 446. This use is common, especially in Aristophanes, with verbs signifying the look of another than the speaker: ble/pein na=pu to look mustard Eq. 631, ble/pein a)pisti/a_n to look unbelief Com. fr. 1. 341 (No. 309); cp. “looked his faith”: Holmes.

examples.translation: talking much nonsense
he shared in the recent exile
victorious in the sea-fight at Salamis
the promises which he made
the charge they bring
war was waged
war was stirred up

title: Subject of Infinitive or Participle
definition: The accusative can express the subject in an infinitive or participle clause. When the subject of the infinitive is different from that of the governing verb, it stands in the accusative; and a predicate noun stands also in the accusative. When the subject of the infinitive is the same as the subject or object of the governing verb, or when it has already been made known in the sentence, it is rarely repeated with the infinitive.

smyth.text: In general the subject of the infinitive, if expressed at all, stands in the accusative; when the subject of the infinitive is the same as the subject or object of the governing verb, or when it has already been made known in the sentence, it is not repeated with the infinitive.

When the subject of the infinitive is the same as that of the governing verb, it is omitted, and a predicate noun stands in the nominative case.

oi)=mai ei)de/nai I think that I know
P. Pr. 312e,

*pe/rshs e)/fh ei)=nai he said he was a Persian
X. A. 4.4.17,

e)gw\ ou)x o(mologh/sw a)/klhtos h(/kein I shall not admit that I have come uninvited
P. S. 174d, o(mologei=s peri\ e)me\ a)/dikos gegenh=sqai; do you admit that you have been guilty as regards me?
X. A. 1.6.8 (cp. 4.2.27 in 2263).
a. The nominative is used when the infinitive, expressing some action or state of the subject of the main verb, has the article in an oblique case. Thus, tou/twn a)ciwqei\s dia\ to\ patriko\s au)tw=| fi/los ei/=nai justifying these requests on the ground that he was his hereditary friend
Aes. 3.52,

tou=to d' e)poi/ei e)k tou= xalepo\s ei)=nai this he effected by reason of his being severe
X. A. 2.6.9, e)pi\ tw=| o(moi=oi toi=s leipome/nois ei)=nai e)kpe/mpontai (colonists) are sent out to be the equals of those who stay at home
T. 1.34.
b. The nominative stands usually in sentences with dei=n, xrh=nai etc., dependent on a verb of saying or thinking. Thus,

h(gou/mhn . . . periei=nai dei=n au)tw=n kai\ megaloyu_xo/teros fai/nesqai I thought I ought to surpass them and to show myself more magnificent
D. 19.235. Here h(gou/mhn dei=n is equivalent to I thought it proper.
c. When the governing verb is a participle in an oblique case, a predicate noun usually agrees with the participle, and rarely stands in the nominative. Thus,

a)pallagei\s tou/twn tw=n fasko/ntwn dikastw=n ei)=nai being rid of those who profess to be judges
P. A. 41a,

ta\_s a)rxa\_s di/dwsi . . . toi=s a)ei\ do/ca_sin a)ri/stois ei)=nai it dispenses the offices to those who always seem to be the most deserving
P. Menex. 238d.

A pronoun subject of the infinitive, if (wholly or partially) identical with the subject of the main verb, is generally expressed when emphatic, and stands in the accusative (cases of the nominative are rare and suspected); but the indirect reflexive sfei=s stands in the nominative or accusative.

oi)=mai e)me\ plei/w xrh/mata ei)rga/sqai h)\ a)/llous su/nduo I think I have made more money than any two others together
P. Hipp. M. 282e, h(ghsa/menos e)mauto\n e)pieike/steron ei)=nai (emphatic for h(ghsa/menos e)pieike/steros ei)=nai) deeming myself to be too honest
P. A. 36b,

tou\s de\ *qhbai/ous h(gei=to . . . e)a/_sein o(/pws bou/letai pra/_ttein e(auto/n he thought the Thebans would let him have his own way
D. 6.9, ou) sfei=s a)dikei=sqai, a)ll' e)kei/nous ma=llon he said that not they (the speaker and the other Lacedaemonians), but they (the Toroneans) rather had been wronged 4. 114 (but sfa=s in 1228 b).
a. After a preceding accusative with the infinitive, a second pronoun referring to a different person, and also subject of an infinitive, must also stand in the accusative whether or not it denotes the same person as the subject of the governing verb. Thus, a)lla\ nomi/zeis h(ma=s me\n a)ne/cesqai/ sou, au)to\s (see below) de\ tuph/sein; kai\ h(ma=s me\n a)poyhfiei=sqai/ sou, de\ (not su\) d' ou' pau/sesqai but do you think that we are going to put up with you, while you strike us yourself? and that we are going to acquit you, while you will not cease your outrageous conduct?
D. 21.204. au)to/s, above and in *kle/wn ou)k e)/fh au)to/s, a)ll' e)kei=non strathgei=n Cleon said that not he himself, but that Nicias was in command
T. 4.28, is not the expressed subject of the infinitive, but au)to/s of direct discourse (au)to\s tuph/seis, au)to\s ou) strathgw=); hence au)to/s is not used here for seauto/n (e(auto/n).

When the subject of the infinitive is different from that of the governing verb, it stands in the accusative; and a predicate noun stands also in the accusative.

nomi/zw ga\r u(_ma=s e)moi\ ei)=nai kai\ patri/da kai\ fi/lous for I think you are to me both fatherland and friends
X. A. 1.3.6,

to\n ga\r kalo\n ka)_gaqo\n a)/ndra eu)dai/mona ei)=nai/ fhmi for I maintain that the noble and good man is happy
P. G. 470e.

A predicate noun takes the case of the subject of an infinitive itself dependent on a subjectless infinitive. Thus,

h(mi=n de\ poiou=si dokei=n sfa=s pantodapou\s fai/nesqai they manage it so that they seem to us to appear in various forms
P. R. 381e.

Several infinitives may be used in succession, one infinitive being the subject of another:

peri\ pollou= poiou/menos mhdeni\ do/cai u(bri/zein bou/lesqai regarding it of great importance not to seem to any one to wish to behave outrageously
L. 23.5.

When the subject of the infinitive is the same as the object (in the genitive or dative) of the governing verb, it is often omitted, and a predicate noun is either attracted into the genitive or dative, or stands in the accusative in agreement with the omitted subject of the infinitive. See 1060-1062.
e)/cestin h(mi=n a)gaqoi=s ei)=nai or e)/cestin h(mi=n a)gaqou\s ei)=nai it is in our power to be good (lit. to be good is possible for us). Thus, deo/meq' ou)=n u(_mw=n . . . a)kroa/_sasqai tw=n legome/nwn, e)nqu_mhqe/ntas o(/ti ktl. we ask you therefore to listen to what is said, considering that, etc. 1. 14. 6. Cp. nu=n soi e)/cestin a)ndri\ gene/sqai quoted in 1062 with

*lakedaimoni/ois e)/cestin u(_mi=n fi/lous gene/sqai it is in your power to become friends to the Lacedaemonians
T. 4.29. The latter construction may be explained as abbreviated for e)/cestin u(_mi=n (u(_ma=s) fi/lous gene/sqai.

The subject of the infinitive is often retained when it is the same as the (omitted) oblique object of the governing verb. Thus,

parh/ggeile ta\ o(/pla ti/qesqai tou\s *(/ellhnas he issued orders that the Greeks should get under arms
X. A. 2.2.21.

examples.greek: νομίζω γὰρ ὑμᾶς ἐμοὶ εἶναι καὶ πατρίδα καὶ φίλους
examples.translation: for I think you are to me both fatherland and friends

examples.greek: τὸν γὰρ καλὸν κἀγαθὸν ἄνδρα εὐδαίμονα εἶναί φημι
examples.translation: for I maintain that the noble and good man is happy

examples.greek: οἶμαι ἐμὲ πλείω χρήματα εἰργάσθαι ἢ ἄλλους σύνδυο
examples.translation: I think I have made more money than any two others together

examples.greek: παρήγγειλε τὰ ὅπλα τίθεσθαι τοὺς Ἕλληνας
examples.translation: he issued orders that the Greeks should get under arms

title: Respect
definition: The accusative of respect or limitation expresses a thing *in respect to which* the verb or adjective is limited. The accusative usually expresses a local relation or the instrument. The word restricted by the accusative of respect usually indicates like or similar to, good or better, bad or worse, a physical or a mental quality, or an emotion. The accusative of respect often specifies qualities and attributes (nature, form, size, name, birth, number, etc.), or it may indicate the sphere in general and is added to verbs denoting a state, and to adjectives.

smyth.text:
To verbs denoting a state, and to adjectives, an accusative may be added to denote a thing in respect to which the verb or adjective is limited.
a. The accusative usually expresses a local relation or the instrument. The word restricted by the accusative usually denotes like or similar to, good or better, bad or worse, a physical or a mental quality, or an emotion.

The accusative of respect is employed
a. Of the parts of the body:

o( a)/nqrwpos to\n da/ktulon a)lgei= the man has a pain in his finger
P. R. 462d,

tuflo\s ta/ t' w)=ta to/n te nou=n ta/ t' o)/mmat' ei)= blind art thou in ears, and mind, and eyes
S. O. T. 371, po/das w)ku\s *)axilleu/s Hom.
N.—The accusative of the part in apposition to the whole (985) belongs here, as is seen by the passive. Cp.

to\n plh=c' au)xe/na him he smote on the neck
*l 240 (ba/le qou=ron *)/arha kat' au)xe/na *f 406) with be/blhai kenew=na thou art smitten in the abdomen E 284.
b. Of qualities and attributes (nature, form, size, name, birth, number, etc.):

diafe/rei gunh\ a)ndro\s th\n fu/sin woman differs from man in nature
P. R. 453b,

ou)de\ e)/oiken qnhta\_s a)_qana/th|si de/mas kai\ ei)=dos e)ri/zein nor is it seemly that mortal women should rival the immortals in form and appearance
e 213, potamo/s, *ku/dnos o)/noma, eu)=ros du/o ple/qrwn a river, Cydnus by name, two plethra in width
X. A. 1.2.23 (so with u(/yos, ba/qos, me/geqos), plh=qos w(s disxi/_lioi about two thousand in number 4. 2. 2,

le/con o(/stis ei)= ge/nos tell me of what race thou art
E. Bacch. 460.
c. Of the sphere in general:

deinoi\ ma/xhn terrible in battle
A. Pers. 27,

ge/nesqe th\n dia/noian transfer yourselves in thought
Aes. 3.153,

to\ me\n e)p' e)moi\ oi)/xomai, to\ d' e)pi\ soi\ se/swsmai so far as I myself was concerned I was lost, but through you am saved
X. C. 5.4.11. Often of indefinite relations:

pa/nta kako/s base in all things
S. O. T. 1421,

tau=ta a)gaqo\s e(/kastos h(mw=n, a(/per sofo/s, a(\ de\ a)maqh/s, tau=ta de\ kako/s each one of us is good in matters in which he is skilled, but bad in those in which he is ignorant
P. Lach. 194d.

Very rarely after substantives: xei=ras ai)xmhth/s a warrior valiant with (thy) arm
p 242,

nea_ni/ai ta\_s o)/yeis youths by their appearance
L. 10.29.
For the acccusative of respect the instrumental dative (1516) is also employed, and also the prepositions ei)s, kata/, pro/s, e.g. diafe/rein a)reth=| or ei)s a)reth/n.
Not to be confused with the accusative of respect is the accusative after intransitive adjectives (1565) or after the passives of 1632.

The accusative of respect is probably in its origin, at least in part, an accusative of the internal object.

## ADVERBIAL ACCUSATIVE

examples.greek: τυφλὸς τά τ᾽ ὦτα τόν τε νοῦν τά τ᾽ ὄμματ᾽ εἶ
examples.translation: you are blind in ears, and mind, and eyes
the man has a pain in his finger
swift-footed Achilles
woman differs from man in nature
about two thousand in number
tell me of what race thou art
terrible in battle
transfer yourselves in thought

title: Time
definition:
The accusative of time indicates duration and the extent of time. It implies that the action of the verb covers the *entire* period.
To mark *how long* a situation has lasted or how much time has elapsed since something happened, an ordinal is used without the article, but often with the addition of οὑτοσί. The current day or year is included. Thus:

smyth.text:
Time.—The accusative denotes extent of time.

e)/meinen h(me/ra_s e(pta/ he remained seven days
X. A. 1.2.6,

cummaxi/a_n e)poih/santo e(kato\n e)/th they made an alliance for a hundred years
T. 3.114.

The accusative of time implies that the action of the verb covers the entire period. When emphasis is laid on the uninterrupted duration of an action, para/ with the accusative (1692. 3. b) and dia/ with the genitive (1685. 1. b) are used. The accusative of time is rarely employed where the dative (1540) is properly in place: th/nde th\n h(me/ra_n
Aes. 3.7.

Duration of life may be expressed by gegonw/s:

e)/th gegonw\s e(bdomh/konta seventy years old
P. A. 17d. (Also by ei)=nai and the genitive, 1327.)

To mark (a) how long a situation has lasted or (b) how much time has elapsed since something happened, an ordinal is used without the article, but often with the addition of ou(tosi/_. The current day or year is included. Thus (a)

th\n mhte/ra teleuth/sa_san tri/ton e)/tos touti/_ my mother who died two years ago
L. 24.6,

e)pidedh/mhke tri/thn h)/dh h(me/ra_n he has been in the city since day before yesterday
P. Pr. 309d. (b)

a)phgge/lqh *fi/lippos tri/ton h)\ te/tarton e)/tos touti\_ *(hrai=on tei=xos poliorkw=n this is the third or fourth year since it was announced that Philip was besieging fort Heraeum
D. 3.4.
On the accusative of extent in degree, see 1609. With a comparative we find polu/ and o)li/gon as well as pollw=| and o)li/gw| (1514); and always ti/, ti\, ou)de/n with the comparative.

Time and degree are often expressed by prepositions with the accusative. See Prepositions under a)mfi/, a)na/, dia/, e)pi/, kata/, para/, pro/s, u(po/.

## TERMINAL ACCUSATIVE (IN POETRY)

examples.translation: he remained seven days
they made an alliance for a hundred years

examples.translation: my mother who died two years ago
he has been in the city since day before yesterday

title: Space
definition: The accusative of space expresses a space, distance or path. It denotes the space or way *over which* an action is extended, or the measure of the space traversed.

smyth.text:
Space.—The accusative denotes the space or way over which an action is extended, and the measure of the space traversed.
a)/gein (stratia\_n)

stena\_s o(dou/s to lead an army over narrow roads
X. C. 1.6.43, e)celau/nei staqmou\s trei=s, parasa/gga_s ei)/kosi kai\ du/o he advances three stages, twenty- two parasangs
X. A. 1.2.5,

a)pe/xei h( *pla/taia tw=n *qhbw=n stadi/ous e(bdomh/konta Plataea is seventy stades distant from Thebes
T. 2.5.
a. This use is analogous to the cognate accusative after verbs of motion (e)co/dous e)celqei=n, plei=n qa/lattan).

examples.translation: to lead an army over narrow roads

examples.greek: ἐξελαύνει σταθμοὺς τρεῖς, παρασάγγας εἴκοσι καὶ δύο
examples.translation: he advances three stages, twenty- two parasangs

examples.greek: ἀπέχει ἡ Πλάταια τῶν Θηβῶν σταδίους ἑβδομήκοντα
examples.translation: Plataea is seventy stades distant from Thebes

title: Direction
definition:
In poetry, the accusative may be used without a preposition to express the goal after verbs of motion.
Of *persons* in Homer (especially with ἱκνέομαι, ἵκω, ἱκάνω \= reach) and in the lyric parts of the drama:

smyth.text:
In poetry after verbs of motion the accusative may be used without a preposition to express the goal.

a)/stu *kadmei=on molw/n having come to the city of Cadmus
S. O. T. 35,

pe/myome/n nin *(ella/da we will convey her to Greece
E. Tro. 883. Of persons in Hom. (especially with i(kne/omai, i(/kw, i(ka/_nw = reach) and in the lyric parts of the drama:

mnhsth=ras a)fi/_keto came unto the suitors
a 332. Cp. “arrived our coast”: Shakesp. In
Hdt. 9.26 fame\n h(me/as i(kne/esqai means we declare that it befits us.

examples.translation: having come to the city of Cadmus
we will convey her to Greece
came unto the suitors

title: Adverbial
definition:
Many accusatives marking limitations of the verbal action serve the same function as adverbs.
Expressing manner: τρόπον τινά in some way, τίνα τρόπον in what way? τόνδε (τοῦτον) τὸν τρόπον in this way, πάντα τρόπον in every way (also παντὶ τρόπῳ), τὴν ταχίστην (ὁδόν) in the quickest way, τὴν εὐθεῖαν (ὁδόν) straightforward.
Many adverbial accusatives express measure and degree: μέγα, μεγάλα greatly, πολύ, πολλά much, τὸ πολύ, τὰ πολλά for the most part, ὅσον as much as, οὐδέν, μηδέν not at all, τοσοῦτον so much, τὶ somewhat, ἀρχήν or τὴν ἀρχήν at all with οὐ or μή.

smyth.text: Many accusatives marking limitations of the verbal action serve the same function as adverbs.

Most of these adverbial accusatives are accusatives of the internal object: thus, in te/los de\ ei)=pe but at last he said, te/los is to be regarded as standing in apposition to an unexpressed object of the verb—words, which were the end. Many adverbial accusatives are thus accusatives in apposition (991) and some are accusatives of respect (1600). It is impossible to apportion all cases among the varieties of the accusatives; many may be placed under different heads. The use of adjectives as adverbs (me/ga plou/sios very rich) is often derived from the cognate accusative with verbs (me/ga ploutei=n).

Manner.—tro/pon tina/ in some way, ti/na tro/pon in what way? to/nde (tou=ton) to\n tro/pon in this way, pa/nta tro/pon in every way (also panti\ tro/pw|), th\n taxi/sthn (o(do/n) in the quickest way, th\n eu)qei=an (o(do/n) straightforward, proi=ka, dwrea/_n gratis (1616), di/khn after the fashion of (

di/khn toco/tou like an archer
P. L. 705e), pro/fasin in pretence (

e)/plee pro/fasin e)p' *(ellhspo/ntou he sailed professedly for the Hellespont
Hdt. 5.33), xa/rin for the sake of (lit. favour）:

ou) th\n *)aqhnai/wn xa/rin e)strateu/onto did not engage in the expedition out of good will to the Athenians
Hdt. 5.99,

tou= xa/rin for what reason?
Ar. Plut. 53,

th\n sh\n h(/kw xa/rin for thy sake I have come
S. Ph. 1413. Cp. 993.

Measure and Degree.—me/ga, mega/la greatly, polu/, polla/ much, to\ polu/, ta\ polla/ for the most part, o(/son as much as, ou)de/n, mhde/n not at all, tosou=ton so much, ti\ somewhat, a)rxh/n or th\n a)rxh/n at all with ou) or mh/ (

e)n tw=| paraxrh=ma ou)k e)/stin a)rxh\n o)rqw=s bouleu/esqai it is utterly impossible to deliberate correctly offhand
Ant. 5.73).

Motive.—ti/ why? tou=to, tau=ta for this reason (cognate accus.): ti/ h)=lqes quid (cur) venisti = ti/na i(=cin h)=lqes; tou=to xai/rw ( = tau/thn th\n xara\_n xai/rw) therefore I rejoice,

au)ta\ tau=ta h(/kw for this very reason have I come
P. Pr. 310e,

tou=t' a)/xqesqe for this reason you are vexed
X. A. 3.2.20.

Time and Succession (1582): to\ nu=n now, to\ pa/lai of old, pro/teron before, to\ pro/teron the former time, prw=ton first, to\ kat' a)rxa/_s in the beginning, to\ prw=ton in the first place, to\ teleutai=on in the last place (for to\ deu/teron in a series use e)/peita or e)/peita de/), to\ loipo/n for the future, a)kmh/n at the point, just, kairo/n in season.

## TWO ACCUSATIVES WITH ONE VERB

he sailed professedly for the Hellespont

title: Oaths
definition:
The accusative of oath indicates the person or thing by which one swears and is accompanied bythe adverbs of swearing such as μά, οὐ μά, ναὶ μά, νή, or verbs of swearing, ὀμνύναι swear by (τοὺς θεούς, pass. Ζεὺς ὀμώμοται) and *swear to* (τὸν ὅρκον, pass. ὁ ὅρκος ὀμώμοται).
μά is negative, except when preceded by ναί. μά may stand alone when a negative precedes (often in a question) or when a negative follows in the next clause:
μά is sometimes omitted after οὐ, and after ναί:

smyth.text:
(III) Verbs of swearing.
o)mnu/nai swear by (tou\s qeou/s, pass. *zeu\s o)mw/motai) and swear to (to\n o(/rkon, pass. o( o(/rkos o)mw/motai). So e)piorkei=n swear falsely by.
a. o)mnu/nai tou\s qeou/s may be an abbreviation of o)mnu/nai o(/rkon (internal object) tw=n qew=n.
b. The accusative is used in asseverations with the adverbs of swearing ma/, ou) ma/, nai\ ma/, nh/.
Nay, by Zeus: ma\ (to\n) *di/a, ou) ma\ (to\n) *di/a.
Yea, by Zeus: nai\ ma\ (to\n) *di/a, nh\ (to\n) *di/a.
ma/ is negative, except when preceded by nai/. ma/ may stand alone when a negative precedes (often in a question) or when a negative follows in the next clause: ma\ to\n *)apo/llw, ou)/k
Ar. Thesm. 269. ma/ is sometimes omitted after ou), and after nai/: ou) to\n *)/olumpon
S. O. T. 1088, nai\ ta\_n ko/ra_n
Ar. Vesp. 1438.
c. The name of the deity may be omitted in Attic under the influence of sudden scrupulousness: ma\ to\n—ou' su/ ge not you, by—
P. G. 466e.

examples.greek: ὀμνύω ὑμῖν θεοὺς πάντας καὶ πάσας
examples.translation: I swear to you by all the gods and goddesses.
No, by Apollo
by heaven, \[you wil\] not.

title: Double Accusative
definition: In addition to a direct object, several verbs take a compliment in the accusative. Double accusatives are common with the verbs meaning to do, to demand, to ask, to name or call, to choose, to persuade, etc. The second accusative could also be internal object (see AccCog.).

smyth.text: Many verbs take both an internal and an external object.

The external object refers to a person, the internal object (cognate accusative, 1563 ff.) refers to a thing. Here the internal object stands in closer relation to the verb.

o( po/lemos a)ei/mnhston paidei/a_n au)tou\s e)pai/deuse the war taught them a lesson they will hold in everlasting remembrance
Aes. 3.148,

tosou=ton e)/xqos e)xqai/rw se I hate thee with such an hate
S. El. 1034,

*me/lhto/s me e)gra/yato th\n grafh\n tau/thn Meletus brought this accusation against me
P. A. 19b, e(/lkos, to/ min ba/le the wound that he dealt him E 795 (1578),

*miltia/dhs o( th\n e)n *maraqw=ni ma/xhn tou\s barba/rous ni_kh/sa_s Miltiades who won the battle at Marathon over the barbarians
Aes. 3.181, to\n a)/ndra tu/ptein ta\_s plhga/_s to strike the man the blows Ant. 4.
g. 1,

kalou=si/ me tou=to to\ o)/noma they give me this appellation
X. O. 7.3.

Passive (1747):

pa=san qerapei/a_n qerapeuo/menos receiving every manner of service
P. Phae. 255a,

tu/ptesqai penth/konta plhga/_s to be struck fifty blows
Aes. 1.139, h( kri/sis, h(\n e)kri/qh the sentence that was pronounced upon him
L. 13.50,

ta\_s ma/xa_s, o(/sa_s *pe/rsai h(tth/qhsan e)w= I omit the battles in which the Persians were defeated
I. 4.145,

o)/noma e(\n keklhme/noi *sikeliw=tai called by the one name of Sicilians
T. 4.64.

So with verbs signifying to do anything to or say anything of a person (1591):

polla\ a)gaqa\ u(_ma=s e)poi/hsen he did you much good
L. 5.3,

tauti/_ me poiou=si that's what they are doing to me
Ar. Vesp. 696,

ta\ toiau=ta e)painw= *)a_ghsi/la_on I praise Agesilaus for such merits
X. Ages. 10.1, tou\s *korinqi/ous polla/ te kai<*> kaka\ e)/lege he said many bad things about the Corinthians
Hdt. 8.61. For the accusative of the thing, eu)= (kalw=s), kakw=s may be substituted; and ei)s and pro/s with the accusative occur.

The accusative of the person may depend on the idea expressed by the combination of verb and accusative of the thing (1612); as in

tou\s polemi/ous ei)rga/sqai kaka/ to have done harm to the enemy
L. 21.8 (here ei)rga/sqai of itself does not mean to do anything to a person).

When the dative of the person is used, something is done for (1474), not to him:

pa/nta e)poi/hsan toi=s a)poqanou=sin they rendered all honours to the dead
X. A. 4.2.23. ei)s or pro/s with the accusative is also employed.

Passive of 1622:

o(/sa a)/lla h( po/lis h)dikei=to all the other wrongs that the State has suffered
D. 18.70.

Verbs of dividing (ne/mein, katane/mein, diairei=n, te/mnein) may take two accusatives, one of the thing divided, the other of its parts (cognate accus.). Thus,

*ku=ros to\ stra/teuma kate/neime dw/deka me/rh Cyrus divided the army into twelve divisions
X. C. 7.5.13. ei)s or kata/ may be used with the accusative of the parts.

title: Cause or Goal
definition:
The accusative could express the cause as a neuter pronoun indicating a situation. Many of these pronouns are very idiomatic: τί; 'why?, wherefore?' τοῦτο, ταῦτα 'for this reason'. The difference with the accusative of goal is very small.
With χάριν for the sake of (lit. favour):

smyth.text:
Motive.—ti/ why? tou=to, tau=ta for this reason (cognate accus.): ti/ h)=lqes quid (cur) venisti = ti/na i(=cin h)=lqes; tou=to xai/rw ( = tau/thn th\n xara\_n xai/rw) therefore I rejoice,

au)ta\ tau=ta h(/kw for this very reason have I come
P. Pr. 310e,

tou=t' a)/xqesqe for this reason you are vexed
X. A. 3.2.20.

examples.translation: For these reasons I have left the gold-decorated palace.

examples.translation: Why was that? So that you could hear men who are the wisest at the moment.
for this very reason have I come
for this reason you are vexed
did not engage in the expedition out of good will to the Athenians
for what reason?
for thy sake I have come

title: Exclamations and direct address
definition:
The vocative is used in exclamations and in direct address:
In ordinary conversation and public speeches, the polite ὦ is usually added. Without ὦ the vocative may express astonishment, joy, contempt, a threat, or a warning, etc.:
But this distinction is not always observed, though in general ὦ has a familiar tone which was unsuited to elevated poetry.

smyth.text:
The vocative is used in exclamations and in direct address:

w)= *zeu= kai\ qeoi/ oh Zeus and ye gods
P. Pr. 310d,

a)/nqrwpe my good fellow
X. C. 2.2.7. The vocative forms an incomplete sentence (904 d).
a. The vocative is never followed immediately by de/ or ga/r.

In ordinary conversation and public speeches, the polite w)= is usually added. Without w)= the vocative may express astonishment, joy, contempt, a threat, or a warning, etc. Thus a)kou/eis *ai)sxi/nh; d'ye hear, Aeschines?
D. 18.121. But this distinction is not always observed, though in general w)= has a familiar tone which was unsuited to elevated poetry.

The vocative is usually found in the interior of a sentence. At the beginning it is emphatic. In prose e)/fh, in poetry w)=, may stand between the vocative and an attributive or between an attributive and the vocative; in poetry w)= may be repeated for emphasis.

In late poetry a predicate adjective may be attracted into the vocative: o)/lbie kw=re ge/noio blessed, oh boy, mayest thou be Theocr. 17. 66. Cp. Matutine pater seu Iane libentius audis Hor. S. 2. 6. 20.

By the omission of su/ or u(_mei=s the nominative with the article may stand in apposition to a vocative: w)= a)/ndoes oi( paro/ntes you, gentlemen, who are present
P. Pr. 337c,

w)= *ku=re kai\ oi( a)/lloi *pe/rsai Cyrus and the rest of you Persians
X. C. 3.3.20; and in apposition to the pronoun in the verb: o( pai=s, a)kolou/qei boy, attend me
Ar. Ran. 521.

The nominative may be used in exclamations as a predicate with the subject unexpressed:

w)= pikro\s qeoi=s oh loathed of heaven
S. Ph. 254,

fi/los w)= *mene/la_e ah dear Menelaus
*d 189; and connected with the vocative by and:

w)= po/lis kai\ dh=me oh city and people
Ar. Eq. 273. In exclamations about a person:

w)\ gennai=os oh the noble man
P. Phae. 227c.
a. ou(=tos is regular in address: ou(=tos, ti/ pa/sxeis, w)= *canqi/a_; ho there, I say, Xanthias, what is the matter with you?
Ar. Vesp. 1; w)= ou(=tos, *ai)/a_s ho there, I say, Ajax
S. Aj. 89.

title: Present of Continuity
definition: The present represents a present state, or an action going on at the moment of speaking. The action might have begun before the present time. The present tense has an imperfective aspect and therefore often indicates incomplete actions. It may also indicate immediate future, or likely and certain actions in the near future. In prophecies a future event may be regarded as present.

examples.translation: I am telling the truth
shall we break off in the middle?

I am on the verge of ruin

title: Customary Action (Iterative)
definition:
The present is used to express a customary or repeated action:
The present indicative may also indicate a general truth and could be used to express an action that is true for all time. The present is an *absolute* tense in such sentences. The future, aorist, and perfect may also express a general truth.

smyth.text:
Present of Customary Action.—The present is used to express a customary or repeated action:

ou(=tos me\n ga\r u(/dwr, e)gw\ d' oi)=non pi/_nw for this man drinks water, whereas I drink wine
D. 19.46.

Present of General Truth.—The present is used to express an action that is true for all time:

a)/gei de\ pro\s fw=s th\n a)lh/qeian xro/nos time brings the truth to light
Men. Sent. 11.
a. The present is an absolute tense in such sentences. The future, aorist, and perfect may also express a general truth.

examples.greek: οὗτος μὲν γὰρ ὕδωρ, ἐγὼ δ᾽ οἶνον πίνω
examples.translation: for this man drinks water, whereas I drink wine
two times five is ten

examples.greek: ἄγει δὲ πρὸς φῶς τὴν ἀλήθειαν χρόνος
examples.translation: time brings the truth to light

title: Conative Present
definition: The present may express an action begun, attempted, or intended. The idea of attempt or intention is an inference from the context and lies in the present only so far as the present does not denote completion.

smyth.text:
Conative Present.—The present may express an action begun, attempted, or intended.

th\n do/can tau/thn pei/qousin u(_ma=s a)pobalei=n they are trying to persuade you to throw away this renown
I. 6.12,

di/dwmi/ soi au)th\n tau/thn gunai=ka I offer you this woman herself as a wife
X. C. 8.5.19,

prodi/doton th\n *(ella/da they are trying to betray Greece
Ar. P. 408.
a. This use is found also in the infinitive and participle:

*fili/ppou e)pi\ *buza/ntion pario/ntos when Philip is preparing to advance against Byzantium
D. 8.66.
b. The idea of attempt or intention is an inference from the context and lies in the present only so far as the present does not denote completion.

examples.greek: τὴν δόξαν ταύτην πείθουσιν ὑμᾶς ἀποβαλεῖν
examples.translation: they are trying to persuade you to throw away this renown
I offer you this woman herself as a wife
they are trying to betray Greece

title: Historical Present
definition:
In lively or dramatic narration, the present is used to represent a past action as going on at the moment of speaking or writing. The historical present may represent either the descriptive imperfect or the narrative aorist. This use does not occur in Homer.
Closely connected with the historical present is the annalistic present, which is used to register historical facts or to note incidents.

smyth.text:
Historical Present.—In lively or dramatic narration the present may be used to represent a past action as going on at the moment of speaking or writing. This use does not occur in Homer.
o( de\ *qemistoklh=s feu/gei e)s *ke/rku_ran . . . diakomi/zetai e)s th\n h)/peiron Themistocles fled (flees) to Corcyra . . . was (is) transported to the mainland
T. 1.136.
a. The historical present may represent either the descriptive imperfect or the narrative aorist.
b. The historical present may be coördinated with past tenses, which may precede or follow it:

a(/ma de\ th=| h(me/ra| th=| po/lei prose/keito kai\ ai(rei= at daybreak he assaulted the town and took it
T. 7.29,

ou(/tw dh\ a)pogra/fontai pa/ntes a)ne/labo/n te ta\ o(/pla accordingly they all enrolled themselves and took the arms
X. C. 2.1.19.
c. The historical present is less frequent in subordinate clauses (
T. 2.91. 3).

Annalistic Present.—Closely connected with the historical present is the annalistic present, which is used to register historical facts or to note incidents.
*da_rei/ou kai\ *parusa/tidos gi/gnontai pai=des du/o of Darius and Parysatis were (are) born two sons
X. A. 1.1.1, pro\ *aeutuxi/dew ga\r (*zeuci/dhmos) teleuta=| . . . *aeutuxi/dhs game/ei *eu)ruda/mhn, e)k th=s oi( . . . gi/_netai quga/thr for Zeuxidemus died before Leutychides . . . L. married Eurydame, from her was born to him a daughter
Hdt. 6.71,

kai\ o( e)niauto\s e)/lhgen, e)n w(=| *karxhdo/nioi ai(rou=si du/o po/leis *(ellhni/das and the year came to an end in which the Carthaginians captured two Greek cities
X. H. 1.1.37.

examples.translation: Themistocles fled (flees) to Corcyra . . . was (is) transported to the mainland

examples.translation: of Darius and Parysatis were (are) born two sons

examples.translation: and the year came to an end in which the Carthaginians captured two Greek cities

title: Resultative and Perfective Present
definition:
The present of certain verbs often expresses an enduring result, and may be translated by the perfect: ἀδικῶ I am guilty (ἄδικός εἰμι), *I have done wrong*, νικῶ, κρατῶ, I am victorious, I have conquered, ἡττῶμαι I am conquered, φεύγω I am the defendant or I am an exile, προδίδωμι I am a traitor, ἁλίσκομαι I am captured, στέρομαι I am deprived, γίγνομαι I am a descendant.
The perfective present is common with verbs of hearing, saying, learning, whose action commenced in the past, but whose effect continues into the present. The present tense with telic verbs has a resultative meaning, such as ἥκω I am come, I have arrived, οἴχομαι I am gone, etc. The present may also indicate an action begun in the past and continued in the present. This use of present tense is accompanied by a definite or indefinite expression of past time.

examples.translation: I Themistocles have come to you
I know where they have gone
I have been long (and am still) wondering
from what I hear (have heard)
as I said

title: Non-indicative (Imperfective Aspect)
definition:
The tenses of the moods other than the indicative rarely have relative temporal value, however, they express the grammatical aspect of the verb. The aspect of a verb indicates how an action extends over time and the way it is presented. For instance, It may present an action as a complete whole, or an incomplete, ongoing process. The present stem has an imperfective aspect, generally expressing actions as ongoing or repeated.
With subjunctive:
With optative:
With Imperative, implying continuance:
With Participles: The present participle denotes that an action is in process, is attempted, or is repeated. The action is generally coincident (rarely antecedent or subsequent) to that of the leading verb.
With infinitives:

smyth.text: The tenses of the moods except the indicative do not express time in independent sentences.

Subjunctive.—The subjunctive mood as such refers to the future. The tenses do not refer to differences of time, and denote only the stage of the action (continuance, simple occurrence, completion with permanent result).
Present (continuance):

ta\ au(tw=n a(/ma e)kporizw/meqa let us at the same time keep developing our resources
T. 1.82; Aorist (simple occurrence):

porisw/meqa ou)=n prw=ton th\n dapa/nhn let us procure the money first
T. 1.83; Perfect (completion with permanent result): i(/na, h)\n mh\ u(pakou/wsi, teqnh/kwsin that, in case they do not submit, they may be put to death (lit. may be dead at once)
T. 8.74. The aorist commonly replaces the more exact perfect because the perfect is rarely used.
a. The future time denoted by present or aorist (ti/ poiw=men; or ti/ poih/swmen; what shall we do?) may refer, according to the sense, either to the next moment or to some later time. Greek has no subjunctive form denoting an intention to do this or that. In dependent constructions (including general conditions) the action of the present is generally coincident (rarely subsequent), that of the aorist is generally anterior (rarely coincident), to the action of the leading verb:

xalepai/nousi, e)peida\n au)toi=s paragge/llw pi/_nein to\ fa/rmakon they are angry whenever I bid them drink the poison
P. Ph. 116c, e)peida\n a(/pant' a)kou/shte, kri/_nate when you (shall) have heard everything, decide
D. 4.14. The use of the aorist of time relatively anterior to the action of the leading verb ( = Lat. future perfect) is, like its other references to relative time, only an inference from the connection of the thought (1850 a).
b. Present and aorist subjunctive are occasionally used in the same sentence without any great difference in sense (
X. C. 1.2.6-7, 5. 5. 13).
c. An independent or dependent subjunctive may be ingressive (1924): h)\n ga\r o( *plou=tos nuni\ ble/yh| for if now Plutus recovers his sight Ar. Pl. 494.
d. In general conditions (2336) the subjunctive refers to general time, denoting what holds true now and at all times.

Optative (not in indirect discourse).—The reference is always to future time. The tenses do not refer to differences of time, and denote only the stage of the action.
Present (continuance): plou/sion de\ nomi/zoimi to\n sofo/n may I (always) count the wise man wealthy
P. Phae. 279b; Aorist (simple occurrence):

ei) ga\r ge/noito would that it might happen
X. C. 6.1.38; Perfect (completion with permanent result): teqnai/hs die (lit. may you be dead)
*z 164.
a. In general conditions (2336) the optative is used of past time.
b. In dependent constructions (including general conditions) the action of the present is generally coincident (rarely anterior), that of the aorist generally anterior (rarely coincident), to the action of the leading verb: ei)/ tis ta/de parabai/noi, e)nagh\s e)/stw tou=) *apo/llwnos if any one violates this, let him be accurst of Apollo
Aes. 3.110, e)peidh\ de\ a)noixqei/h (to\ desmwth/rion), ei)sh=|men para\ to\n *swkra/th whenever the prison was opened, we (always) went in to Socrates
P. Ph. 59d. The aorist is often preferred to the more exact perfect because the perfect was rarely used.
c. An independent or dependent optative may be ingressive (1924): ei) polemh/saimen di' *)wrwpo/n, ou)de\n a)\n h(ma=s paqei=n h(gou=mai if we should enter upon a war on account of Oropus, I think we should suffer nothing
D. 5.16.

Optative (in indirect discourse).—When the optative in indirect discourse represents the indicative after a past tense of a verb of saying or thinking, each tense does denote time (as well as stage of action) relatively to that of the leading verb.
a. The present optative represents the imperfect as well as the present indicative.
b. The future optative (first in Pindar) occurs only in indirect discourse after verbs of saying and thinking, in object clauses after o(/pws, 2212, and in other indirect expressions of thought.
c. When the optative in indirect discourse represents the subjunctive (2619 b), its tenses denote only stage of action.

a. Present opt. = present indic.: a)nhrw/ta_ ti/ bou/lointo he demanded what they wanted ( = ti/ bou/lesqe;)
X. A. 2.3.4.
b. Present opt. = imperf. indic.: dihgou=nto o(/ti e)pi\ tou\s polemi/ous ple/oien they explained that they kept sailing against the enemy ( = e)ple/omen)
X. H. 1.7.5.
c. Future opt. = future indic.: o(/ ti poih/soi ou)de\ tou/tois ei)=pe he did not tell even these what he would do ( = poih/sw)
X. A. 2.2.2.
d. Aorist opt. = aorist indic.: h)rw/ta_ ti/ pa/qoien he asked what had happened to them ( = ti/ e)pa/qete;)
X. C. 2.3.19.
e. Perfect opt. = perfect indic.: e)/legon o(/ti oi( meta\ *dhmosqe/nous paradedw/koien sfa=s au)tou/s they said that the troops of Demosthenes had surrendered ( = paradedw/ka_si)
T. 7.83.

Imperative.—The imperative always implies future time. The tenses do not refer to differences of time, and denote only the stage of the action.
a. Present (continuance):

tou\s gonei=s ti(_ma_ honour thy parents
I. 1.16, pa/nta ta)_lhqh= le/ge tell (go on and tell in detail) the whole truth
L. 1.18,

tou\s i(/ppous e)kei/nois di/dote offer the horses to them
X. C. 4.5.47.
b. Aorist (simple occurrence): ble/yon pro\s ta\ o)/rh look (cast a glance) toward the mountains
X. A. 4.1.20, ei)pe/ state (in a word)
P. A. 24d,

h(mi=n tou\s i(/ppous do/te give the horses to us
X. C. 4.5.47.
c. Perfect (completion with permanent result): teta/xqw let him take his place (and stay there)
P. R. 562a, ei)rh/sqw let it have been said (once for all) 503 b.
N.—The perfect active and middle are generally used as presents (

teqna/tw let him be put to death
P. L. 938c,

me/mnhsqe remember
D. 40.30). The perfect passive (in the third person) is used of a fixed decision concerning what is to be done or has been done.

Infinitive (not in indirect discourse).—The tenses of the infinitive (without a)/n) not in indirect discourse have no time of themselves and express only the stage of the action; their (relative) time depends on the context and is that of the leading verb (present, past, or future). The infinitive may have the article (2025 ff.).
a. Present (continuance):

ou)de\ bouleu/esqai e)/ti w(/ra_, a)lla\ bebouleu=sqai it is time no longer to be making up one's mind, but to have it made up
P. Cr. 46a.
b. Aorist (simple occurrence):

tou= piei=n e)piqu_mi/a_ the desire of obtaining drink
T. 7.84, h)/rcato gene/sqai began to be 1. 103, but h)/rxeto gi/gnesqai 3. 18 (the tense of gi/gnomai depends on that of a)/rxomai; not h)/rcato gi/gnesqai), dei= tou\s u(pe\r au)tou= le/gontas mi_sh=sai (ingressive) one must conceive an aversion for those who speak in his behalf
D. 9.53.
c. Perfect (completion with permanent result): see a. Often of certainty of action.
d. Future.—When the context shows that stress is laid on the idea of futurity, the future infinitive, referring to future time relative to the main verb, is sometimes used instead of the present or aorist:

ou)k a)pokwlu/_sein dunatoi\ o)/ntes not being able to prevent
T. 3.28,

pollou= de/w kat' e)mautou= e)rei=n I am far from intending to speak to my own disadvantage
P. A. 37b. On the future infinitive with me/llw see 1959.
N. 1.—The action set forth by a dependent present or aorist infinitive (without a)/n) not in indirect discourse has no time except that which is implied by the context. With verbs signifying to advise or to command, and when the infinitive expresses purpose, the reference is to future time. Usually the action of the present and aorist is coincident with or antecedent to that of the main verb. The action of an aorist infinitive with the article and a subject is not always relatively past. The perfect (without a)/n) has no time apart from the context; its action is usually antecedent.
N. 2.—On the use of the present and aorist with verbs of promising, etc., see 1868; with me/llw, see 1959.
N. 3.—Observe that verbs denoting continuance (as me/nw remain) often appear in the aorist, while verbs of transitory action (as i(_e/nai send, hurl) often appear in the present.
N. 4.—Present and aorist occasionally occur in close conjunction without any great difference in meaning, as

prosh/kei u(_mi=n tou/tou katayhfi/zesqai . . ., dei= u(_ma=s qa/naton au)tou= katayhfi/sasqai it is fitting that you vote ag

Infinitive (in indirect discourse).—The tenses of the infinitive in indirect discourse denote the same time relative to that of the leading verb (present, past, or future) as was denoted by the corresponding tenses of the indicative in direct discourse which they represent.
a. The present infinitive represents also the imperfect, the perfect infinitive represents also the pluperfect indicative.
b. The action of the present is usually coincident, that of the aorist anterior, to the action of the leading verb.
c. The future infinitive is found chiefly in indirect discourse and in analogous constructions. With me/llw, see 1959. It may have the article (2026).

Participle (not in indirect discourse).—The participle, as a verbal adjective, is timeless. The tenses of the participle express only continuance, simple occurrence, and completion with permanent result. Whether the action expressed by the participle is antecedent, coincident, or subsequent to that of the leading verb (in any tense) depends on the context. The future participle has a temporal force only because its voluntative force points to the future.
a. Present (continuative). The action set forth by the present participle is generally coincident (rarely antecedent or subsequent) to that of the leading verb:

e)rgazo/menai me\n h)ri/stwn, e)rgasa/menai de\ e)dei/pnoun the women took their noonday meal while they continued their work, but took their supper when they had stopped work
X. M. 2.7.12.
1. Antecedent action ( = imperf.):

oi( *ku/_reioi pro/sqen su\n h(mi=n tatto/menoi nu=n a)festh/ka_sin the forces of Cyrus that were formerly marshalled with us have now deserted
X. A. 3.2.17,

tou\s to/te paro/ntas ai)tia/_sontai sumbou/lous they will accuse those who were their counsellors at that time
P. G. 519a, oi( *kori/nqioi me/xri tou/tou proqu/_mws pra/_ssontes a)nei=san th=s filoneiki/a_s the Corinthians, who up to that time had been acting zealously, now slackened in their vehemence
T. 5.32. An adverb (pro/teron, pro/sqen, to/te, pote/) often accompanies the participle, which is sometimes called the participle of the imperfect.
2. Subsequent action (especially when the leading verb denotes motion): e)/pemyan pre/sbeis a)gge/llontas th\n tou= *plhmuri/ou lh=yin they despatched messengers to announce the capture of Plemyrium
T. 7.25. An attributive present part. w. nu=n may refer to the absolute present, though the main verb is past:

th\n nu=n *boiwti/a_n kaloume/nhn w)/|khsan they settled in the country now called Boeotia
T. 1.12.
3. The present participle denotes that an action is in process, is attempted, or is repeated.
b. Future (chiefly voluntative):

ou) sunh/lqomen w(s basilei= polemh/sontes we have not come together for the purpose of waging war with the king
X. A. 2.3.21.
c. Aorist (simple occurrence). The action set forth by the aorist participle is generally antecedent to that of the leading verb; but it is sometimes coincident or nearly so, when it defines, or is identical with, that of the leading verb, and the subordinate action is only a modification of the main action.
1. Antecedent:

deipnh/sa_s e)xw/rei after supper he advanced
T.

may I (always) count the wise man wealthy
honour thy parents

offer the horses to them

examples.greek: οἱ Κορίνθιοι μέχρι τούτου προθύμως πράσσοντες ἀνεῖσαν τῆς φιλονεικίας
examples.translation: the Corinthians, who up to that time had been acting zealously, now slackened in their vehemence
