examples.translation: it is time no longer to be making up one's mind, but to have it made up

title: Imperfect of Continuance
definition:
The imperfect represents an action as ongoing in the past.
The imperfect of verbs of sending, going, saying, exhorting, etc., which imply continuous action, is often used where one might expect the aorist of concluded action. Thus, in ἔπεμπον, the action is regarded as unfinished since the goal is not reached.
With a negative, the imperfect often denotes resistance or refusal (would not or could not), while the negative aorist denotes unrestricted denial of a fact.

smyth.text:
Imperfect of Continuance.—The imperfect thus represents an action as continuing in the past: die/fqeiran *)aqhnai/wn pi/nte kai\ ei)/kosi, oi(\ cunepoliorkou=nto they put to death twenty-five of the Athenians who were besieged (i.e. from the beginning to the end of the siege)
T. 3.68.

The imperfect of verbs of sending, going, saying, exhorting, etc., which imply continuous action, is often used where we might expect the aorist of concluded action. Thus, in e)/pempon, the action is regarded as unfinished since the goal is not reached:

a)/ggelon e)/pempon kai\ tou\s nekrou\s u(pospo/ndous a)pe/dosan they sent a messenger and surrendered the dead under a truce
T. 2.6. In e)ke/leuon gave orders, urged, requested the command, etc., is regarded as not yet executed. In

e)/legen au)toi=s toia/de he spoke to them as follows
X. H. 1.6.4 (followed by the speech and e)pei\ de\ tau=t' ei)=pen 1. 6. 12) the speech is not thought of as a finished whole, but as developed point by point, as in e)pe)idh\ de\ ou(=tos tau=ta e)/legen, e)/leca but when he had said this, I said
Ant. 6.21.
a. In messenger's speeches the speaker may go back to the time of receiving a command:

i)e/nai s' e)ke/leuon oi( strathgoi\ th/meron the generals order you to depart to-day
Ar. Ach. 1073.

The imperfect, when accompanied by an expression of past time, is used of actions which had been in progress for some time and were still in progress (cp. 1885):

to\ *(ph/gion e)pi\ polu\n xro/non e)stasi/aze Rhegium had been for a long time in a state of faction
T. 4.1. If the action is regarded as completed the pluperfect is used.

Imperfect of Resistance or Refusal.—With a negative, the imperfect often denotes resistance or refusal (would not or could not). The aorist with a negative denotes unrestricted denial of a fact.

th\n pro/klhsin ou)k e)de/xesqe you would not accept the proposal
T. 3.64 (th\n i(ketei/a_n ou)k e)de/canto they did not receive the supplication 1. 24),

o( me\n ou)k e)ga/mei, o( de\ e)/ghmen the one would not marry, the other did
D. 44.17,

ou)de\ fwnh\n h)/kouon, ei)/ tis a)/llo ti bou/loito le/gein they would not even listen to a syllable if ever any one wished to say anything to the contrary
D. 18.43. So ou)k ei)/a_ he would not allow (he was not for allowing).

If simple positive and negative are contrasted, the aorist is preferred with the latter: ta\ u(pa/rxonta/ te sw/|zein (positive with present) kai\ e)pignw=nai mhde/n (negative with aorist) to preserve what you have, and to form no new plans
T. 1.70. But where the verb itself contains or implies a negative idea, the present is used:

parei=nai kai\ mh\ a)podhmei=n to be present and not to be abroad
Aes. 2.59.

examples.greek: διέφθειραν Ἀθηναίων πέντε καὶ εἴκοσι, οἳ ξυνεπολιορκοῦντο
examples.translation: they put to death twenty-five of the Athenians who were besieged (i.e. from the beginning to the end of the siege)
Antiochus was reigning

examples.greek: ἄγγελον ἔπεμπον καὶ τοὺς νεκροὺς ὑποσπόνδους ἀπέδοσαν
examples.translation: they sent a messenger and surrendered the dead under a truce
you would not accept the proposal (compare to: τὴν ἱκετείαν οὐκ ἐδέξαντο **T.1. 24**; ⇾ they did not receive the supplication)

examples.greek: ὁ μὲν οὐκ ἐγάμει, ὁ δὲ ἔγημεν
examples.translation: the one would not marry, the other did

examples.greek: οὐδὲ φωνὴν ἤκουον, εἴ τις ἄλλο τι βούλοιτο λέγειν
examples.translation: they would not even listen to a syllable if ever any one wished to say anything to the contrary

title: Customary Action (Iterative)
definition: The imperfect is used to express frequently repeated or customary past actions. ἄν may be used with this imperfect to express the repetition emphatically. Homer and Herodotus have iterative imperfects and aorists stems in \-σκον and \-σκομην denoting a customary or repeated past action.

examples.greek: ἐπεὶ εἶδον αὐτὸν οἵπερ πρόσθεν προσεκύνουν, καὶ τότε προσεκύνησαν
examples.translation: when they caught sight of him, the very men who before this were wont to prostrate themselves before him, prostrated themselves on this occasion also

examples.greek: (Σωκράτης) τοὺς ἑαυτοῦ ἐπιθυμοῦντας οὐκ ἐπράττετο χρήματα
examples.translation: Socrates was not in the habit of demanding money from those who were passionately attached to him

examples.greek: ἐπεθύμει ἄν τις ἔτι πλείω αὐτοῦ ἀκούειν
examples.translation: people would (used to) desire to hear still more from him
I used to ask

title: Conative Imperfect
definition: The imperfect may express an action attempted, intended, or expected in the past that eventually did not occur. The conative imperfect is used with telic verbs.

smyth.text:
Conative Imperfect.—The imperfect may express an action attempted, intended, or expected, in the past.
e)/peiqon au)tou/s, kai\ ou(\s e)/peisa, tou/tous e)/xwn e)poreuo/mhn I tried to persuade them, and I marched away with those whom I succeeded in persuading
X. C. 5.5.22, *(alo/nnhson e)di/dou: o( d' a)phgo/reue mh\ lamba/nein Philip offered (proposed to give) Halonnesus, but he (Demosthenes) dissuaded them from accepting it
Aes. 3.83,

*qhbai=oi katedoulou=nt' au)tou/s the Thebans tried to enslave them
D. 8.74,

h)pei/gonto e)s th\n *ke/rku_ran they were for pushing on to Corcyra
T. 4.3.
a. Here may be placed the imperfect equivalent in sense to e)/mellon with the infinitive. Thus, foneu\s ou)=n au)tw=n e)gigno/mhn e)gw\ mh\ ei)pw\n u(_ui=n a(\ h)/kousa. e)/ti de\ tria_kosi/ous *)aqhnai/wn a)pw/lluon I was on the point of becoming their murderer (interfecturus eram) had I not told you what I heard. And besides I threatened three hundred Athenians with death
And. 1.58. So a)pwllu/mhn I was threatened with death.

examples.greek: ἔπειθον αὐτούς, καὶ οὓς ἔπεισα, τούτους ἔχων ἐπορευόμην
examples.translation: I tried to persuade them, and I marched away with those whom I succeeded in persuading

examples.greek: Ἁλόννησον ἐδίδου: ὁ δ᾽ ἀπηγόρευε μὴ λαμβάνειν
examples.translation: Philip *offered* (proposed to give) *Halonnesus*, *but he* (Demosthenes) *dissuaded* them from accepting it
the Thebans tried to enslave them
they were for pushing on to Corcyra

title: Imperfect of Completed Action
definition: The imperfect with telic verbs[^59] draws attention toward the consequences of the action, while the present of these verbs suggests that the action is not completed yet. Thus, ἧκον I had come (rarely I came), ᾠχόμην I had departed, as ἐνίκων I was victorious, ἡττώμην I was defeated.

smyth.text:
Imperfect for Pluperfect.—The imperfect has the force of the pluperfect in the case of verbs whose present is used in the sense of the perfect (1886).
Thus, h(=kon I had come (rarely I came), w)|xo/mhn I had departed, as e)ni/_kwn I was victorious, h(ttw/mhn I was defeated (1752). So (*)olu/mpia) oi(=s *)androsqe/nhs pagkra/tion e)ni/_ka_ the Olympic games, at which Androsthenes was the victor (= had won) in the pancratium
T. 5.49.

examples.greek: ὃ μὲν δή σφι τὰ ἐντεταλμένα ἀπήγγελλε, τοῖσι δὲ ἕαδε μὲν βοηθέειν Ἀθηναίοισι ...
examples.translation: He delivered the message he had been ordered to say, and they resolved to send help to the Athenians
the Olympic games, at which Androsthenes was the victor (= had won) in the pancratium

examples.greek: τὸ πλοῖον ἧκεν, ἐν ᾧ ἐπλέομεν
examples.translation: the vessel arrived in which we (had) sailed

title: Imperfect of Description
definition:
The imperfect can explain the background circumstances under which an action has taken place. It describes manners and customs; the situation, circumstances, and details of events; and the development of actions represented as continuing in past time. The imperfect often has a dramatic or panoramic force: it enables the reader to follow the course of events as they occurred, as if he were a spectator of the scene depicted.
In descriptions of places and scenery and in other statements of existing facts the imperfect is often used by assimilation to the time of the narrative (usually set forth in the main verb).
The imperfect may refer to a topic previously discussed. This is called the *philosophical imperfect*:

smyth.text:
Imperfect of Description.—The imperfect describes manners and customs; the situation, circumstances, and details, of events; and the development of actions represented as continuing in past time.
e)kei=no/s te tou\s u(f' e(autw=| w(/sper e(autou= pai=das e)ti/_ma_, oi(/ te a)rxo/menoi *ku=ron w(s pate/ra e)se/bonto he (Cyrus) treated his subjects with honour as if they were his own children, and his subjects reverenced Cyrus like a father
X. C. 8.8.2, eu)qu\s a)nebo/hsa/n te pa/ntes kai\ prospeso/ntes e)ma/xonto, e)w/qoun, e)wqou=nto, e)/paion, e)pai/onto immediately all raised a shout and falling upon each other fought, pushed and were pushed, struck and were struck 7. 1. 38, e)pei\ de\ tau=ta e)rrh/qh, e)poreu/onto: tw=n de\ a)pantw/ntwn oi( me\n a)pe/qnh|skon, oi( de\ e)/feugon pa/lin ei)/sw, oi( de\ e)bo/wn and when these words had been spoken, they proceeded to advance; and of those who met them some were killed, others fled back indoors, and others shouted 7. 5. 26,

e)strath/gei de\ au)tw=n *)aristeu/s Aristeus was their commander
T. 1.60; cp.
X. C. 4.2.28, X. Ag. 2. 12,
X. A. 4.3.8-25, Isocr. 1. 9, 7. 51-53,
D. 18.169 ff.,
Aes. 3.192.
N.—The imperfect often has a dramatic or panoramic force: it enables the reader to follow the course of events as they occurred, as if he were a spectator of the scene depicted.

The imperfect is thus often used to explain, illustrate, offer reasons for an action, and to set forth accompanying and subordinate circumstances that explain or show the result of the main action. Descriptive adverbs are often used with the imperfect.
e)ntau=qa e)/meinen h(me/ra_s pe/nte: kai\ toi=s stratiw/tais w)fei/leto misqo\s ple/on h)\ triw=n mhnw=n, kai\ polla/kis i)o/ntes e)pi\ ta\_s qu/ra_s a)ph/|toun: o( de\ e)lpi/das le/gwn dih=ge kai\ dh=los h)=n a)niw/menos there he remained for five days; and the soldiers whose pay was in arrears for more than three months kept going to headquarters and demanding their dues; but he kept expressing his expectation (of making payment) and was plainly annoyed
X. A. 1.2.11. See also 1907 a.

Inchoative Imperfect.—The imperfect may denote the beginning of an action or of a series of actions: e)peidh\ de\ kairo\s h)=n, prose/ballon but when the proper time arrived, they began an (proceeded to) attack
T. 7.51.

Imperfect for Present.—In descriptions of places and scenery and in other statements of existing facts the imperfect, instead of the present, is often used by assimilation to the time of the narrative (usually set forth in the main verb).

a)fi/_konto e)pi\ to
 potamo
 o(\s w(/rize th
 tw=n *makrw/nwn xw/ra_n kai\ th
 tw=n *skuqhnw=n they came to the river which divided the country of the Macrones from that of the Scytheni
X. A. 4.8.1, e)celau/nei e)pi\ potamo
 plh/rh i)xqu/wn, ou(\s oi( *su/roi qeou\s e)no/mizon he marched to a river full of fish, which the Syrians regarded as gods 1. 4. 9.

—Imperfect of a Truth Just Recognized.—The imperfect, usually some form of ei)=nai, with a)/ra, is often used to denote that a present fact or truth has just been recognized, although true before: ou)de\n a)/r' h)=n pra=gma it is, as it appears, no matter after all
P. S. 198e,

tou=t' a)/r' h)=n a)lhqe/s this is true after all
E. I. T. 351,

a)/ra h)pi/stw you know, sure enough
X. H. 3.4.9. a)/ra sure enough, after all appears with other tenses (
P. Cr. 49a,
P. Ph. 61a,
D. 19.160).

The imperfect may refer to a topic previously discussed: h)=n h( mousikh\ a)nti/strofos th=s gumnastikh=s ei) me/mnhsai music is (as we have seen) the counterpart of gymnastics, if you remember the discussion
P. R. 522a. This is called the philosophical imperfect.
The epistolary imperfect is rare in Greek. See 1942 b.

e)/dei, e)xrh=n.—The imperfect of verbs expressing obligation or duty may refer to present time and imply that the obligation or duty is not fulfilled:

si_gh/sa_s h(ni/k' e)/dei le/gein keeping silence when he ought to speak
D. 18.189. So with e)xrh=n it were proper, ei)ko\s h)=n it were fitting (1774). But the imperfect may also express past obligation without denying the action of the infinitive, as e)/dei me/nein he was obliged to remain (and did remain)
D. 19.124, o(/per e)/dei dei=cai quod erat demonstrandum Euclid 1. 5 (1779).

examples.greek: εὐθὺς ἀνεβόησάν τε πάντες καὶ προσπεσόντες ἐμάχοντο, ἐώθουν, ἐωθοῦντο, ἔπαιον, ἐπαίοντο
examples.translation: immediately all raised a shout and falling upon each other fought, pushed and were pushed, struck and were struck

examples.greek: ἐπεὶ δὲ ταῦτα ἐρρήθη, ἐπορεύοντο: τῶν δὲ ἀπαντώντων οἱ μὲν ἀπέθνῃσκον, οἱ δὲ ἔφευγον πάλιν εἴσω, οἱ δὲ ἐβόων
examples.translation: and when these words had been spoken, they proceeded to advance; and of those who met them some were killed, others fled back indoors, and others shouted

examples.greek: ἀφίκοντο ἐπὶ τὸν ποταμὸν ὃς ὥριζε τὴν τῶν Μακρώνων χώραν καὶ τὴν τῶν Σκυθηνῶν
examples.translation: they came to the river which divided the country of the Macrones from that of the Scytheni

examples.greek: ἐξελαύνει ἐπὶ ποταμὸν πλήρη ἰχθύων, οὓς οἱ Σύροι θεοὺς ἐνόμιζον
examples.translation: he marched to a river full of fish, which the Syrians regarded as gods

examples.greek: ἦν ἡ μουσικὴ ἀντίστροφος τῆς γυμναστικῆς εἰ μέμνησαι
examples.translation: music is (as we have seen) the counterpart of gymnastics, if you remember the discussion

title: Imperfect of Consecutive Action
definition:
The imperfect may refer to an action that immediately follows another action. This use of imperfect is sometimes referred to as inchoative or inceptive imperfect; however, this use of imperfect does not exactly refer the beginning point of an action , but it expressses the action in process.
→ “ὡς δὲ πορευομένων ἐξεκύμαινέ τι τῆς φάλαγγος, τὸ ὑπολειπόμενον ἤρξατο δρόμῳ θεῖν: καὶ ἅμα ἐφθέγξαντο πάντες οἷον τῷ Ἐνυαλίῳ ἐλελίζουσι, καὶ πάντες δὲ **ἔθεον**” **X. A. 1.8.18**; ⇾ And when, as they proceeded, a part of the phalanx billowed out, those who were thus left behind began to run; at the same moment they all set up the sort of war-cry which they raise to Enyalius, and next, they were all running.

smyth.text:
Inchoative Imperfect.—The imperfect may denote the beginning of an action or of a series of actions: e)peidh\ de\ kairo\s h)=n, prose/ballon but when the proper time arrived, they began an (proceeded to) attack
T. 7.51.

examples.translation: but when the proper time arrived, they began an (proceeded to) attack

title: Future Events or Expectations
definition: The future denotes an action that will take place at some future time. The future tense indicates that according to the opinion, expectation, hope, fear, or purpose of the speaker or the agent, the action would happen in the future. Depending on the context, the action of the future could be both continuative (like the present) or, similar to the aorist, express simple attainment. For instance, πείσω means I shall try to persuade, or I shall convince (resultative), βασιλεύσω I shall be king, shall reign or I shall become king (ingressive).

examples.translation: he shall receive a talent as his reward

examples.greek: Θηβαῖοι ἔχουσι μὲν ἀπεχθῶς, ἔτι δ᾽ ἐχθροτέρως σχήσουσιν
examples.translation: the Thebans are hostile and will become still more so

title: Hypothesis or General Truth
definition:
The future may be used to express an action possible in the moment of speaking, hypothetical scenarios, inferences, or present intention. In this sense, instead of indicating that the action would happen in the actual future, the future tense implies that the statement could be verified in the future.
The future may indicate a general truth (also known as gnomic future).
The future tense in commonly used in deliberative questions:

smyth.text:
Gnomic Future.—The future may express a general truth: a)nh\r e)pieikh\s ui(o\n a)pole/sa_s r(a=|sta oi)/sei tw=n a)/llwn a reasonable man, if he loses a son, will (is expected to) bear it more easily than other men
P. R. 603e (cp. 1434).
a. Hdt. uses the future in descriptions of customs and in directions to travellers (1. 173, 2. 29).

Future for Present.—The future may be used instead of the present of that which is possible at the moment of speaking:

eu(rh/somen tou\s filoti/_mous tw=n a)ndrw=n . . . a)nti\ tou= zh=n a)poqnh/|skein eu)klew=s ai(roume/nous we shall find that ambitious men choose a glorious death in preference to life
I. 9.3.
a. The future may denote present intention:

ai)=re plh=ktron, ei) maxei= raise your spur if you mean to fight
Ar. Av. 759 (in this use me/llw is more common (1959)). So in the tragic ti/ le/ceis; what do you mean?
E. Med. 1310.

Deliberative Future.—The future is often used in deliberative questions: ti/ e)rou=men h)\ ti/ fh/somen; what shall we say or what shall we propose?
D. 8.37.
a. The deliberative future may occur in connection with the deliberative subjunctive (1805): ei)/pwmen h)\ si_gw=men; h)\ ti/ dra/_somen; shall we speak or keep silent? or what shall we do?
E. Ion 758.

examples.greek: εὑρήσομεν τοὺς φιλοτίμους τῶν ἀνδρῶν . . . ἀντὶ τοῦ ζῆν ἀποθνῄσκειν εὐκλεῶς αἱρουμένους
examples.translation: we shall find that ambitious men choose a glorious death in preference to life
raise your spur if you mean to fight
what do you mean?

examples.greek: “ἀνὴρ ἐπιεικὴς υἱὸν ἀπολέσας ῥᾷστα **οἴσει** τῶν ἄλλων **P. R. 603e**; ⇾ a reasonable man, if he loses a son, will (is expected to) bear it more easily than other men
examples.translation: a reasonable man, if he loses a son, will (is expected to) bear it more easily than other men

examples.greek: “τί **ἐροῦμεν** ἢ τί **φήσομεν**; **D. 8.37**; ⇾ what shall we say or what shall we propose?
examples.translation: what shall we say or what shall we propose?

title: Jussive Future
definition: The future in the second person may function similar to the imperative, and express an urgent command, prohibition, concession or permission. The tone of the jussive future is generally familiar. In combination with οὐ μή , it indicates urgent prohibition. This use of the future tense is post-homeric.

smyth.text:
Jussive Future.—The future may express a command, like the imperative; and, in the second person, may denote concession or permission. The negative is ou). The tone of the jussive future (which is post-Homeric) is generally familiar.

w(\s ou)=n poih/sete you will do thus
P. Pr. 338a, a)nagnw/setai to\n no/mon—a)nagi/gnwske the clerk will read the law—read
D. 24.39,

au)to\s gnw/sei you will judge for yourself
P. Phil. 12a,

spoudh\ e)/stai th=s o(dou= you will have to hurry on the march
T. 7.77, u(_mei=s ou)=n, e)a\_n swfronh=te, ou) tou/tou a)ll' u(_mw=n fei/sesqe now, if you are wise, you will spare, not him, but yourselves
X. H. 2.3.34.

The future with ou) interrogative is used in questions in an imperative sense to express urgency, warning, or irony: ou)k e)/cimen . . . ou)k e)pi\ th\n e)kei/nou pleuso/meqa; shall we not go forth . . . shall we not set sail against his country?
D. 4.44, ou) fula/cesqe; will you not be on your guard? 6. 25. In exhortations addressed to oneself: ou)k a)pallaxqh/somai qu_mou=; shall I not cease from my passion?
E. Med. 878.
a. mh/ with the future in a prohibitive sense is used in a few suspected passages (
L. 29.13,
D. 23.117).

ou) mh/ with the second person singular of the future in the dramatic poets denotes a strong prohibition; as ou) mh\ diatri/_yeis don't dawdle (you shall not dawdle)
Ar. Ran. 462. ou) mh/ with any person of the future indicative occasionally denotes an emphatic future denial; as

tou\s ponhrou\s ou) mh/ pote belti/_ous poih/sete you will never make the bad better
Aes. 3.177.

o(/pws and o(/pws mh/ are used with the future in urgent exhortations and prohibitions:

o(/pws ou)=n e)/sesqe a)/cioi th=s e)leuqeri/a_s prove yourselves then worthy of freedom
X. A. 1.7.3,

o(/pws toi/nun peri\ tou= pole/mou mhde\n e)rei=s say nothing therefore about the war
D. 19.92. For the fuller form of this use after sko/pei, skopei=te. see 2213.

o(/pws mh/ (negative o(/pws mh\ ou)) may express the desire to avert something; as o(/pws mh\ ai)sxroi\ fainou/meqa mind we don't appear base
X. C. 4.2.39, a)ll' o(/pws mh\ ou)x oi(=o/s t' e)/somai but (I fear that) I shall not be able
P. R. 506d. Cp. 1802, 1803, 2229.

On a)/n (ke/) with the future indicative, see 1793. On the periphrastic future see 1959; on the future in dependent clauses, see 2203, 2211, 2220 a, 2229, 2231, 2328, 2549-2551, 2554, 2558, 2559, 2565 a, 2573 c.

## AORIST INDICATIVE

examples.translation: you will do thus
the clerk will read the law—read
you will judge for yourself
you will have to hurry on the march

examples.greek: “ὑμεῖς οὖν, ἐὰν σωφρονῆτε, οὐ τούτου ἀλλ᾽ ὑμῶν **φείσεσθε** **X. H. 2.3.34**; ⇾ now, if you are wise, you will spare, not him, but yourselves
examples.translation: now, if you are wise, you will spare, not him, but yourselves

title: Non-indicative
definition:
The tenses of the moods other than the indicative rarely have relative temporal value, however, they express the grammatical aspect of the verb. The aspect of a verb indicates the way an action extends over time and the way it is presented. For instance, It may present an action as a complete whole, or an incomplete, ongoing process. The future stem does not have an aspectual value, meaning that it is neutral and makes no distinction between completed or imperfect actions. The future participle refers to an action posterior to the main verb.
With participles: The future participle is often voluntative and expresses purpose. In combination with ὡς, it indicates the intention of the subject.
The verb ἔρχομαι with future participle is idiomatic, and often translates to “about to” or “going to”.
With infinitives: When the context shows that stress is laid on the idea of futurity, the future infinitive, referring to future time relative to the main verb, is sometimes used instead of the present or aorist.

smyth.text: The tenses of the moods except the indicative do not express time in independent sentences.

Subjunctive.—The subjunctive mood as such refers to the future. The tenses do not refer to differences of time, and denote only the stage of the action (continuance, simple occurrence, completion with permanent result).
Present (continuance):

ta\ au(tw=n a(/ma e)kporizw/meqa let us at the same time keep developing our resources
T. 1.82; Aorist (simple occurrence):

porisw/meqa ou)=n prw=ton th\n dapa/nhn let us procure the money first
T. 1.83; Perfect (completion with permanent result): i(/na, h)\n mh\ u(pakou/wsi, teqnh/kwsin that, in case they do not submit, they may be put to death (lit. may be dead at once)
T. 8.74. The aorist commonly replaces the more exact perfect because the perfect is rarely used.
a. The future time denoted by present or aorist (ti/ poiw=men; or ti/ poih/swmen; what shall we do?) may refer, according to the sense, either to the next moment or to some later time. Greek has no subjunctive form denoting an intention to do this or that. In dependent constructions (including general conditions) the action of the present is generally coincident (rarely subsequent), that of the aorist is generally anterior (rarely coincident), to the action of the leading verb:

xalepai/nousi, e)peida\n au)toi=s paragge/llw pi/_nein to\ fa/rmakon they are angry whenever I bid them drink the poison
P. Ph. 116c, e)peida\n a(/pant' a)kou/shte, kri/_nate when you (shall) have heard everything, decide
D. 4.14. The use of the aorist of time relatively anterior to the action of the leading verb ( = Lat. future perfect) is, like its other references to relative time, only an inference from the connection of the thought (1850 a).
b. Present and aorist subjunctive are occasionally used in the same sentence without any great difference in sense (
X. C. 1.2.6-7, 5. 5. 13).
c. An independent or dependent subjunctive may be ingressive (1924): h)\n ga\r o( *plou=tos nuni\ ble/yh| for if now Plutus recovers his sight Ar. Pl. 494.
d. In general conditions (2336) the subjunctive refers to general time, denoting what holds true now and at all times.

Optative (not in indirect discourse).—The reference is always to future time. The tenses do not refer to differences of time, and denote only the stage of the action.
Present (continuance): plou/sion de\ nomi/zoimi to\n sofo/n may I (always) count the wise man wealthy
P. Phae. 279b; Aorist (simple occurrence):

ei) ga\r ge/noito would that it might happen
X. C. 6.1.38; Perfect (completion with permanent result): teqnai/hs die (lit. may you be dead)
*z 164.
a. In general conditions (2336) the optative is used of past time.
b. In dependent constructions (including general conditions) the action of the present is generally coincident (rarely anterior), that of the aorist generally anterior (rarely coincident), to the action of the leading verb: ei)/ tis ta/de parabai/noi, e)nagh\s e)/stw tou=) *apo/llwnos if any one violates this, let him be accurst of Apollo
Aes. 3.110, e)peidh\ de\ a)noixqei/h (to\ desmwth/rion), ei)sh=|men para\ to\n *swkra/th whenever the prison was opened, we (always) went in to Socrates
P. Ph. 59d. The aorist is often preferred to the more exact perfect because the perfect was rarely used.
c. An independent or dependent optative may be ingressive (1924): ei) polemh/saimen di' *)wrwpo/n, ou)de\n a)\n h(ma=s paqei=n h(gou=mai if we should enter upon a war on account of Oropus, I think we should suffer nothing
D. 5.16.

Optative (in indirect discourse).—When the optative in indirect discourse represents the indicative after a past tense of a verb of saying or thinking, each tense does denote time (as well as stage of action) relatively to that of the leading verb.
a. The present optative represents the imperfect as well as the present indicative.
b. The future optative (first in Pindar) occurs only in indirect discourse after verbs of saying and thinking, in object clauses after o(/pws, 2212, and in other indirect expressions of thought.
c. When the optative in indirect discourse represents the subjunctive (2619 b), its tenses denote only stage of action.

a. Present opt. = present indic.: a)nhrw/ta_ ti/ bou/lointo he demanded what they wanted ( = ti/ bou/lesqe;)
X. A. 2.3.4.
b. Present opt. = imperf. indic.: dihgou=nto o(/ti e)pi\ tou\s polemi/ous ple/oien they explained that they kept sailing against the enemy ( = e)ple/omen)
X. H. 1.7.5.
c. Future opt. = future indic.: o(/ ti poih/soi ou)de\ tou/tois ei)=pe he did not tell even these what he would do ( = poih/sw)
X. A. 2.2.2.
d. Aorist opt. = aorist indic.: h)rw/ta_ ti/ pa/qoien he asked what had happened to them ( = ti/ e)pa/qete;)
X. C. 2.3.19.
e. Perfect opt. = perfect indic.: e)/legon o(/ti oi( meta\ *dhmosqe/nous paradedw/koien sfa=s au)tou/s they said that the troops of Demosthenes had surrendered ( = paradedw/ka_si)
T. 7.83.

Imperative.—The imperative always implies future time. The tenses do not refer to differences of time, and denote only the stage of the action.
a. Present (continuance):

tou\s gonei=s ti(_ma_ honour thy parents
I. 1.16, pa/nta ta)_lhqh= le/ge tell (go on and tell in detail) the whole truth
L. 1.18,

tou\s i(/ppous e)kei/nois di/dote offer the horses to them
X. C. 4.5.47.
b. Aorist (simple occurrence): ble/yon pro\s ta\ o)/rh look (cast a glance) toward the mountains
X. A. 4.1.20, ei)pe/ state (in a word)
P. A. 24d,

h(mi=n tou\s i(/ppous do/te give the horses to us
X. C. 4.5.47.
c. Perfect (completion with permanent result): teta/xqw let him take his place (and stay there)
P. R. 562a, ei)rh/sqw let it have been said (once for all) 503 b.
N.—The perfect active and middle are generally used as presents (

teqna/tw let him be put to death
P. L. 938c,

me/mnhsqe remember
D. 40.30). The perfect passive (in the third person) is used of a fixed decision concerning what is to be done or has been done.

Infinitive (not in indirect discourse).—The tenses of the infinitive (without a)/n) not in indirect discourse have no time of themselves and express only the stage of the action; their (relative) time depends on the context and is that of the leading verb (present, past, or future). The infinitive may have the article (2025 ff.).
a. Present (continuance):

ou)de\ bouleu/esqai e)/ti w(/ra_, a)lla\ bebouleu=sqai it is time no longer to be making up one's mind, but to have it made up
P. Cr. 46a.
b. Aorist (simple occurrence):

tou= piei=n e)piqu_mi/a_ the desire of obtaining drink
T. 7.84, h)/rcato gene/sqai began to be 1. 103, but h)/rxeto gi/gnesqai 3. 18 (the tense of gi/gnomai depends on that of a)/rxomai; not h)/rcato gi/gnesqai), dei= tou\s u(pe\r au)tou= le/gontas mi_sh=sai (ingressive) one must conceive an aversion for those who speak in his behalf
D. 9.53.
c. Perfect (completion with permanent result): see a. Often of certainty of action.
d. Future.—When the context shows that stress is laid on the idea of futurity, the future infinitive, referring to future time relative to the main verb, is sometimes used instead of the present or aorist:

ou)k a)pokwlu/_sein dunatoi\ o)/ntes not being able to prevent
T. 3.28,

pollou= de/w kat' e)mautou= e)rei=n I am far from intending to speak to my own disadvantage
P. A. 37b. On the future infinitive with me/llw see 1959.
N. 1.—The action set forth by a dependent present or aorist infinitive (without a)/n) not in indirect discourse has no time except that which is implied by the context. With verbs signifying to advise or to command, and when the infinitive expresses purpose, the reference is to future time. Usually the action of the present and aorist is coincident with or antecedent to that of the main verb. The action of an aorist infinitive with the article and a subject is not always relatively past. The perfect (without a)/n) has no time apart from the context; its action is usually antecedent.
N. 2.—On the use of the present and aorist with verbs of promising, etc., see 1868; with me/llw, see 1959.
N. 3.—Observe that verbs denoting continuance (as me/nw remain) often appear in the aorist, while verbs of transitory action (as i(_e/nai send, hurl) often appear in the present.
N. 4.—Present and aorist occasionally occur in close conjunction without any great difference in meaning, as

prosh/kei u(_mi=n tou/tou katayhfi/zesqai . . ., dei= u(_ma=s qa/naton au)tou= katayhfi/sasqai it is fitting that you vote ag

Infinitive (in indirect discourse).—The tenses of the infinitive in indirect discourse denote the same time relative to that of the leading verb (present, past, or future) as was denoted by the corresponding tenses of the indicative in direct discourse which they represent.
a. The present infinitive represents also the imperfect, the perfect infinitive represents also the pluperfect indicative.
b. The action of the present is usually coincident, that of the aorist anterior, to the action of the leading verb.
c. The future infinitive is found chiefly in indirect discourse and in analogous constructions. With me/llw, see 1959. It may have the article (2026).

Participle (not in indirect discourse).—The participle, as a verbal adjective, is timeless. The tenses of the participle express only continuance, simple occurrence, and completion with permanent result. Whether the action expressed by the participle is antecedent, coincident, or subsequent to that of the leading verb (in any tense) depends on the context. The future participle has a temporal force only because its voluntative force points to the future.
a. Present (continuative). The action set forth by the present participle is generally coincident (rarely antecedent or subsequent) to that of the leading verb:

e)rgazo/menai me\n h)ri/stwn, e)rgasa/menai de\ e)dei/pnoun the women took their noonday meal while they continued their work, but took their supper when they had stopped work
X. M. 2.7.12.
1. Antecedent action ( = imperf.):

oi( *ku/_reioi pro/sqen su\n h(mi=n tatto/menoi nu=n a)festh/ka_sin the forces of Cyrus that were formerly marshalled with us have now deserted
X. A. 3.2.17,

tou\s to/te paro/ntas ai)tia/_sontai sumbou/lous they will accuse those who were their counsellors at that time
P. G. 519a, oi( *kori/nqioi me/xri tou/tou proqu/_mws pra/_ssontes a)nei=san th=s filoneiki/a_s the Corinthians, who up to that time had been acting zealously, now slackened in their vehemence
T. 5.32. An adverb (pro/teron, pro/sqen, to/te, pote/) often accompanies the participle, which is sometimes called the participle of the imperfect.
2. Subsequent action (especially when the leading verb denotes motion): e)/pemyan pre/sbeis a)gge/llontas th\n tou= *plhmuri/ou lh=yin they despatched messengers to announce the capture of Plemyrium
T. 7.25. An attributive present part. w. nu=n may refer to the absolute present, though the main verb is past:

th\n nu=n *boiwti/a_n kaloume/nhn w)/|khsan they settled in the country now called Boeotia
T. 1.12.
3. The present participle denotes that an action is in process, is attempted, or is repeated.
b. Future (chiefly voluntative):

ou) sunh/lqomen w(s basilei= polemh/sontes we have not come together for the purpose of waging war with the king
X. A. 2.3.21.
c. Aorist (simple occurrence). The action set forth by the aorist participle is generally antecedent to that of the leading verb; but it is sometimes coincident or nearly so, when it defines, or is identical with, that of the leading verb, and the subordinate action is only a modification of the main action.
1. Antecedent:

deipnh/sa_s e)xw/rei after supper he advanced
T.

title: Resultative Aorist
definition:
The aorist expresses the mere occurrence of an action in the past. The action is regarded as an event or single fact without reference to the length of time it occupied. As a narrative tense it is often used to state the chief events and facts, while the other past tenses set forth subordinate actions and attendant circumstances. In contrast to the imperfect (and present) the aorist denotes the result, end, or effect of an action.
The same verb may be a resultative aorist or an ingressive aorist; for instance, ἔβαλον I let fly a missile (ingressive), and *I hit* (resultative); κατέσχον I got possession of (ingressive), and *I kept back* (resultative).

smyth.text:
The aorist expresses the mere occurrence of an action in the past. The action is regarded as an event or single fact without reference to the length of time it occupied.

e)ni/_khsan oi( *kerku_rai=oi kai\ nau=s pe/nte kai\ de/ka die/fqeiran the Corcyraeans were victorious and destroyed fifteen ships
T. 1.29,

*paiw/nios e)poi/hse Paeonius fecit
I.G.A. /lref>, e)/docen th=| boulh=| it was voted by (seemed good to) the Senate
C.I.A. /lref>
a. The uses of the aorist may be explained by the figure of a point in time:
1. The starting point (ingressive aorist, 1924); 2. The end point (resultative aorist, 1926); 3. The whole action (beginning to end) concentrated to a point (complexive aorist, 1927).

Ingressive Aorist.—The aorist of verbs whose present denotes a state or a continued action, expresses the entrance into that state or the beginning of that action.
a. This holds true of the other moods. Greek has no special form to denote entrance into a state in present time (1853).

Most of the verbs in question are denominatives, and the forms are chiefly those of the first aorist:—

a)/rxw ruleh)=rca became ruler

basileu/w am king, rulee)basi/leusa became king, ascended the throne

ble/pw look ate)/bleya cast a glance

dakru/_w weepe)da/kru_sa burst into tears

douleu/w am a slavee)dou/leusa became a slave

e)rw= loveh)ra/sqhn fell in love

qarrw= am courageouse)qa/rrhsa plucked up courage

nosw= am ille)no/shsa fell ill

ploutw= am riche)plou/thsa became rich

polemw= make ware)pole/mhsa began the war

si_gw= am silente)si/_ghsa became silent
a. Rarely with the second aorist: e)/sxon took hold, took possession of, got, as

*peisistra/tou teleuth/santos *(ippi/a_s e)/sxe th\n a)rxh/n when Peisistratus died Hippias succeeded to his power
T. 6.54. So h)|sqo/mhn became aware, e)/sthn took my stand (perfect e(/sthka am standing).
b. The aorist of these verbs denotes also a simple occurrence of the action as an historical fact: e)basi/leusa was king, ruled, e)no/shsa was ill. Thus,

e)kei=noi pe/nte kai\ tettara/konta e)/th tw=n *(ellh/nwn h)=rcan they held the supremacy over Greece for forty-five years
D. 3.24 (cp. 1927 b).

Resultative Aorist.—In contrast to the imperfect (and present) the aorist denotes the result, end, or effect of an action.
Thus, h)/gagon I brought, e)bou/leusa I decided (e)bou/leuon I was deliberating), e)/qhca I sharpened, e)/peson I struck in falling (e)/pi_pton I was in the act of falling), e)/peisa I succeeded in persuading (1895).
a. The same verb may be a resultative aorist or an ingressive aorist. Thus, e)/balon I let fly a missile (ingressive), and I hit (resultative); kate/sxon I got possession of (ingressive), and I kept back (resultative).
b. e)/kteina/ se
E. Ion 1291 means I tried to kill you, since ktei/nw denotes properly only the act of the agent, and does not, like kill, also connote the effect of the action upon another.

Complexive Aorist.—The complexive aorist is used to survey at a glance the course of a past action from beginning to end:

tou/tw| tw=| tro/pw| th\n po/lin e)tei/xisan it was in this manner that they fortified the city
T. 1.93. It may sum up the result of a preceding narrative (often containing imperfects, as
T. 2.47. 4; 3. 81). The complexive aorist appears also in other moods than the indicative.
a. This is often called the ‘concentrative’ aorist, because it concentrates the entire course of an action to a single point. When used of rapid or instantaneous action this aorist is often called ‘momentary.’
b. The complexive aorist is used either of a long or of a short period of time:

te/ssara kai\ de/ka e)/th e)ne/meinan ai( spondai/ the peace lasted fourteen years
T. 2.2, o)li/gon xro/non cune/meinen h( o(maixmi/a_ the league lasted a short time 1. 18, h)=lqon, ei)=don, e)ni/_khsa veni, vidi, vici (“Caesar's brag of came, and saw, and conquered”) Plutarch, Caes. 50.

The aorist is commonly used with definite numbers. The imperfect is, however, often employed when an action is represented as interrupted or as proceeding from one stage to another. Thus,

e)ntau=qa e)/meine *ku=ros h(me/ra_s tria/_konta Cyrus remained thirty days there
X. A. 1.2.9;

te/ttaras mh=nas o(/lous e)sw/|zonto oi( *fwkei=s tou\s u(/steron, h( de\ tou/tou yeudologi/a_ meta\ tau=q' u(/steron au)tou\s a)pw/lesen for the four whole ensuing months the Phocians remained safe, but the falsehood of this man afterwards effected their ruin
D. 19.78.

The aorist enumerates and reports past events. It may be employed in brief continuous narration (
X. A. 1.9.6). As a narrative tense it is often used to state the chief events and facts, while the other past tenses set forth subordinate actions and attendant circumstances.

title: Ingressive Aorist
definition: The aorist of verbs whose present denotes a state or a continued action, expresses the entrance into that state or the beginning of that action. The ingressive aorist is used with atelic verbs[^68], particularly with stative verbs and indicates the beginning of a state; for instance, ἄρχω rule: ἦρξα became ruler, βασιλεύω am king, rule: ἐβασίλευσα became king, ascended the throne, or νοσῶ am ill: ἐνόσησα fell ill.

title: Complexive Aorist
definition: The complexive aorist is used to survey at a glance the course of a past action from beginning to end and often is accompanied with an expression of the duration. It may sum up the result of a preceding narrative. This is often called the concentrative aorist, because it concentrates the entire course of an action to a single point.

title: Gnomic Aorist
definition:
Gnomic aorist (γνώμη maxim, proverb) indicates a general truth. This use of the aorist does not seem to simply states a past occurrence, but it expresses habits, general tendencies, procedures, or typical events.
Akin to the gnomic aorist is the aorist employed in general descriptions, imaginary scenes and in descriptions of manners and custom. The aorist is used in similes in poetry, and usually contains the point of comparison.

smyth.text:
Gnomic Aorist (gnw/mh maxim, proverb).—The aorist may express a general truth. The aorist simply states a past occurrence and leaves the reader to draw the inference from a concrete case that what has occurred once is typical of what often occurs: paqw\n de/ te nh/pios e)/gnw a fool learns by experience Hesiod, Works and Days, 218,

ka/llos me\n ga\r h)\ xro/nos a)nh/lwsen h)\ no/sos e)ma/ra_ne for beauty is either wasted by time or withered by disease
I. 1.6.
a. The gnomic aorist often alternates with the present of general truth (1877): ou) ga\r h( plhgh\ pare/sthse th\n o)rgh/n, a)ll' h( a)ti_mi/a_: ou)de\ to\ tu/ptesqai toi=s e)leuqe/rois e)sti\ deino/n . . . a)lla\ to\ e)f' u(/brei for it is not the blow that causes anger, but the disgrace; nor is it the beating that is terrible to freemen, but the insult
D. 21.72. Cp.
P. R. 566e.
b. The gnomic aorist is regarded as a primary tense (1858):

oi( tu/rannoi plou/sion o(\n a)\n bou/lwntai paraxrh=m' e)poi/hsan tyrants make rich in a moment whomever they wish
D. 20.15.

Akin to the gnomic aorist is the aorist employed in general descritions. So in imaginary scenes and in descriptions of manners and custom Thus, e)peida
 a)fi/kwntai oi( teteleuthko/tes ei)s to
 to/pon, oi(= o( dai/mwn e(/kaston komi/z prw=ton me
 diedika/santo oi(/ te kalw=s kai\ o(si/ws biw/santes kai\ oi( mh/ when the de<*> reach the place whither each is severally conducted by his genius, first of all the have judgment pronounced upon them as they have lived well and devoutly not
P. Ph. 113d, fa=ros de\ au)thmero
 e)cufh/nantes oi( i(_re/es kat' w)=n e)/dhsan e(no\s au)t<*> mi/trh| tou\s o)fqalmou/s after having woven a mantle on the same day the pries bind the eyes of one of their number with a snood
Hdt. 2.122.

Aorist in Similes.—The aorist is used in similes in poetry, and usually contains the point of comparison. It may alternate with the present. Thus

h)/ripe d' w(s o(/te tis dru=s h)/ripen he fell as falls an oak
*p 482, oi(=os d' e)k nefe/wn a)na fai/netai ou)/lios a)sth\r | pamfai/nwn, to/te d' au)=tis e)/du_ ne/fea skio/enta, | w(\s *(/ektwr ktl and as from out of the clouds all radiant appears a baneful star, and then again sinks within the shadowy clouds, so Hector, etc.
*a 62.
a. The aorist in 1931, 1935 is used of time past (in 1934 of the future), from the point of view of an assumed or ideal present.

title: Suggestive Questions and Requests
definition: The aorist is used in questions with τί οὖν ου and τί οὐ to express surprise that something has not been done. The question is here equivalent to a command or a suggestion.

smyth.text:
Aorist for Future.—The aorist may be substituted for the futur when a future event is vividly represented as having actually occurred: a)pwl<*> mhn a)/r', ei)/ me dh\ lei/yeis I am undone if thou dost leave me
E. Alc. 386.

Aorist in Similes.—The aorist is used in similes in poetry, and usually contains the point of comparison. It may alternate with the present. Thus

h)/ripe d' w(s o(/te tis dru=s h)/ripen he fell as falls an oak
*p 482, oi(=os d' e)k nefe/wn a)na fai/netai ou)/lios a)sth\r | pamfai/nwn, to/te d' au)=tis e)/du_ ne/fea skio/enta, | w(\s *(/ektwr ktl and as from out of the clouds all radiant appears a baneful star, and then again sinks within the shadowy clouds, so Hector, etc.
*a 62.
a. The aorist in 1931, 1935 is used of time past (in 1934 of the future), from the point of view of an assumed or ideal present.

Aorist for Present.—The aorist is used in questions with ti/ ou)=n ou and ti/ ou) to express surprise that something has not been done. The question is here equivalent to a command or proposal: ti/ ou)=n ou)xi\ kai\ su\ u(pe/mnhsa/s me, why don't you recall it to my mind?
X. Hi. 1.3. The (less lively) present, and the future, may also be used.

examples.translation: why don't you recall it to my mind?

examples.translation: let us hear your account of the conversation at once, if nothing prevents you

title: Customary Action (Iterative)
definition: The aorist with ἄν may indicate repetitions and habits. Additionally, Homer and Herodotus have iterative imperfects and aorists in \-σκον and \-σκομην denoting a customary or repeated past action. Homer has iterative forms in the imperfect and 1 and 2 aorist active and middle. Herodotus has no iteratives in the 1 aorist and few in the 2 aorist.

smyth.text:
Iterative Aorist.—With a)/n the aorist may denote repetition (1790)

ei)=pen a)/n he used to say
X. C. 7.1.14. Distinguish 2303.

Iterative Imperfects and Aorists in -sko/e-.—Homer and Herodotus have iterative imperfects and aorists in -skon and -skomhn denoting a customary or repeated past action. Homer has iterative forms in the imperfect and 1 and 2 aorist active and middle. Herodotus has no iteratives in the 1 aorist and few in the 2 aorist; and only from w-verbs. Herodotus regularly and Homer usually omit the augment. -aw verbs have -aa-skon or -a-skon; -ew verbs -ee-skon, in Hom. also -e-skon. -a-skon is rare in other verbs than those in -aw. The vowel preceding the suffix is always short.
a. The suffix -sko/e- is added to the tense-stem. Imperf.: feu/ge-ske (feu/gw flee), e)/xe-skon (e)/xw have), ni_ka/-skomen (ni_ka/w conquer), goa/a-ske (goa/w bewail), kru/pta-ske (kru/ptw hide), kale/e-skon (kale/w call), zwnnu/sketo (zw/nnu_mi gird) ; 1 aor.: a)po-tre/ya-ske (a)potre/pw turn away）; 2 aor.: fu/ge-ske, sta/-ske stood.

title: Dramatic Aorist
definition:
The first person singular of the aorist is used in the answers and reactions in tragedy and comedy, often indicating a state of mind or an act expressing a state of mind (especially approval or disapproval) occurring to the speaker in the moment just passed. The  dramatic aorist is sometimes called instantaneous aorist.
Sometimes this use appears outside of dialogue:

smyth.text:
Dramatic Aorist.—The first person singular of the aorist is used in the dialogue parts of tragedy and comedy to denote a state of mind or an act expressing a state of mind (especially approval or disapproval) occurring to the speaker in the moment just passed. This use is derived from familiar discourse, but is not found in good prose. In translation the present is employed. Thus, h(/sqhn, e)ge/lasa I am delighted, I can't help laughing
Ar. Eq. 696,

e)deca/mhn to\ r(hqe/n I welcome the omen
S. El. 668 (prose de/xomai to\n oi)wno/n). So e)ph/|nesa I approve, cunh=ka I understand. Sometimes this use appears outside of dialogue (

a)pe/ptusa I spurn
A. Pr. 1070, Ag. 1193).

examples.translation: I am delighted, I can't help laughing
I welcome the omen
I spurn

title: Non-indicative (Perfective Aspect)
definition:
The tenses of the moods other than the indicative rarely have relative temporal value, however, they express the aspect of the verb. The aspect of a verb indicates the way an action extends over time and the way it is presented. For instance, It may present an action as a complete whole, or an incomplete, ongoing process. The aorist has a perfective aspect, presenting the verb as completed, or an uninterrupted whole.

With Infinitives:

smyth.text: The tenses of the moods except the indicative do not express time in independent sentences.

Subjunctive.—The subjunctive mood as such refers to the future. The tenses do not refer to differences of time, and denote only the stage of the action (continuance, simple occurrence, completion with permanent result).
Present (continuance):

ta\ au(tw=n a(/ma e)kporizw/meqa let us at the same time keep developing our resources
T. 1.82; Aorist (simple occurrence):

porisw/meqa ou)=n prw=ton th\n dapa/nhn let us procure the money first
T. 1.83; Perfect (completion with permanent result): i(/na, h)\n mh\ u(pakou/wsi, teqnh/kwsin that, in case they do not submit, they may be put to death (lit. may be dead at once)
T. 8.74. The aorist commonly replaces the more exact perfect because the perfect is rarely used.
a. The future time denoted by present or aorist (ti/ poiw=men; or ti/ poih/swmen; what shall we do?) may refer, according to the sense, either to the next moment or to some later time. Greek has no subjunctive form denoting an intention to do this or that. In dependent constructions (including general conditions) the action of the present is generally coincident (rarely subsequent), that of the aorist is generally anterior (rarely coincident), to the action of the leading verb:

xalepai/nousi, e)peida\n au)toi=s paragge/llw pi/_nein to\ fa/rmakon they are angry whenever I bid them drink the poison
P. Ph. 116c, e)peida\n a(/pant' a)kou/shte, kri/_nate when you (shall) have heard everything, decide
D. 4.14. The use of the aorist of time relatively anterior to the action of the leading verb ( = Lat. future perfect) is, like its other references to relative time, only an inference from the connection of the thought (1850 a).
b. Present and aorist subjunctive are occasionally used in the same sentence without any great difference in sense (
X. C. 1.2.6-7, 5. 5. 13).
c. An independent or dependent subjunctive may be ingressive (1924): h)\n ga\r o( *plou=tos nuni\ ble/yh| for if now Plutus recovers his sight Ar. Pl. 494.
d. In general conditions (2336) the subjunctive refers to general time, denoting what holds true now and at all times.

Optative (not in indirect discourse).—The reference is always to future time. The tenses do not refer to differences of time, and denote only the stage of the action.
Present (continuance): plou/sion de\ nomi/zoimi to\n sofo/n may I (always) count the wise man wealthy
P. Phae. 279b; Aorist (simple occurrence):

ei) ga\r ge/noito would that it might happen
X. C. 6.1.38; Perfect (completion with permanent result): teqnai/hs die (lit. may you be dead)
*z 164.
a. In general conditions (2336) the optative is used of past time.
b. In dependent constructions (including general conditions) the action of the present is generally coincident (rarely anterior), that of the aorist generally anterior (rarely coincident), to the action of the leading verb: ei)/ tis ta/de parabai/noi, e)nagh\s e)/stw tou=) *apo/llwnos if any one violates this, let him be accurst of Apollo
Aes. 3.110, e)peidh\ de\ a)noixqei/h (to\ desmwth/rion), ei)sh=|men para\ to\n *swkra/th whenever the prison was opened, we (always) went in to Socrates
P. Ph. 59d. The aorist is often preferred to the more exact perfect because the perfect was rarely used.
c. An independent or dependent optative may be ingressive (1924): ei) polemh/saimen di' *)wrwpo/n, ou)de\n a)\n h(ma=s paqei=n h(gou=mai if we should enter upon a war on account of Oropus, I think we should suffer nothing
D. 5.16.

Optative (in indirect discourse).—When the optative in indirect discourse represents the indicative after a past tense of a verb of saying or thinking, each tense does denote time (as well as stage of action) relatively to that of the leading verb.
a. The present optative represents the imperfect as well as the present indicative.
b. The future optative (first in Pindar) occurs only in indirect discourse after verbs of saying and thinking, in object clauses after o(/pws, 2212, and in other indirect expressions of thought.
c. When the optative in indirect discourse represents the subjunctive (2619 b), its tenses denote only stage of action.

a. Present opt. = present indic.: a)nhrw/ta_ ti/ bou/lointo he demanded what they wanted ( = ti/ bou/lesqe;)
X. A. 2.3.4.
b. Present opt. = imperf. indic.: dihgou=nto o(/ti e)pi\ tou\s polemi/ous ple/oien they explained that they kept sailing against the enemy ( = e)ple/omen)
X. H. 1.7.5.
c. Future opt. = future indic.: o(/ ti poih/soi ou)de\ tou/tois ei)=pe he did not tell even these what he would do ( = poih/sw)
X. A. 2.2.2.
d. Aorist opt. = aorist indic.: h)rw/ta_ ti/ pa/qoien he asked what had happened to them ( = ti/ e)pa/qete;)
X. C. 2.3.19.
e. Perfect opt. = perfect indic.: e)/legon o(/ti oi( meta\ *dhmosqe/nous paradedw/koien sfa=s au)tou/s they said that the troops of Demosthenes had surrendered ( = paradedw/ka_si)
T. 7.83.

Imperative.—The imperative always implies future time. The tenses do not refer to differences of time, and denote only the stage of the action.
a. Present (continuance):

tou\s gonei=s ti(_ma_ honour thy parents
I. 1.16, pa/nta ta)_lhqh= le/ge tell (go on and tell in detail) the whole truth
L. 1.18,

tou\s i(/ppous e)kei/nois di/dote offer the horses to them
X. C. 4.5.47.
b. Aorist (simple occurrence): ble/yon pro\s ta\ o)/rh look (cast a glance) toward the mountains
X. A. 4.1.20, ei)pe/ state (in a word)
P. A. 24d,

h(mi=n tou\s i(/ppous do/te give the horses to us
X. C. 4.5.47.
c. Perfect (completion with permanent result): teta/xqw let him take his place (and stay there)
P. R. 562a, ei)rh/sqw let it have been said (once for all) 503 b.
N.—The perfect active and middle are generally used as presents (

teqna/tw let him be put to death
P. L. 938c,

me/mnhsqe remember
D. 40.30). The perfect passive (in the third person) is used of a fixed decision concerning what is to be done or has been done.

Infinitive (not in indirect discourse).—The tenses of the infinitive (without a)/n) not in indirect discourse have no time of themselves and express only the stage of the action; their (relative) time depends on the context and is that of the leading verb (present, past, or future). The infinitive may have the article (2025 ff.).
a. Present (continuance):

ou)de\ bouleu/esqai e)/ti w(/ra_, a)lla\ bebouleu=sqai it is time no longer to be making up one's mind, but to have it made up
P. Cr. 46a.
b. Aorist (simple occurrence):

tou= piei=n e)piqu_mi/a_ the desire of obtaining drink
T. 7.84, h)/rcato gene/sqai began to be 1. 103, but h)/rxeto gi/gnesqai 3. 18 (the tense of gi/gnomai depends on that of a)/rxomai; not h)/rcato gi/gnesqai), dei= tou\s u(pe\r au)tou= le/gontas mi_sh=sai (ingressive) one must conceive an aversion for those who speak in his behalf
D. 9.53.
c. Perfect (completion with permanent result): see a. Often of certainty of action.
d. Future.—When the context shows that stress is laid on the idea of futurity, the future infinitive, referring to future time relative to the main verb, is sometimes used instead of the present or aorist:

ou)k a)pokwlu/_sein dunatoi\ o)/ntes not being able to prevent
T. 3.28,

pollou= de/w kat' e)mautou= e)rei=n I am far from intending to speak to my own disadvantage
P. A. 37b. On the future infinitive with me/llw see 1959.
N. 1.—The action set forth by a dependent present or aorist infinitive (without a)/n) not in indirect discourse has no time except that which is implied by the context. With verbs signifying to advise or to command, and when the infinitive expresses purpose, the reference is to future time. Usually the action of the present and aorist is coincident with or antecedent to that of the main verb. The action of an aorist infinitive with the article and a subject is not always relatively past. The perfect (without a)/n) has no time apart from the context; its action is usually antecedent.
N. 2.—On the use of the present and aorist with verbs of promising, etc., see 1868; with me/llw, see 1959.
N. 3.—Observe that verbs denoting continuance (as me/nw remain) often appear in the aorist, while verbs of transitory action (as i(_e/nai send, hurl) often appear in the present.
N. 4.—Present and aorist occasionally occur in close conjunction without any great difference in meaning, as

prosh/kei u(_mi=n tou/tou katayhfi/zesqai . . ., dei= u(_ma=s qa/naton au)tou= katayhfi/sasqai it is fitting that you vote ag

Infinitive (in indirect discourse).—The tenses of the infinitive in indirect discourse denote the same time relative to that of the leading verb (present, past, or future) as was denoted by the corresponding tenses of the indicative in direct discourse which they represent.
a. The present infinitive represents also the imperfect, the perfect infinitive represents also the pluperfect indicative.
b. The action of the present is usually coincident, that of the aorist anterior, to the action of the leading verb.
c. The future infinitive is found chiefly in indirect discourse and in analogous constructions. With me/llw, see 1959. It may have the article (2026).

Participle (not in indirect discourse).—The participle, as a verbal adjective, is timeless. The tenses of the participle express only continuance, simple occurrence, and completion with permanent result. Whether the action expressed by the participle is antecedent, coincident, or subsequent to that of the leading verb (in any tense) depends on the context. The future participle has a temporal force only because its voluntative force points to the future.
a. Present (continuative). The action set forth by the present participle is generally coincident (rarely antecedent or subsequent) to that of the leading verb:

e)rgazo/menai me\n h)ri/stwn, e)rgasa/menai de\ e)dei/pnoun the women took their noonday meal while they continued their work, but took their supper when they had stopped work
X. M. 2.7.12.
1. Antecedent action ( = imperf.):

oi( *ku/_reioi pro/sqen su\n h(mi=n tatto/menoi nu=n a)festh/ka_sin the forces of Cyrus that were formerly marshalled with us have now deserted
X. A. 3.2.17,

tou\s to/te paro/ntas ai)tia/_sontai sumbou/lous they will accuse those who were their counsellors at that time
P. G. 519a, oi( *kori/nqioi me/xri tou/tou proqu/_mws pra/_ssontes a)nei=san th=s filoneiki/a_s the Corinthians, who up to that time had been acting zealously, now slackened in their vehemence
T. 5.32. An adverb (pro/teron, pro/sqen, to/te, pote/) often accompanies the participle, which is sometimes called the participle of the imperfect.
2. Subsequent action (especially when the leading verb denotes motion): e)/pemyan pre/sbeis a)gge/llontas th\n tou= *plhmuri/ou lh=yin they despatched messengers to announce the capture of Plemyrium
T. 7.25. An attributive present part. w. nu=n may refer to the absolute present, though the main verb is past:

th\n nu=n *boiwti/a_n kaloume/nhn w)/|khsan they settled in the country now called Boeotia
T. 1.12.
3. The present participle denotes that an action is in process, is attempted, or is repeated.
b. Future (chiefly voluntative):

ou) sunh/lqomen w(s basilei= polemh/sontes we have not come together for the purpose of waging war with the king
X. A. 2.3.21.
c. Aorist (simple occurrence). The action set forth by the aorist participle is generally antecedent to that of the leading verb; but it is sometimes coincident or nearly so, when it defines, or is identical with, that of the leading verb, and the subordinate action is only a modification of the main action.
1. Antecedent:

deipnh/sa_s e)xw/rei after supper he advanced
T.

title: Completed action
definition:
The perfect denotes a completed action the effects of which still continue in the present:
“ἐφοβήθην, καὶ ἔτι καὶ νῦν **τεθορύβημαι**” **Aes. 2.4**; ⇾ I was struck with fear, and even at the present moment am still in a state of agitation
When the perfect marks the enduring result rather than the completed act, it may not indicate any clear reference to the preceding action; for instance, κέκλημαι (have received a name) am called, my name is, κέκτημαι (have acquired) possess, μέμνημαι (have recalled) remember, τέθνηκα (have passed away) am dead, οἶδα (have found out) know. These are often translated to a present tense and therefore, they are sometimes called “perfect with present meaning”; however, they are not fundamentally different from other perfect verbs.

examples.translation: the rooms have been constructed (their construction is finished)
he has taken away (and still holds) their cities

examples.greek: τί βουλεύεσθον ποιεῖν; οὐδέν, ἔφη ὁ Χαρμίδης, ἀλλὰ βεβουλεύμεθα
examples.translation: what are you conspiring to do? Nothing, said Charmides; we have already conspired

title: Intensive Perfect
definition:
The perfects tense with atelic verbs[^77] may indicate an emphasis of the degree of the state expressed by the verb. These are often called intensive perfects. Such are: verbs of the *senses* (δέδορκα gaze, πέφρικα shudder), of *sustained sound* (κέκραγα bawl, λέληκα shout, βέβρυχα roar), of *emotion* (πεφόβημαι am filled with alarm, γέγηθα am glad, μέμηλε cares for), of *gesture* (κέχηνα keep the mouth agape), and many others (σεσίγηκα am still, etc.).
With certain telic verbs, the perfect tense may emphasize the responsibility of the subject for the results of the verb.

smyth.text:
‘Intensive’ Perfect.—Many perfects seem to denote an action rather than a state resulting from an action, and to be equivalent to strengthened presents. These are often called intensive perfects.
Such are: verbs of the senses (de/dorka gaze, pe/fri_ka shudder), of sustained sound (ke/kra_ga bawl, le/lhka shout, be/bru_xa roar), of emotion (pefo/bhmai am filled with alarm, ge/ghqa am glad, me/mhle cares for), of gesture (ke/xhna keep the mouth agape), and many others (sesi/_ghka am still, etc.).
a. But most if not all of the verbs in question may be regarded as true perfects, i.e. they denote a mental or physical state resulting from the accomplishment of the action; thus, pe/fri_ka I have shuddered and am now in a state of shuddering.
b. Certain verbs tend to appear in the perfect for emphasis: te/qnhka am dead, a)po/lwla perish, pe/pra_ka sell (have sold).

examples.greek: πολλὰ δὲ θαυμάζων τῶν εἰωθότων λέγεσθαι παρ᾽ ὑμῖν, οὐδενὸς ἧττον, ὦ ἄνδρες Ἀθηναῖοι, τεθαύμακα, ὃ καὶ πρώην τινὸς ἤκουσ᾽ εἰπόντος ἐν τῇ βουλῇ
examples.translation: I often wonder at the sort of speeches that are delivered here, but nothing, men of Athens, has surprised me more than what I heard uttered in the Council the other day

examples.greek: γέγραφε δὲ καὶ ταῦτα ὁ αὐτὸς Θουκυδίδης Ἀθηναῖος
examples.translation: the same Thucydides of Athens is the author of this a well.

title: Perfect for Future Perfect
definition:
The perfect may be used instead of the future perfect to anticipate an action that has not occurred yet; however, it is presented as already having had an effect . This use of the perfect tense is sometimes called the rhetorical perfect.
Especially with the phrase τὸ ἐπί τινι, the perfect anticipates the certain occurrence of an event:

smyth.text:
Perfect for Future Perfect.—The perfect may be used vividly for the future perfect to anticipate an action not yet done: ka)\_n tou=to ni_kw=men, pa/nq' h(mi=n pepoi/htai and if we conquer in that quarter, everything has been (will have been) accomplished by us
X. A. 1.8.12.
a. Especially with the phrase to\ e)pi/ tini, the perfect anticipates the certain occurrence of an event:

to\ e)pi\ tou/tw| a)polw/lamen for all he could do, we had perished
X. A. 6.6.23.

for all he could do, we had perished

Optative (in indirect discourse).—When the optative in indirect discourse represents the indicative after a past tense of a verb of saying or thinking, each tense does denote time (as well as stage of action) relatively to that of the leading verb.
a. The present optative represents the imperfect as well as the present indicative.
b. The future optative (first in Pindar) occurs only in indirect discourse after verbs of saying and thinking, in object clauses after o(/pws, 2212, and in other indirect expressions of thought.
c. When the optative in indirect discourse represents the subjunctive (2619 b), its tenses denote only stage of action.

a. Present opt. = present indic.: a)nhrw/ta_ ti/ bou/lointo he demanded what they wanted ( = ti/ bou/lesqe;)
X. A. 2.3.4.
b. Present opt. = imperf. indic.: dihgou=nto o(/ti e)pi\ tou\s polemi/ous ple/oien they explained that they kept sailing against the enemy ( = e)ple/omen)
X. H. 1.7.5.
c. Future opt. = future indic.: o(/ ti poih/soi ou)de\ tou/tois ei)=pe he did not tell even these what he would do ( = poih/sw)
X. A. 2.2.2.
d. Aorist opt. = aorist indic.: h)rw/ta_ ti/ pa/qoien he asked what had happened to them ( = ti/ e)pa/qete;)
X. C. 2.3.19.
e. Perfect opt. = perfect indic.: e)/legon o(/ti oi( meta\ *dhmosqe/nous paradedw/koien sfa=s au)tou/s they said that the troops of Demosthenes had surrendered ( = paradedw/ka_si)
T. 7.83.

Imperative.—The imperative always implies future time. The tenses do not refer to differences of time, and denote only the stage of the action.
a. Present (continuance):

tou\s gonei=s ti(_ma_ honour thy parents
I. 1.16, pa/nta ta)_lhqh= le/ge tell (go on and tell in detail) the whole truth
L. 1.18,

tou\s i(/ppous e)kei/nois di/dote offer the horses to them
X. C. 4.5.47.
b. Aorist (simple occurrence): ble/yon pro\s ta\ o)/rh look (cast a glance) toward the mountains
X. A. 4.1.20, ei)pe/ state (in a word)
P. A. 24d,

h(mi=n tou\s i(/ppous do/te give the horses to us
X. C. 4.5.47.
c. Perfect (completion with permanent result): teta/xqw let him take his place (and stay there)
P. R. 562a, ei)rh/sqw let it have been said (once for all) 503 b.
N.—The perfect active and middle are generally used as presents (

teqna/tw let him be put to death
P. L. 938c,

me/mnhsqe remember
D. 40.30). The perfect passive (in the third person) is used of a fixed decision concerning what is to be done or has been done.

Infinitive (not in indirect discourse).—The tenses of the infinitive (without a)/n) not in indirect discourse have no time of themselves and express only the stage of the action; their (relative) time depends on the context and is that of the leading verb (present, past, or future). The infinitive may have the article (2025 ff.).
a. Present (continuance):

ou)de\ bouleu/esqai e)/ti w(/ra_, a)lla\ bebouleu=sqai it is time no longer to be making up one's mind, but to have it made up
P. Cr. 46a.
b. Aorist (simple occurrence):

tou= piei=n e)piqu_mi/a_ the desire of obtaining drink
T. 7.84, h)/rcato gene/sqai began to be 1. 103, but h)/rxeto gi/gnesqai 3. 18 (the tense of gi/gnomai depends on that of a)/rxomai; not h)/rcato gi/gnesqai), dei= tou\s u(pe\r au)tou= le/gontas mi_sh=sai (ingressive) one must conceive an aversion for those who speak in his behalf
D. 9.53.
c. Perfect (completion with permanent result): see a. Often of certainty of action.
d. Future.—When the context shows that stress is laid on the idea of futurity, the future infinitive, referring to future time relative to the main verb, is sometimes used instead of the present or aorist:

ou)k a)pokwlu/_sein dunatoi\ o)/ntes not being able to prevent
T. 3.28,

pollou= de/w kat' e)mautou= e)rei=n I am far from intending to speak to my own disadvantage
P. A. 37b. On the future infinitive with me/llw see 1959.
N. 1.—The action set forth by a dependent present or aorist infinitive (without a)/n) not in indirect discourse has no time except that which is implied by the context. With verbs signifying to advise or to command, and when the infinitive expresses purpose, the reference is to future time. Usually the action of the present and aorist is coincident with or antecedent to that of the main verb. The action of an aorist infinitive with the article and a subject is not always relatively past. The perfect (without a)/n) has no time apart from the context; its action is usually antecedent.
N. 2.—On the use of the present and aorist with verbs of promising, etc., see 1868; with me/llw, see 1959.
N. 3.—Observe that verbs denoting continuance (as me/nw remain) often appear in the aorist, while verbs of transitory action (as i(_e/nai send, hurl) often appear in the present.
N. 4.—Present and aorist occasionally occur in close conjunction without any great difference in meaning, as

prosh/kei u(_mi=n tou/tou katayhfi/zesqai . . ., dei= u(_ma=s qa/naton au)tou= katayhfi/sasqai it is fitting that you vote ag

Infinitive (in indirect discourse).—The tenses of the infinitive in indirect discourse denote the same time relative to that of the leading verb (present, past, or future) as was denoted by the corresponding tenses of the indicative in direct discourse which they represent.
a. The present infinitive represents also the imperfect, the perfect infinitive represents also the pluperfect indicative.
b. The action of the present is usually coincident, that of the aorist anterior, to the action of the leading verb.
c. The future infinitive is found chiefly in indirect discourse and in analogous constructions. With me/llw, see 1959. It may have the article (2026).

Participle (not in indirect discourse).—The participle, as a verbal adjective, is timeless. The tenses of the participle express only continuance, simple occurrence, and completion with permanent result. Whether the action expressed by the participle is antecedent, coincident, or subsequent to that of the leading verb (in any tense) depends on the context. The future participle has a temporal force only because its voluntative force points to the future.
a. Present (continuative). The action set forth by the present participle is generally coincident (rarely antecedent or subsequent) to that of the leading verb:

e)rgazo/menai me\n h)ri/stwn, e)rgasa/menai de\ e)dei/pnoun the women took their noonday meal while they continued their work, but took their supper when they had stopped work
X. M. 2.7.12.
1. Antecedent action ( = imperf.):

oi( *ku/_reioi pro/sqen su\n h(mi=n tatto/menoi nu=n a)festh/ka_sin the forces of Cyrus that were formerly marshalled with us have now deserted
X. A. 3.2.17,

tou\s to/te paro/ntas ai)tia/_sontai sumbou/lous they will accuse those who were their counsellors at that time
P. G. 519a, oi( *kori/nqioi me/xri tou/tou proqu/_mws pra/_ssontes a)nei=san th=s filoneiki/a_s the Corinthians, who up to that time had been acting zealously, now slackened in their vehemence
T. 5.32. An adverb (pro/teron, pro/sqen, to/te, pote/) often accompanies the participle, which is sometimes called the participle of the imperfect.
2. Subsequent action (especially when the leading verb denotes motion): e)/pemyan pre/sbeis a)gge/llontas th\n tou= *plhmuri/ou lh=yin they despatched messengers to announce the capture of Plemyrium
T. 7.25. An attributive present part. w. nu=n may refer to the absolute present, though the main verb is past:

th\n nu=n *boiwti/a_n kaloume/nhn w)/|khsan they settled in the country now called Boeotia
T. 1.12.
3. The present participle denotes that an action is in process, is attempted, or is repeated.
b. Future (chiefly voluntative):

ou) sunh/lqomen w(s basilei= polemh/sontes we have not come together for the purpose of waging war with the king
X. A. 2.3.21.
c. Aorist (simple occurrence). The action set forth by the aorist participle is generally antecedent to that of the leading verb; but it is sometimes coincident or nearly so, when it defines, or is identical with, that of the leading verb, and the subordinate action is only a modification of the main action.
1. Antecedent:

deipnh/sa_s e)xw/rei after supper he advanced
T.

title: Past Perfect
definition:
The pluperfect is the past of the perfect, therefore, it indicates a past fixed state resulting from a completed action. Unlike many other languages, Greek does not necessarily need to use pluperfect for expressing an action that happened prior to an aforementioned time in the past, and it can use the aspectual value of other past tenses for this purpose. The pluperfect expresses absolute tense.
Similar to imperfect, the pluperfect is also used for describing the background circumstances of an action:

smyth.text:
The pluperfect is the past of the perfect, hence it denotes a past fixed state resulting from a completed action: e)bebouleu/mhn I had (was) resolved.
a. When the perfect is translated by the present, the pluperfect is rendered by the imperfect: e)kekth/mhn was in possession, e)teqnh/kei he was dead, h)/|dh knew, e)memnh/mhn remembered. Cp. 1946.

Pluperfect of Immediate Occurrence.—The pluperfect may denote that a past action occurred so immediately or suddenly that it was accomplished almost at the same moment as another action: w(s de\ e)lh/fqhsan, e)le/lunto ai( spondai/ and when they were captured the truce was (already) at an end
T. 4.47 (the fact of their capture was equivalent to the immediate rupture of the truce).

examples.greek: ἦλθον οἱ Ἰνδοὶ ἐκ τῶν πολεμίων οὓς ἐπεπόμφει Κῦρος ἐπὶ κατασκοπήν

title: Future Completed Action
definition:
The future perfect denotes a future state resulting from a completed action: ἀναγεγράψομαι I shall stand enrolled, δεδήσεται he shall be kept in prison.
Most future perfects are middle in form, passive in meaning. The active future perfect is usually periphrastic, meaning that it is formed by combining the perfect active participle with ἔσομαι shall be; for instance, γεγραφὼς ἔσομαι I shall have written. Exceptions are two perfects with a present meaning, ἕστηκα I stand (ἵστημι set) and τέθνηκα I am dead (θνῄσκω), which form the future perfects ἑστήξω I shall stand, τεθνήξω I shall be dead.

smyth.text:
The future perfect denotes a future state resulting from a completed action: a)nagegra/yomai I shall stand enrolled, dedh/setai he shall be kept in prison;

h( qu/ra_ keklh/|setai the door will be kept shut
Ar. Lys. 1071.
a. Most future perfects are middle in form, passive in meaning (581).
b. The active future perfect is usually periphrastic (600):

ta\ de/ont' e)so/meqa e)gnwko/tes we shall have determined on our duty
D. 4.50.

When stress is laid upon complete fulfilment, the future perfect may imply rapidity, immediate consequence, or certainty, of action accomplished in the future: fra/ze, kai\ pepra/_cetai speak, and it shall be done instanter Ar. Pl. 1027, eu)qu\s *)ariai=os a)festh/cei: w(/ste fi/los h(mi=n ou)dei\s lelei/yetai Ariaeus will soon withdraw, so that we shall have no friend left
X. A. 2.4.5.

The future perfect usually has a passive force. The active meaning is found where the perfect middle or active has an active meaning (1946, 1947).
kekth/somai shall possess (ke/kthmai possess), kekra/_comai shall cry out (ke/kra_ga cry out), kekla/gcomai shall scream (ke/klagga scream), memnh/somai shall remember (me/mnhmai remember), pepau/somai shall have ceased (pe/paumai have ceased).

Future Perfect Active.—The future perfect active of most verbs is formed by combining the perfect active participle with e)/somai shall be. Thus, gegrafw\s e)/somai I shall have written, cp. scriptus ero. For the two verbs which do not use this periphrasis, see 584.
a. The perfect middle participle is used in the case of deponent verbs: a)poleloghme/nos e)/somai
And. 1.72.

title: Active Voice
definition:
The active voice represents the subject as performing the action of the verb: λούω I wash. Under *action* is included *being*, as ἡ ὁδὸς μακρά ἐστι the way is long.
Active verbs may be *transitive* or *intransitive.* Verbs capable of taking a direct object are called transitive and other verbs are intransitive. Many verbs are used in the active voice both transitively and intransitively. The distinction between transitive and intransitive verbs is a grammatical convenience, and is not founded on an essential difference of nature.
The active may be causative, and used of an action performed at the bidding of the subject:

smyth.text:
The active voice represents the subject as performing the action of the verb: lou/w I wash.
a. Under action is included being, as h( o(do\s makra/_ e)sti the way is long.
Active verbs are transitive or intransitive (920).
The action of a transitive verb is directed immediately upon an object, as tu/ptw to\n pai=da I strike the boy.
The object of a transitive verb is always put in the accusative (1553).

The action of an intransitive verb is not directed immedi-ately upon an object. The action may be restricted to the subject, as a)lgw= I am in pain, or it may be defined by an oblique case or by a preposition with its case, as a)lgw= tou\s po/das I have a pain in my feet, a)fi/_keto ei)s th\n po/lin he arrived at the city.

Many verbs are used in the active voice both transitively and intransitively. So, in English, turn, move, change. Cp. 1557 ff.
a. The distinction between transitive and intransitive verbs is a grammatical convenience, and is not founded on an essential difference of nature.

Active verbs ordinarily transitive are often used intransitively:
a. By the ellipsis of a definite external object, which in some cases may be employed, as a)/gein (to\ stra/teuma) march, ai)/rein (th\n a)/gku_ran) hoist the anchor, (ta\_s nau=s) get under sail, start, a)pai/rein (ta\_s nau=s, to\n strato/n) sail away, march away, dia/gein (to\n bi/on) live, e)lau/nein (to\n i(/ppon) ride, (to\ a(/rma) drive, (to\n strato/n) march, katalu/_ein (tou\s i(/ppous, ta\ u(pozu/gia) halt, kate/xein (th=n nau=n) put in shore, prose/xein (to\n nou=n) pay attention, teleuta=n (to\n bi/on) die. The original sense has often been so completely forgotten that it becomes possible to say

ai)/rein tw=| stratw=| set out with the army
T. 2.12,

e)lau/nwn i(drou=nti tw=| i(/ppw| riding with his horse in a sweat
X. A. 1.8.1.
b. pra/_ttein, e)/xein with adverbs often mean to keep, to be: eu)= pra/_ttein fare well, kalw=s e)/xein be well (bene se habere), e)/xein ou(/tws be so. So when a reflexive pronoun is apparently omitted:

e)/x' au)tou= stop there!
D. 45.26.
c. Many other transitive verbs may be used absolutely, i.e. with no definite object omitted, as ni_ka=n be a victor, a)dikei=n be guilty. Cp. ‘amare’ be in love, ‘drink’ be a drunkard. This is especially the case in compounds, e.g. of a)lla/ttein, a)nu/ein, dido/nai, kli/_nein, lamba/nein, lei/pein, meignu/nai.
d. In poetry many uncompounded transitive verbs are used intransitively. Many intransitive verbs become transitive when compounded with a prep., especially when the compound has a transferred sense, 1559. In some verbs 1st aorist and 1st perfect are transitive, 2d aorist and 2d perfect are intransitive.

Instead of the active, a periphrasis with gi/gnesqai may be used, often to express solemnity.

mhnu_tai\ gi/gnontai they turned informers
T. 3.2, mh\ u(bristh\s ge/vh| ‘do not be guilty of outrage’
S. Aj. 1092.

Transitive and Intransitive Verbs.—Verbs capable of taking a direct object are called transitive because their action passes over to an object Other verbs are called intransitive.
a. But many intransitive verbs, as in English, are used transitively (1558, 1559), and verbs usually transitive often take an indirect object (1341 ff., 1460 ff., 1471 ff.).

## KINDS OF SIMPLE SENTENCES
