title: Indirect Reflexive Middle
definition:
In the indirect reflexive middle, the subject of the verb is affected by the verb, often as a beneficiary. The Indirect Reflexive Middle represents the subject as acting *for himself, with reference to himself*, or *with something belonging to himself*. *Self* is often the indirect object. So πορίζεσθαι provide for oneself (πορίζειν provide), φυλάττεσθαι guard against (φυλάττειν keep guard), αἱρεῖσθαι choose (take for oneself). The middle often denotes that the subject acts with something belonging to himself (material objects, means, powers). It is often used for acts done willingly.
Some middle verbs may indicate that the subject has something done by another for himself. This use is often called the causative middle.

smyth.text: The Indirect Reflexive Middle represents the subject as acting for himself, with reference to himself, or with something belonging to himself. Self is often here the indirect object. So pori/zesqai provide for oneself (pori/zein provide), fula/ttesqai guard against (fula/ttein keep guard), ai(rei=sqai choose (take for oneself), pare/xesqai furnish (pare/xein offer, present).

Cases in which the object is to be removed from the sphere of the subject may be resolved into the dative for oneself (1483）:

th\n r(a|qu_mi/a_n a)poqe/sqai to lay aside your indolence
D. 8.46,

e)tre/yanto tou\s i(ppe/a_s they routed the cavalry
T. 6.98, tou\s e)xqrou\s a)mu/_nesqai to ward off the enemy for themselves, i.e. to defend themselves against the enemy 1. 144.

The middle often denotes that the subject acts with something belonging to himself (material objects, means, powers). It is often used of acts done willingly. Thus, pare/xesqai furnish from one's own resources, e)pagge/llesqai promise, make profession of, ti/qesqai th\n yh=fon give one's vote, ti/qesqai ta\ o(/pla ground arms, a)podei/casqai gnw/mhn set forth one's opinion, lamba/nesqai/ tinos put one's hand on (seize) something. Thus,

e)spasme/noi ta\ ci/fh having drawn their swords
X. A. 7.4.16,

pai=das e)kkekomisme/noi h)=san they had removed their children
T. 2.78,

tropai=on sthsa/menoi having set up a trophy
X. H. 2.4.7,

o(/pla pori/sasqai to procure arms for themselves
T. 4.9, o(pli/_ta_s metepe/myato he sent for hoplites 7. 31,

gunai=ka h)gago/mhn I married
L. 1.6.

Under the indirect middle belong the periphrases of poiei=sqai with verbal nouns instead of the simple verb (cp. 1754). poiei=n with the same nouns means to bring about, effect, fashion, etc.
ei)rh/nhn poiei=sqai make peace (of one nation at war with another).
ei)rh/nhn poiei=n bring about a peace (between opponents, nations at war: of an individual).
qh/ra_n poiei=sqai ( = qhra=n hunt, qh/ra_n poiei=n arrange a hunt.
lo/gon poiei=sqai ( = le/gein) deliver a speech, lo/gon poiei=n compose a speech.
naumaxi/a_n poiei=sqai ( = naumaxei=n) fight a naval battle.
naumaxi/a_n poiei=n bring on a naval battle (of the commander).
o(do\n poiei=sqai ( = o(deu/ein) make a journey, o(do\n poiei=n build a road.
po/lemon poiei=sqai wage war, po/lemon poiei=n bring about a war.
sponda\_s poiei=sqai conclude (make) a treaty , or truce.
sponda\_s poiei=n bring about a treaty , or truce.

The Causative Middle denotes that the subject has something done by another for himself:

e)gw\ ga/r se tau=ta e)didaca/mhn for I had you taught this
X. C. 1.6.2, parati/qesqai si=ton to have food served up 8. 6. 12, o(/soi o(/pla a)fh/|rhntai, taxu\ a)/lla poih/sontai all who have had their arms taken from them will soon get others made 6. 1. 12, e(autw=| skhnh\n kateskeua/sato he had a tent prepared for himself 2. 1. 30.
a. This force does not belong exclusively to the middle; cp. 1711.

Differences between Active and Middle.—As contrasted with the active, the middle lays stress on the conscious activity, bodily or mental participation, of the agent.
In verbs that possess both active and middle: bouleu/esqai deliberate, bouleu/ein plan, staqma=n measure, staqma=sqai calculate, skopei=n look at, skopei=sqai consider, e)/xesqai cling to, pau/esqai cease (1734. 14). The force of the middle often cannot be reproduced in translation (a)kou/esqai, ti_ma=sqai, a)riqmei=sqai, a)porei=sqai), and in some other cases it may not have been felt, as in o(ra=sqai in poetry (proora=sqai occurs in prose).
a. Many such verbs form their futures from the middle: a)kou/somai, a)/|somai, a(marth/somai. See 805.
b. In verbs in -euw, the middle signifies that the subject is acting in a manner appropriate to his state or condition: poli_teu/ein be a citizen, poli_teu/esqai act as a citizen, perform one's civic duties; presbeu/ein be an envoy, presbeu/esqai negotiate as envoy or send envoys (of the State in its negotiations). But this force of the middle is not always apparent.

title: Direct Reflexive Middle
definition:
The Direct Reflexive Middle represents the subject as acting directly *on themselves*. *Self* is here the direct object. Direct reflexive middle verbs often express external and natural acts, such as grooming: ἀλείφεσθαι anoint oneself or λοῦσθαι wash oneself. The part affected may be added in the accusative.
“**ἐπαίσατο** τὸν μηρόν” **X. C. 7.3.6**; ⇾ he smote his thigh
The reflexive pronoun may be used with the middle often for emphasis:
“ἑαυτὸν **ἀποκρύπτεσθαι**” **P. R. 393c**; ⇾ to hide himself

smyth.text:
The Direct Reflexive Middle represents the subject as acting directly on himself. Self is here the direct object. So with verbs expressing external and natural acts, as the verbs of the toilet: a)lei/fesqai anoint oneself, lou=sqai wash oneself; and kosmei=sqai adorn oneself, stefanou=sqai crown oneself; gumna/zesqai exercise oneself.
a. The direct reflexive idea is far more frequently conveyed by the active and a reflexive pronoun, 1723.
b. The part affected may be added in the accusative:

e)pai/sato to\n mhro/n he smote his thigh
X. C. 7.3.6.

So with many other verbs, as i(/stasqai stand (place oneself), tre/pesqai turn (lit. turn oneself), dhlou=sqai show oneself, ta/ttesqai post oneself, a)pologei=sqai defend oneself (argue oneself off), fai/nesqai show oneself, appear, paraskeua/zesqai prepare onself, a)po/llusqai destroy oneself, perish.

Middle and Reflexive.—The reflexive pronoun may be used with the middle:

e(auto\n a)pokru/ptesqai to hide himself
P. R. 393c; often for emphasis, as in contrasts: oi( me/n fa_si basile/a_ keleu=sai/ tina e)pisfa/cai au)to\n *ku/_rw|, oi( d' e(auto\n e)pisfa/casqai some say that the king issued orders for some one to slay him (Artapates) over (the body of) Cyrus, while others say that he slew himself with his own hand
X. A. 1.8.29, cp. also ti/ th\n po/lin prosh=ke poiei=n, a)rxh\n kai\ turanni/da tw=n *(ellh/nwn o)rw=san e(autw=| kataskeuaco/menon *fi/lippon; what did it beseem the city to do when it saw Philip compassing for himself dominion and despotic sway over the Greeks?
D. 18.66.

examples.translation: He has not bathed since his birth

title: Speech Act Middle
definition:
Verbs expressing certain kinds of speech are often middle-only. Most speech act middle verbs have a rather specific lexical meaning, while more general or neutral verbs of saying tend to be active.
The subject of a speech act middle could be involved in the speech act in different ways, for example, as a beneficiary or an experiencer. Some middle verbs of speech may indicate a strong emotional or mental involvement of the subject.

examples.greek: τῇ δεκάτῃ δ᾽ ἀγορὴν δὲ καλέσσατο λαὸν Ἀχιλλεύς
examples.translation: but on the tenth Achilles called the people to assembly

examples.greek: ἀλλ᾽ ἔκ τοι ἐρέω καὶ ἐπὶ μέγαν ὅρκον ὀμοῦμαι
examples.translation: But I will speak out to you, and will swear thereto a mighty oath
So spoke the son of Peleus

examples.greek: ὅ σφιν ἐὺ φρονέων ἀγορήσατο καὶ μετέειπεν
examples.translation: He with good intent addressed the gathering and spoke among them

title: Body Motions
definition: The middles of body motion represent the subject changing their physical state voluntarily, thus being both the agent and the patient; for instance, ἅλλεσθαι jump, πέτεσθαι fly or ὀρχεῖσθαι dance. Under this category belongs the middle of collective motion. The middle of collective motion is used for verbs express a change of position of a group, such as gathering.

examples.greek: θάμβησεν δ᾽ Ἀχιλεύς, μετὰ δ᾽ ἐτράπετ᾽, αὐτίκα δ᾽ ἔγνω Παλλάδ᾽ Ἀθηναίην
examples.translation: Achilles was seized with wonder, and turned around, and immediately recognized Pallas Athene.

examples.greek: Μυρμιδόνων δ᾽ ἐπί τε κλισίας καὶ νῆας ἱκέσθην
examples.translation: … and came to the tents and the ships of the Myrmidons.

examples.greek: οἳ μὲν ἐκήρυσσον, τοὶ δ᾽ ἠγείροντο μάλ᾽ ὦκα
examples.translation: they made summons, and the men gathered full quickly.

examples.greek: οὗτος κἂν εἰς μαχαίρας κυβιστήσειε κἂν εἰς πῦρ ἅλοιτο
examples.translation: the man would do a somersault into a ring of knives; he would jump into fire.

title: Mental Activity, Process or Perception
definition:
Middle verbs of mental activity or process indicate intentional  or unintentional involvement of a subject in a mental or emotional activity; for instance, βούλομαι want or prefer, ἥδομαι enjoy or be glad, ἡγέομαι believe or consider. The subject could be involved in the verb as the agent or the experiencer.
The crucial difference between the mental activity and the mental process type is that mental activities are intentional while the mental process is unintentional. However, many verbs may indicate both mental processes and activities. Verbs of perception are also included in this category, expressing intentional or unintentional perception of a subject through their sensory organs.

examples.greek: ὅς κ᾽ εἴποι ὅ τι τόσσον ἐχώσατο Φοῖβος Ἀπόλλων
examples.translation: … who might say why Phoebus Apollo is so angry.
listening to the singer
the Hellenes are planning flight in their fear …

title: Reciprocal Middle
definition: Reciprocal middle verbs involve events that naturally need more than one participant, acting toward each other in the same manner, meaning that the relation between each participant to the other one is the same; for instance, with verbs of contending, conversing (questioning, replying), *greeting*, *embracing*, etc. The reciprocal middle is often found with compounds of διά.

smyth.text:
Reciprocal Middle.—With a dual or plural subject the middle may indicate a reciprocal relation. So with verbs of contending, conversing (questioning, replying), greeting, embracing, etc. The reciprocal middle is often found with compounds of dia/.

oi( a)_qlhtai\ h)gwni/zonto the athletes contended
T. 1.6, katasta/ntes e)ma/xonto when they had got into position they fought 1. 49, a)nh\r a)ndri\ diele/gonto they conversed man with man 8. 93,

e)pimei/gnusqai a)llh/lois to have friendly intercourse with one another
X. C. 7.4.5,

tau=ta dianemou=ntai they will divide this up among themselves
L. 21.14. So ai)tia=sqai accuse, lu_mai/nesqai maltreat, me/mfesqai blame, a(milla=sqai vie, parakeleu/esqai encourage one another.
a. The active may also be employed, as polemei=n wage war.
b. Some of these verbs have a passive aorist form, as diele/xqhn (812).

The reciprocal relation may also be expressed (1) by the use of the reflexive pronoun (cp. 1724) with the active:

fqonou=sin e(autoi=s they are mutually envious
X. M. 3.5.16; (2) by the use of a)llh/lwn, etc., with the active:

a)mfisbhtou=men a)llh/lois we are at variance with one another
P. Phae. 263a; (3) by repetition of the noun: ptwxo\s ptwxw=| fqone/ei = beggars envy each other Hesiod W. D. 26. The reflexive pronouns and a)llh/lwn, etc., may also be added to the middle.

examples.translation: the athletes contended
when they had got into position they fought
they conversed man with man
to have friendly intercourse with one another
they will divide this up among themselves

title: Spontaneous Process Middle
definition: The subjects of spontaneous process middle verbs go through internal, physical changes of state without initiating it directly. The importance difference from passive is that in spontaneous process middles the agent is unknown or unidentifiable. Most middles of this type also have a causative counterpart in the active voice; for instance, ἀπόλλυμαι perish and ἀπόλλυμι destroy.

examples.greek: (...) πέλας τῶν κήπων (...), ἐν τοῖσι φύεται αὐτόματα ῥόδα
examples.translation: (...) near the gardens (...), where roses grow of themselves

examples.greek: αἰεὶ δὲ πυραὶ νεκύων καίοντο θαμειαί
examples.translation: and constantly the pyres of the dead burned thick.

title: Passive voice
definition:
The passive voice represents the subject as acted on. The passive has been developed from the middle. With the exception of some futures and the aorist, the middle forms do duty as passives: αἱρεῖται takes for himself, i.e. *chooses*, and *is chosen*; κέχυται has poured itself, has been poured. The agent of the passive is regularly expressed by ὑπό and the genitive; sometimes by ἀπό, διά, ἐκ, παρά, πρός with the genitive, or by ὑπό with the dative (in poetry).
The passive may have the sense *allow oneself to be, get oneself:*
The dative, or a prepositional phrase, is regularly used with the passive to denote the instrument, means, or cause. The agent may be viewed as the instrument. The instrument of an action, when regarded as the agent, is personified, and may be expressed by ὑπό with the genitive.

smyth.text:
The passive voice represents the subject as acted on: e)w/qoun, e)wqou=nto, e)/paion, e)pai/onto they pushed, were pushed, they struck, were struck
X. C. 7.1.38.
a. The passive has been developed from the middle. With the exception of some futures and the aorist, the middle forms do duty as passives: ai(rei=tai takes for himself, i.e. chooses, and is chosen. (For this development of the passive, cp. the reflexive use in se trouver, sich finden.) So ke/xutai has poured itself, has been poured. In Homer there are more perfect middles used passively than any other middle tenses. Cp. 802.
b. Uncompounded e)sxo/mhn sometimes retained its use as a passive. e)sxe/qhn is late.

The passive may have the sense allow oneself to be, get oneself:

e)ca/gonte/s te kai\ e)cago/uenoi carrying and allowing ourselves to be carried across the border
P. Cr. 48d,

a)pexqh/sei *gorgi/a| you will incur the hatred of Gorgias
P. Phil. 58c.
Many future middle forms are used passively (807 ff.).

The future middle forms in -somai are developed from the present stem, and express durative action; the (later) future passives in -h/somai, -qh/somai are developed from the aorists in -hn and -qhn, and are aoristic. This difference in kind of action is most marked when the future middle forms are used passively, but it is not always found. toi=s a)/llois cumma/xois para/deigma safe\s katasth/sate, o(\s a)\n a)fi/sthtai, qana/tw| zhmiwso/menon give to the rest of the allies a plain example that whoever revolts shall be punished (in each case) with death
T. 3.40, e)a\_n a(lw=|, qana/tw| zhmiwqh/setai if he is convicted, he will be punished (a single occurrence) with death
D. 23.80, o( di/kaios masti_gw/setai, streblw/setai, dedh/setai, e)kkauqh/setai tw)fqalmw/ the just man will be scourged, racked, fettered, will have his eyes burnt out
P. R. 361e, ti_mh/somai I shall enjoy honour, ti_mhqh/somai I shall be honoured (on a definite occasion), w)felh/somai I shall receive lasting benefit, w)felhqh/somai I shall be benefited (on a definite occasion). Cp. 808, 809, 1911.

The second aorist passive was originally a second aorist active (of the -mi form) that was used intransitively to distinguish it from the transitive first aorist, as e)/fhna showed, e)fa/nhn appeared; e)/fqeira destroyed, e)fqa/rhn am destroyed; e)ce/plhca was terrified, e)cepla/ghn was alarmed. So e)da/hn learned, e)rru/hn flowed. Cp. e)/sthsa placed, e)/sthn stood (819).

In Hom. all the second aorist forms in -hn are intransitive except e)plh/ghn and e)tu/phn was struck. Most of the forms in -qhn are likewise intransitive in Hom., as e)fa/nqhn appeared (in Attic was shown).

The perfect passive in the third singular with the dative of the agent (1488) is often preferred to the perfect active of the first person. Thus pe/pra_ktai/ moi it has been done by me is more common than pe/pra_ga or pe/pra_xa I have done.

The passive may be passive of the middle as well as passive of the active: ai(rei=tai is taken or is chosen, bia/zetai does violence or suffers violence (is forced), h(|re/qh was taken or was chosen, e)gra/fh was written or was indicted (ge/grammai is commonly middle). The use of the passive as passive of the middle is post-Homeric.
a. When deponent verbs have a passive force, the future and aorist have the passive form: e)bia/sqhn I suffered violence (was forced), but e)biasa/mhn I did violence. This holds when there was once an active form. Cp. also ti_mwrei=sqai, metape/mpesqai, yhfi/zesqai, kuklei=sqai.
b. The aorist passive may have a middle sense (814).

Active Verbs with Aorist Passive in a Middle Sense.—The aorist passive of some active verbs has a reflexive or middle sense, either sometimes or always. Thus eu)frai/nw gladden, hu)fra/nqhn rejoiced, ki_ne/w move, e)ki_nh/qhn was moved or moved myself, fai/nw show, e)fa/nhn showed myself, appeared (e)fa/nqhn usually was shown).
a. These verbs are often called middle passives.
b. The middle and the passive form of the future of such verbs is often found, the middle being frequently preferred.

examples.translation: they pushed, were pushed, they struck, were struck
envied by Odysseus

examples.greek: οὐκ ἠξίουν οὗτοι ἡγεμονεύεσθαι ὑφ᾽ ἡμῶν
examples.translation: they did not think it right to be governed by us
carrying and allowing ourselves to be carried across the border
he is captured by a trireme

title: Assertions and Questions
definition:
The indicative states particular or general suppositions, makes affirmative or negative assertions and expressing beliefs, facts or assumptions. The indicative is also used for expressing requests, suggestions and questions.
In assumptions:
The indicative may be used to express a doubtful assertion about a present or past action (negative μή or μὴ οὐ). Such sentences are often regarded as questions with the effect of doubtful affirmation.
The indicative mood is frequently used in different types of subordinate clause, including temporal, conditional or relative clauses. The indicative in the subordinate clause may indicate a general assumption or statement, or it may be a modal indicative, for instance, in relative or conditional clauses referring to a counterfactual action.

smyth.text:
The indicative states particular or general suppositions, makes affirmative or negative assertions, which may or may not be absolutely true. Thus, in assumptions, e)ch/marte/ tis a)/_kwn: suggnw/mh a)nti\ ti_mwri/a_s tou/tw| suppose some one involuntarily committed an offence; for him there is pardon rather than punish- ment
D. 18.274, and often after kai\ dh/, as

kai\ dh\ teqna=si and suppose they are dead
E. Med. 386.

The indicative may be used to express a doubtful assertion about a present or past action (negative mh/ or mh\ ou)): a)ll' a)/ra . . . mh\ o( *kth/sippos h)=n o( tau=t' ei)pw/n but I suspect (i.e. perhaps) after all it was Ctesippus who said this
P. Eu. 290e,

a)lla\ mh\ tou=to ou) kalw=s w(mologh/samen but perhaps we did not do well in agreeing to this
P. Men. 89c. Such sentences are often regarded as questions with the effect of doubtful affirmation.

The indicative may be used alone where in English we employ an auxiliary verb: pisteu/wn de\ qeoi=s pw=s ou)k ei)=nai qeou\s e)no/mizen; since he trusted in the gods how could (or should) he believe there were no gods?
X. M. 1.1.5,

o)li/gou ei(=lon th\n po/lin a little more and they would have taken the city
T. 8.35, a)pwllu/meqa we might have perished (we were in danger of perishing)
X. A. 5.8.2. Cp. 2319.

The apodosis may be the simple indicative or any other form of the simple sentence appropriate to the thought.
a. Simple Indicative: ei) tou=t' e)/xei kalw=s, e)kei=no ai)sxrw=s if this is excellent, that is disgraceful
Aes. 3.188, ei) me\n (*)asklhpio\s)

qeou= h)=n, ou)k h)=n ai)sxrokerdh/s: ei) d' ai)sxrokerdh/s, ou)k h)=n qeou= if Asclepius was the son of a god, he was not covetous; if he was covetous, he was not the son of a god
P. R. 408c, ei)/ te/ ti a)/llo . . . e)ge/neto e)piki/ndu_non toi=s *(/ellhsi, pa/ntwn . . . mete/sxomen and if any other danger befell the Greeks, we took our share in all
T. 3.54,

h)= kalo\n . . . te/xnhma a)/ra ke/kthsai, ei)/per ke/kthsai in truth you do possess a noble art, if indeed you do possess it
P. Pr. 319a, ei)/per ge *da_rei/ou . . . e)sti pai=s . . . , ou)k a)maxei\ tau=t' e)gw\ lh/yomai if indeed he is a son of Darius, I shall not gain this without a battle
X. A. 1.7.9, *kle/arxos ei) para\ tou\s o(/rkous e)/lu_e ta\_s sponda/_s, th\n di/khn e)/xei assuming that Clearchus broke the truce contrary to his oath, he has his deserts 2. 5. 41, ei) de\ du/o e)c e(no\s a)gw=nos gege/nhsqon, ou)k e)gw\ ai)/tios but if two trials have been made out of one, I am not responsible
Ant. 5.85.
b. Indicative with a)/n (unreal indicative, 1786):

kai/toi to/te . . . to\n *(uperei/dhn, ei)/per a)lhqh= mou nu=n kathgorei=, ma=llon a)\n ei)ko/tws h)\ to/nd' e)di/wken and yet, if indeed his present charge against me is true, he would have had more reason for prosecuting Hyperides than he now has for prosecuting my client
D. 18.223 (here a)\n e)di/wken implies ei) e)di/wken, 2303). So also an unreal indicative without a)/n, 1774:

tou=to, ei) kai\ ta)/lla pa/nt' a)posterou=sin . . . a)podou=nai prosh=ken even if they steal everything else, they should have restored this
D. 27.37. In the above examples each clause has its proper force.
c. Subjunctive of exhortation or prohibition (cp. the indicative dei= or xrh/ with the infinitive, 1807):

o(/qen de\ a)peli/pomen e)pane/lqwmen, ei)/ soi h(dome/nw| e)sti/n but let us return to the point whence we digressed, if it is agreeable to you
P. Ph. 78b, ei) me\n i)/ste me toiou=ton . . . mhde\ fwnh\n a)na/sxhsqe if you know that I am such a man . . . do not even endure the sound of my voice
D. 18.10.
d. Optative of wish (cp. the indicative e)lpi/zw):

ka/kist' a)poloi/mhn, *canqi/a_n ei) mh\ filw= may I perish most vilely, if I do not love Xanthias
Ar. Ran. 579.
e. Potential optative: qauma/zo

Subordinate clauses are of three classes:
1. Substantival clauses: in which the subordinate clause plays the part of a substantive and is either the subject or the object:

dh=lon h)=n | o(/ti e)ggu/s pou basileu\s h)=n it was plain that the king was somewhere hard by
X. A. 2.3.6, ou)k i)/ste | o(/ ti poiei=te you do not know what you are doing 1. 5. 16.
2. Adjectival (attributive) clauses: in which the subordinate clause plays the part of an adjective, and contains a relative whose antecedent (expressed or implied) stands in the principal clause:

le/ge dh\ th\n e)pistolh\n | h(\n e)/pemye *fi/lippos come read the letter which Philip sent
D. 18.39 ( = th\n u(po\ *fili/ppou pemfqei=san).
3. Adverbial clauses: in which the subordinate clause plays the part of an adverb or adverbial expression modifying the principal clause in like manner as an adverb modifies a verb.

kraugh\n pollh\n e)poi/oun kalou=ntes a)llh/lous, w(/ste kai\ tou\s polemi/ous a)kou/ein they made a loud noise by calling each other so that even the enemy heard them
X. A. 2.2.17 (here w(/ste . . . a)kou/ein may be regarded as having the force of an adverb: and in a manner audible even to the enemy); pw=s a)\n ou)=n o)rqw=s dika/saite peri\ au)tw=n; ei) tou/tous e)a/_sete to\n nomizo/menon o(/rkon diomosame/nous kathgorh=sai ktl. how then would you judge correctly about them? if you permit (i.e. by permitting) them to make their accusations after having sworn the customary oath, etc.
Ant. 5.90. Cp. 1095 end.

The future indicative is used, especially in poetry, after o(/pws (rarely after w(s, o)/fra, and mh/) in the same sense as the subjunctive.
ou)de\ di' e(\n a)/llo tre/fontai h)\ o(/pws maxou=ntai nor are they maintained for any other single purpose than for fighting (lit. how they shall fight)
X. C. 2.1.21, si_ga=q', o(/pws mh\ peu/setai/ (fut.) tis . . . glw/sshs xa/rin de\ pa/nt' a)paggei/lh| (subj.)

ta/de keep silence, lest some one hear and report all this for the sake of talk
A. Ch. 265. In prose the future occurs with o(/pws in Xenophon and Andocides. This usage is an extension of that after verbs of effort (2211).

examples.translation: Clearchus was an exile
but what do you think of horses?

examples.greek: ἐξήμαρτέ τις ἄκων: συγγνώμη ἀντὶ τιμωρίας τούτῳ
examples.translation: suppose someone involuntarily committed an offence; for him there is pardon rather than punishment

examples.greek: ἀλλ᾽ ἄρα . . . μὴ ὁ Κτήσιππος ἦν ὁ ταῦτ᾽ εἰπών
examples.translation: but I suspect (i.e. perhaps) after all it was Ctesippus who said this

examples.greek: ἀλλὰ μὴ τοῦτο οὐ καλῶς ὡμολογήσαμεν
examples.translation: but perhaps we did not do well in agreeing to this

examples.greek: δῆλον ἦνι ὅτι ἐγγύς που βασιλεὺς ἦν
examples.translation: it was plain that the king was somewhere hard by

examples.greek: δοὐδὲ δι᾽ ἓν ἄλλο τρέφονται ἢ ὅπως μαχοῦνται
examples.translation: nor are they maintained for any other single purpose than for fighting (lit. how they shall fight)

title: Unfulfilled Obligation
definition: With impersonal verbs indicating obligation, propriety, necessity, or possibility, the indicative without ἄν is used to express an unfulfilled obligation.  Such expressions are ἔδει, χρῆν (or ἐχρῆν), προσῆκε, καιρὸς ἦν, ἄξιον ἦν, εἰκὸς ἦν, δίκαιον ἦν, αἰσχρὸν ἦν, ἐξῆν, καλῶς εἶχεν, verbals in \-τόν or \-τέον with ἦν, etc. Here, the indicative denotes that an action contrary to what has happened (often expressed by an infinitive) was or is required. This use of the indicative is a variation of the counterfactual indicative.

smyth.text:
Unfulfilled Obligation (Propriety, Possibility).—With the imperfect indicative of impersonal expressions denoting obligation, propriety, necessity, or possibility, the action of a dependent infinitive is usually not realized. (Examples 1775-1776.)
Such expressions are e)/dei, xrh=n (or e)xrh=n), prosh=ke, kairo\s h)=n, a)/cion h)=n, ei)ko\s h)=n, di/kaion h)=n, ai)sxro\n h)=n, e)ch=n, kalw=s ei)=xen, verbals in -to/n or -te/on with h)=n, etc.
a. For the use of these expressions (also with a)/n) in the apodosis of unreal conditions, see 2313, 2315.

Present.—Thus, e)/dei se tau=ta poiei=n you ought to be doing this (but are not doing it),

tou/sde mh\ zh=n e)/dei these men ought not to be alive
S. Ph. 418,

ti/ si_ga=|s; ou)k e)xrh=n si_ga=n why art thou silent? Thou shouldst not be silent
E. Hipp. 297,

ei)ko\s h)=n u(_ma=s . . . mh\ malakw=s, w(/sper nu=n, cummaxei=n you should not be slack in your alliance, as you are at present
T. 6.78.

Past.—e)/dei se tau=ta poih=sai (or poiei=n) you ought to have done this (but did not do it), e)ch=n soi e)lqei=n you might have gone (but did not go), e)nh=n au)tw=| tau=ta poih=sai he could have done this (almost equivalent to the potential indicative tau=ta e)poi/hsen a)/n, 1784),

e)/dei ta\ e)ne/xura to/te labei=n I ought to have taken the pledges then
X. A. 7.6.23,

a)/cion h)=n a)kou=sai it would have been worth hearing
P. Eu. 304d,

me/nein e)ch=n he might have remained
D. 3.17.

The Greek usage simply states the obligation (propriety, possibility) as a fact which existed in the past (and may continue to exist in the present). In English we usually express the non-fulfilment of the action.

Present or past time is denoted when the present infinitive is used. When the reference is to present time, the action of the present infinitive is always denied. Past time is denoted when the aorist infinitive is used.

The expressions in 1774 may also refer to simple past obligation (propriety, possibility) and have the ordinary force of past indicatives: e)/dei me/nein he had to remain (and did remain)
D. 19.124. The context determines the meaning; thus ti/ to\n su/mboulon e)xrh=n poiei=n; (
D. 18.190) by itself might mean either what was it the duty of the statesman to do or what was it the duty of the statesman to have done?

examples.translation: I ought to have taken the pledges then
it would have been worth hearing
he might have remained
why art thou silent? Thou shouldst not be silent
these men ought not to be alive

title: Unattainable Wish
definition:
The past indicative with εἴθε or with εἰ γάρ, without ἄν, is used to express a present or past wish which cannot be realized. The imperfect refers to present time, the aorist to past time (negative μή).
An unattainable wish may also be expressed by ὤφελον (ought) with the present or aorist infinitive:

smyth.text:
Unattainable Wish.—A wish, referring to the present or past, which cannot be realized, is expressed by a past tense of the indicative with ei)/qe or with ei) ga/r (negative mh/). The imperfect refers to present time, the aorist to past time (cp. 2304, 2305).
ei)/q' ei)=xes belti(_ous fre/nas would that thou hadst (now) a better heart
E. El. 1061,

ei)/qe soi to/te sunegeno/mhn would that I had then been with thee
X. M. 1.2.46.

An unattainable wish may also be expressed by w)/felon (ought) with the present or aorist infinitive: w)/fele *ku=ros zh=n would that Cyrus were (now) alive (Cyrus ought to be alive)
X. A. 2.1.4 (1775). The negative is mh/:

mh/pot' w)/felon lipei=n th\n *sku=ron would that I had never left Scyros
S. Ph. 969. ei)/qe or ei) ga/r (poet. ai)/qe, w(s) may be used before w)/felon: ei) ga\r w)/felon oi(=oi/ te ei)=nai oi( polloi\ kaka\ e)rga/zesqai would that the multitude were able to do evil Pl. Cr. 44 d.

e)boulo/mhn followed by an infinitive may express an unattainable wish: e)boulo/mhn me\n ou)k e)ri/zein e)nqa/de I would that I were not contending here (as I am)
Ar. Ran. 866. (e)boulo/mhn a)/n vellem, 1789.)

The indicative is also used in other than simple sentences: in final sentences (2203); in object sentences after verbs of effort (2211), of caution (2220 a), of fearing (2231, 2233); in consecutive sentences with w(/ste so that (2274), in conditional sentences (2300, 2303, 2323, 2326); in temporal sentences (2395); in object sentences after o(/ti and w(s with a verb of saying, etc. (2577 ff.).

## INDICATIVE WITH a)/n

examples.translation: would that thou hadst (now) a better heart
would that I had then been with thee
would that Cyrus were (now) alive (Cyrus ought to be alive)

examples.greek: εἰ γὰρ ὤφελον οἷοί τε εἶναι οἱ πολλοὶ κακὰ ἐργάζεσθαι
examples.translation: would that the multitude were able to do evil

title: Counterfactual Indicative
definition: The indicative of the historical tenses with ἄν (κέν) may indicate counterfactual (or unreal) actions. The imperfect refers to the present or the past, the aorist to the past (rarely to the present), the pluperfect to the present (less commonly to the past). This use of the indicative with ἄν undicating unreality is closely connected to past potential use of the indicative. The past potential use of the indicative with ἄν (κέν) expresses past potentiality, probability (cautious statement), or necessity.

examples.greek: τότε δ᾽ αὐτὸ τὸ πρᾶγμ᾽ ἂν ἐκρίνετο ἐφ᾽ αὑτοῦ
examples.translation: but the case would then have been decided on its own merits
and in that case it were far better

examples.greek: ἐβουλόμην ἂν Σίμωνα τὴν αὐτὴν γνώμην ἐμοὶ ἔχειν
examples.translation: I should have liked Simon to be (or I wish Simon were) of the same mind as myself
which they could not have expected

examples.greek: τίς γὰρ ἂν ᾠήθη ταῦτα γενέσθαι;
examples.translation: for who would have expected these things to happen?
one might (could, would) have known

examples.greek: ὑπό κεν ταλασίφρονά περ δέος εἷλεν
examples.translation: fear might have seized even a man of stout heart

title: Hortatory Subjunctive
definition: The hortatory subjunctive (present or aorist) is used to express a request or a proposal (negative μή). The hortatory use of the subjunctive compensates for the absence of an imperative of the first person and is more common in the first person plural than first person singular.

smyth.text:
Hortatory Subjunctive.—The hortatory subjunctive (present or aorist) is used to express a request or a proposal (negative mh/).
a. Usually in the first person plural: nu=n i)/wmen kai\ a)kou/swmen tou= a)ndro/s let us go now and hear the man P. Prot. 314 b, mh/pw e)kei=se i)/wmen let's not go there yet 311 a. a)/ge, fe/re (dh/), in Hom. a)/ge (dh/), sometimes precedes, as a)/ge skopw=men come, let us consider
X. C. 5.5.15. i)/qi (dh/) rarely precedes.
b. Less frequently in the first person singular, which is usually preceded (in affirmative sentences) by fe/re (dh/), in Hom. by a)/ge (dh/):

fe/re dh\ peri\ tou= yhfi/smatos ei)/pw let me now speak about the bill
D. 19.234.

The first person singular in negative exhortations (rare and poetic) may convey a warning or a threat: mh/ se, ge/ron, koi/lh|sin para\ nhusi\ kixei/w old man, let me not find thee by the hollow ships A 26. This use is often regarded as prohibitive (1800).
The hortatory use of the subjunctive compensates for the absence of an imperative of the first person.

The Negative in Questions.—The use of mh/ (not ou)) in questions is due to the fact that the construction of 1805 is simply the interrogative form of the hortatory subjunctive: fw=men let us say, mh\ fw=men; are we not to say? Distinguish po/teron bi/a_n fw=men h)\ mh\ fw=men ei)=nai; shall we say that it is force or that it is not?
X. M. 1.2.45, from fw=men tau=t' o)rqw=s le/gesqai h)\ ou)/ shall we say that this is well said or not? (ou)/ = ou)k o)rqw=s le/gesqai)
P. G. 514c.

examples.greek: νῦν ἴωμεν καὶ ἀκούσωμεν τοῦ ἀνδρός
examples.translation: let us go now and hear the man
let's not go there yet
come, let us consider

examples.greek: φέρε δὴ περὶ τοῦ ψηφίσματος εἴπω
examples.translation: let me now speak about the bill

title: Prohibitive Subjunctive
definition:
The subjunctive (in the second and third persons of the aorist) is often used to express prohibitions (negative μή). The third person is less common and usually represents the second person (see example below).
οὐ μή with the subjunctive of the second person in the dramatic poets occasionally expresses a strong prohibition:

smyth.text:
Prohibitive Subjunctive.—The subjunctive (in the second and third persons of the aorist) is often used to express prohibitions (negative mh/).
a. Usually in the second person:

mhde\n a)qu_mh/shte do not lose heart
X. A. 5.4.19. For the aorist subjunctive the present imperative may be employed (1840): mh\ poih/sh|s (or mh\ poi/ei) tau=ta do not do this (not mh\ poih=|s).
b. Less commonly in the third person, which usually represents the second:

u(pola/bh| de\ mhdei/s and let no one suppose
T. 6.84 ( = mh\ u(pola/bhte do not suppose).
c. The third person of the present subjunctive is rare: mh\ toi/nun tis oi)/htai ( = mh\ oi)w/meqa) let not any one think P. L. 861 E.
N.—ou) mh/ with the subjunctive of the second person in the dramatic poets occasionally expresses a strong prohibition:

ou) mh\ lhrh/sh|s don't talk nonsense
Ar. Nub. 367.

examples.translation: do not lose heart
and let no one suppose ( \= μὴ ὑπολάβητε do not suppose).
don't talk nonsense

title: Doubtful Assertion
definition:
The present subjunctive with μή may express a doubtful assertion, with μὴ οὐ a doubtful negation. The idea of apprehension or anxiety (real or assumed) is due to the situation. A touch of irony often marks this use, which is chiefly Platonic. With μή (of what may be true):
In Homer μή with the independent subjunctive is used to indicate fear and warning, or to suggest danger:

smyth.text:
Doubtful Assertion.—The present subjunctive with mh/ may express a doubtful assertion, with mh\ ou) a doubtful negation. The idea of apprehension or anxiety (real or assumed) is due to the situation. A touch of irony often marks this use, which is chiefly Platonic. With mh/ (of what may be true): mh\ a)groiko/teron h)=| to\ a)lhqe\s ei)pei=n I suspect it's rather bad form (lit. too rude) to tell the truth
P. G. 462e. With mh\ ou) (of what may not be true):

a)lla\ mh\ ou)x ou(/tws e)/xh| but I rather think this may not be so
P. Crat. 436b,

mh\ ou)k h)=| didakto\n a)reth/ virtue is perhaps not a thing to be taught
P. Men. 94e.

In Hom. mh/ with the independent subjunctive is used to indicate fear and warning, or to suggest danger: mh/ ti xolwsa/menos r(e/ch| kako\n ui(=as *)axaiw=n may he not (as I fear he may) in his anger do aught to injure the sons of the Achaeans B 195. Usually with the aorist, rarely with the present subjunctive (
o 19). The constructions of 1801, 1802 are used as object clauses after verbs of fearing (2221).

o(/pws mh/ is occasionally so used with the aorist subjunctive, and with an idea of command: o(/pws mh\ fh/sh| tis may no one say (as I fear he may)
X. S. 4. 8. See 1921.

From the use in 1801 is probably developed the construction of ou) mh/ with the aorist (less often the present) subjunctive to denote an emphatic denial; as

ou) mh\ pau/swmai filosofw=n I will not cease from searching for wisdom
P. A. 29d,

ou)ke/ti mh\ du/nhtai basileu\s h(ma=s katalabei=n the king will no longer be able to overtake us
X. A. 2.2.12.

examples.greek: μὴ ἀγροικότερον ᾖ τὸ ἀληθὲς εἰπεῖν
examples.translation: I suspect it's rather bad form (lit. too rude) to tell the truth
but I rather think this may not be so
virtue is perhaps not a thing to be taught

examples.greek: μή τι χολωσάμενος ῥέξῃ κακὸν υἷας Ἀχαιῶν
examples.translation: may he not (as I fear he may) in his anger do aught to injure the sons of the Achaeans

title: Deliberative Subjunctive
definition:
The deliberative subjunctive (present or aorist) is used for expressing doubt of the speaker about what to do or say (negative μή). It is often used  in the first person.
The subjunctive question does not refer to a future fact, but to what is, under the present circumstances, advantageous or proper to do or say. βούλει, βούλεσθε (poet. θέλεις, θέλετε) often precede the subjunctive.

smyth.text:
From the use in 1801 is probably developed the construction of ou) mh/ with the aorist (less often the present) subjunctive to denote an emphatic denial; as

ou) mh\ pau/swmai filosofw=n I will not cease from searching for wisdom
P. A. 29d,

ou)ke/ti mh\ du/nhtai basileu\s h(ma=s katalabei=n the king will no longer be able to overtake us
X. A. 2.2.12.

Deliberative Subjunctive.—The deliberative subjunctive (present or aorist) is used in questions when the speaker asks what he is to do or say (negative mh/).
a. Usually in the first person: ei)/pwmen h)\ si_gw=men; shall we speak or keep silence?
E. Ion 758, ti/ dra/_sw; poi= fu/gw; what am I to do? whither shall I fly?
E. Med. 1271, mh\ fw=men; shall we not say?
P. R. 554b.
b. The (rare) second person is used in repeating a question: A. ti/ soi piqw/meqa; B. o(/ ti pi/qhsqe; A. In what shall we take your advice? B. In what shall you take my advice?
Ar. Av. 164.
c. The third person is generally used to represent the first person; commonly with ti\s, as ti/ tis ei)=nai tou=to fh=|; how shall anyone say this is so? ( = ti/ fw=men;)
D. 19.88.
N.—The subjunctive question does not refer to a future fact, but to what is, under the present circumstances, advantageous or proper to do or say.

bou/lei, bou/lesqe (poet. qe/leis, qe/lete) do you wish often precede the subjunctive: bou/lei soi ei)/pw; do you wish me to say to you?
P. G. 521d. This is a fusion of two distinct questions: bou/lei do you wish? and ei)/pw shall I say?

The deliberative subjunctive may be replaced by a periphrasis with dei= or xrh/ and the infinitive, or by the verbal adjective in -te/on e)sti/. Thus, h(mei=s de\ prosme/nwmen; h)\ ti/ xrh\ poiei=n; and shall we wait? or what must we do?
S. Tr. 390, ti/ poihte/on; ( = ti/ poiw=men;) what are we to do?
Ar. P. 922.
a. For the deliberative future see 1916.
Deliberation in the past may be expressed by e)/dei, xrh=n (e)xrh=n), e)/mellon with the infinitive, and by -te/on (verbal adj.) h)=n.

The Negative in Questions.—The use of mh/ (not ou)) in questions is due to the fact that the construction of 1805 is simply the interrogative form of the hortatory subjunctive: fw=men let us say, mh\ fw=men; are we not to say? Distinguish po/teron bi/a_n fw=men h)\ mh\ fw=men ei)=nai; shall we say that it is force or that it is not?
X. M. 1.2.45, from fw=men tau=t' o)rqw=s le/gesqai h)\ ou)/ shall we say that this is well said or not? (ou)/ = ou)k o)rqw=s le/gesqai)
P. G. 514c.

examples.translation: shall we speak or keep silence?
what am I to do? whither shall I fly?
shall we not say?
do you wish me to say to you?

title: Anticipatory Subjunctive (Homeric)
definition: In Homer the subjunctive is often closely akin to the future indicative, and refers by anticipation to a future event (negative οὐ).

smyth.text:
Anticipatory Subjunctive (Homeric Subjunctive).—In Homer the subjunctive is often closely akin to the future indicative, and refers by anticipation to a future event (negative ou)): ou) ga/r pw toi/ous i)/don a)_ne/ras, ou)de\ i)/dwmai for never yet saw I such men, nor shall I see them A 262,

kai/ nu/ tis w(=d' ei)/ph|si and one will say
c 275. a)/n (ke/n) usually limits this subjunctive in Hom. (1813).
a. This futural subjunctive is retained in Attic only in subordinate clauses (2327), and in ti/ pa/qw (1811).

The subjunctive is used in ti/ pa/qw; what will become of me; what am I to do? (lit. what shall I undergo?) as
P. Eu. 302d. So ti/ ge/nwmai; quid me fiet? Thus, w)/ moi e)gw/, ti/ pa/qw; ti/ nu/ moi mh/kista ge/nhtai; ah, woe's me! what is to become of me? what will happen unto me at the last?
e 465. The subjunctive here is not deliberative, but refers to a future event.

The subjunctive without a)/n is also used in dependent clauses of purpose (2196), after verbs of fearing (2225), in the protasis of conditional (2327, 2339) and conditional relative sentences (2567 b).

## SUBJUNCTIVE WITH a)/n

examples.greek: οὐ γάρ πω τοίους ἴδον ἀνέρας, οὐδὲ ἴδωμαι
examples.translation: for never yet saw I such men, nor shall I see them
and one will say

title: Emphatic Denial
definition: The subjunctive with οὐ μή can indicate an emphatic denial, expressing a strong belief that something will not happen.

smyth.text:
From the use in 1801 is probably developed the construction of ou) mh/ with the aorist (less often the present) subjunctive to denote an emphatic denial; as

ou) mh\ pau/swmai filosofw=n I will not cease from searching for wisdom
P. A. 29d,

ou)ke/ti mh\ du/nhtai basileu\s h(ma=s katalabei=n the king will no longer be able to overtake us
X. A. 2.2.12.

examples.greek: οὐκέτι μὴ δύνηται βασιλεὺς ἡμᾶς καταλαβεῖν
examples.translation: the king will no longer be able to overtake us
I will not cease from searching for wisdom
he will certainly not obey

title: In subordinate clause
definition:
The subjunctive mood is frequently used in different types of subordinate clause, including temporal, conditional or relative clauses. Indefinite subjunctive with ἄν is used to represent actions that are occurring repeatedly or generically. Prospective subjunctive with ἄν indicates an action that is definitely or probably occurring in the future. Subjunctive dependent clauses regularly take ἄν except in the older language. The omission of ἄν is sometimes due to clerical error, sometimes perhaps to a sense of euphony, sometimes to a survival of the older construction.
The present and aorist indicative and subjunctive (usually without ἄν) are regularly used in similes with ὡς, ὡς εἰ, ὡς εἴ τε as if, ὡς ὅτε, ὡς ὁπότε as when.

examples.greek: ὃς ἂν δακρῦσαι μάλιστα τὴν θύσασαν παραχρῆμα ποιήσῃ πόλιν, οὗτος τὰ νικητήρια φέρει
examples.translation: and the man that succeeds at once in drawing most tears from the sacrificing city carries off the palm of victory.

examples.greek: ὡς ἐγώ ὁπότερος ἂν σφῷν νῦν με μᾶλλον εὖ ποιῇ, τούτῳ παραδώσω τῆς πυκνὸς τὰς ἡνίας
examples.translation: to whichever of you shall treat me best I hand over the reins of state.

examples.greek: οἱ δ᾽, ὥς τ᾽ αἰγυπιοὶ . . . πέτρῃ ἐφ᾽ ὑψηλῇ μεγάλα κλάζοντε μάχωνται, ὣς οἱ κεκλήγοντες ἐπ᾽ ἀλλήλοισιν ὄρουσαν
examples.translation: and they, like vultures who contend with loud screams on a lofty cliff, even so they rushed screaming against each other

title: Optative of Wish
definition:
The optative without ἄν is used to express a wish referring to the future.  (negative μή). The optative of wish, or cupitive optative, is often introduced by εἰ γάρ, εἴθε (Hom. αἰ γάρ, αἴθε), or by εἰ, ὡς (both poetical).
The optative introduced by εἰ γάρ, etc. is sometimes explained as a protasis with the conclusion omitted:
An unattainable wish, referring to the present, may be expressed by the present optative in Homer:
Under wishes are included execrations and protestations:
The optative may indicate rhetorical wishes, willingness, or indifferance as in imprecations.

smyth.text:
Optative of Wish.—In independent sentences the optative without a)/n is used to express a wish referring to the future (negative mh/): w)= pai=, ge/noio patro\s eu)tuxe/steros ah, boy, mayest thou prove more fortunate than thy sire
S. Aj. 550. From this use is derived the name of the mood (Lat. opto wish).
a. So even in relative sentences:

e)a/_n pote, d\ mh\ ge/noito, la/bwsi th\n po/lin if ever they capture the city, which Heaven forbid
L. 31.14.
b. Under wishes are included execrations and protestations:

e)coloi/mhn may I perish
Ar. Ach. 324,

kai/ s' e)pidei/cw, h)\ mh\ zw/|hn, dwrodokh/santa and I will prove that you took bribes, or may I not live
Ar. Eq. 833.

The optative of wish is often introduced by ei) ga/r, ei)/qe (Hom. ai' ga/r, ai)/qe), or by ei), w(s (both poetical):

ei) ga\r ge/noito would that it might happen
X. C. 6.1.38,

w(s o)/loito may he perish
S. El. 126. (w(s is properly an exclamation: how.)

The optative introduced by ei) ga/r, etc. is sometimes explained as a protasis with the conclusion omitted: ei)/qe fi/los h(mi=n ge/noio oh, if you would become our friend
X. H. 4.1.38. Cp. 2352 e.
An unattainable wish, referring to the present, may be expressed by the present optative in Homer: ei)/q' h(bw/oimi would that I were young again H 157.

Unattainable wishes, when they refer to the future, may be expressed by the optative:

ei)/ moi ge/noito fqo/llos e)n braxi/_osi would that I had a voice in my arms
E. Hec. 836. Wishes represented as hopeless are expressed in the postHomeric language by the past tenses of the indicative (1780) or by w)/felon (1781).

Hom. often uses the optative with a concessive or permissive force: e)/peita de\ kai/ ti pa/qoimi after that I may (lit. may I) suffer come what will
*f 274.

examples.translation: ah, boy, mayest thou prove more fortunate than thy sire
may he perish
oh, if you would become our friend
would that it might happen
would that I were young again
may I perish

examples.greek: ἐν πυρὶ δὴ βουλαί τε γενοίατο μήδεά τ᾽ ἀνδρῶν
examples.translation: into the fire let us cast all counsels and plans of warriors

title: Command or Request
definition: The optative may express a command, exhortation, or request in the second-person with a force nearly akin to the imperative. In the first-person, it is used to express compliance to a wish or command or taking permission to do something.

smyth.text:
Imperative Optative.—The optative may express a command or exhortation with a force nearly akin to the imperative:

*xeiri/sofos h(goi=to let Chirisophus lead
X. A. 3.2.37.

examples.translation: let Chirisophus lead
I will speak then

title: Potential Optative
definition: The potential optative with ἄν states a future possibility, propriety, or likelihood. The potential optative, which in Attic regularly takes ἄν, is occasionally found in Homer and later poetry in an earlier form, without that particle. The potential optative is sometimes used to soften the statement of an opinion or fact, or to express irony.

smyth.text:
Potential Optative.—The potential optative, which in Attic regu larly takes a)/n (1824), is occasionally found in Homer and later poetry in an earlier form, without that particle:

r(ei=a qeo/s g' e)qe/lwn kai\ thlo/qen a)/ndra saw/sai easily might a god, if he so willed, bring a man safe even from afar
g 231,

qa=sson h)\ le/goi tis quicker than a man could speak
E. Hipp. 1186. This construction is suspected in prose.
a. Usually in negative sentences or in questions expecting a negative answer (with ou)): ou) me\n ga/r ti kakw/teron a)/llo pa/qoimi for I could not (conceivably) suffer anything worse T 321, tea/_n, *zeu=, du/nasin ti/s a)ndrw=n u(perbasi/a_ kata/sxoi; thy power, oh Zeus, what trespass of man can check?
S. Ant. 604.

The optative after ou)k e)/stin o(/stis (o(/pws, o(/poi) in the dramatists is probably potential:

ou)k e)/sq' o(/pws le/caimi ta\ yeudh= kala/ I could not call false tidings fair
A. Ag. 620. a)/n is usually employed in this construction.

The optative without a)/n (ke/n) is also used elsewhere, as in purpose clauses (2196) and clauses of fearing (2225) after a secondary tense; in the apodosis of conditional sentences (2300 d, 2326 d, 2333), in relative sentences (2566, 2568); and as the representative of the indicative (2615) or subjunctive (2619) in indirect discourse after secondary tenses.

## OPTATIVE WITH a)/n

Potential Optative.—The potential optative with a)/n states a future possibility, propriety, or likelihood, as an opinion of the speaker; and may be translated by may, might, can (especially with a negative), must, would, should (rarely will, shall). So in Latin velim, videas, cognoscas, credas.

gnoi/hs d' a)\n o(/ti tou=q' ou(/tws e)/xei you may see that this is so
X. C. 1.6.21,

a(/pantes a)\n o(mologh/seian all would agree
I. 11.5, h(de/ws a)\n e)roi/mhn I (would gladly ask) should like to ask
D. 18.64,

ou)k a)\n la/bois thou canst not take
S. Ph. 103,

le/goim' a)\n ta/de I will tell this
A. Supp. 928. The second person singular is often indefinite (one), as gnoi/hs a)/n (cognoscas) = gnoi/h tis a)/n.
a. The potential optative ranges from possibility to fixed resolve. The aorist optative with a)/n and a negative is very common.
b. When stress is laid on the idea of possibility and power, necessity and obligation, Greek uses du/namai, dei= or xrh/ with the infinitive (statement of fact).
c. The potential optative with a)/n is also used in dependent sentences; in purpose clauses (2202 b), in object clauses after verbs of effort (2216) and verbs of fearing (2232), in causal clauses (2243), in result clauses (2278), in the apodosis of conditional (see 2356) and conditional relative sentences (2566). In indirect discourse the infinitive with a)/n or the participle with a)/n may represent the optative with a)/n (1845 ff.).

Usually these optatives are not limited by any definite condition present to the mind, and it is unnecessary to supply any protasis in thought. In some cases a protasis is dormant in a word of the sentence (such as dikai/ws, ei)ko/tws). Thus, in

ou(\s a)xari/stous ei)=nai dikai/ws a)\n u(polamba/noite whom you would justly consider to be ungrateful
Aes. 3.196, dikai/ws may stand for ei) dikai/ws u(polamba/noite: if you should consider the matter justly. So ou)/te e)sqi/ousi plei/w h)\ du/nantai fe/rein: diarragei=en ga\r a)/n ktl. they neither eat more than they can bear, for otherwise (if they should eat more: ei) e)sqi/oien plei/w) they would burst
X. C. 8.2.21. The potential optative is also used as the main clause of less vivid conditions (2329) in which the protasis has the optative by assimilation to the mood of the apodosis.

The potential optative with a)/n is used to soften the statement of an opinion or fact, or to express irony: e(/tero/n ti tou=t' a)\n ei)/h this is (would be) another matter
D. 20.116, nosoi=m' a)/n, ei) no/shma tou\s e)xqrou\s stugei=n I must be mad, if it is madness to hate one's foes
A. Pr. 978. So often with i)/sws or ta/xa perhaps.
a. With a negative, the potential optative may have the force of a strong assertion:

ou) ga\r a)\n a)pe/lqoim', a)lla\ ko/yw th\n qu/ra_n for I will not go away, but I will knock at the door
Ar. Ach. 236.

bouloi/mhn a)/n (velim) is often used as a softened optative of wish: bouloi/mhn a)\n tou=to ou(/tw gene/sqai I could wish that this might be the result (ou(/tw ge/noito may it result thus)
P. A. 19a. For e)boulo/mhn a)/n see 1789.

The present and aorist are used of what will be, or what will prove to be, true (future realization of a present fact): a)reth\ a)/ra, w(s e)/oiken, u(gi/eia/ tis a)\n ei)/h virtue then, it seems, will (prove to) be a kind of health
P. R. 444d. The perfect is used of what will prove to be the case as regards a completed action: pw=s a)\n lelh/qoi; how can it have escaped my knowledge?
X. S. 3. 6. Usually the perfect is here equivalent to the present.

examples.greek: γνοίης δ᾽ ἂν ὅτι τοῦθ᾽ οὕτως ἔχει
examples.translation: you may see that this is so
all would agree
I (would gladly ask) should like to ask
thou canst not take
I will tell this
quicker than a man could speak

title: In subordinate clause
definition:
The optative mood is frequently used in different types of subordinate clause, including temporal, conditional or relative clauses. In subordinate clauses in the secondary or historic sequence, the optative may replace the original mood. This use of optative is limited to the subordinate clauses of the secondary sequence (imperfect, aorist, pluperfect) and does not appear in primary sequence (present, perfect, future) and is called the oblique optative. The indefinite subordinate clauses of historic sequence may use the iterative optative (without ἄν) to express a habitual or repeated action.
When an optative of the principal clause refers to *future* time (potential optative and optative of wish), the subordinate clause takes the optative by assimilation.

smyth.text:
Assimilation to the Optative.—When an optative of the principal clause refers to future time (potential optative and optative of wish), the subordinate clause takes the optative by assimilation in the following cases.
a. Conditional relative clauses (regularly): pw=s ga\r a)/n (1832) tis, a(/ ge mh\ e)pi/staito, tau=ta sofo\s ei)/h; for how could any one be wise in that which he does not know?
X. M. 4.6.7, ti/s mi_sei=n du/nait' a)/n u(f' ou(= ei)dei/h kalo/s te kai\ a)gaqo\s nomizo/menos; who could hate one by whom he knew that he was regarded as both beautiful and good?
X. S. 8. 17,

e)/rdoi tis h(\n e(/kastos ei)dei/h te/xnhn would that every man would practise the craft that he understood
Ar. Vesp. 1431, ti/s a)\n . . . mo/loi (1832),

o(/stis diaggei/leie ta)_m' ei)/sw kaka/ would that some one would come to report within my tale of woe
E. Hel. 435.
N. 1.—If the relative has a definite antecedent, assimilation does not take place; but not all relative clauses with an indefinite antecedent are assimilated. Cp.

w(/sper a)\n u(_mw=n e(/kastos ai)sxunqei/h th\n ta/cin lipei=n h(\n a)\n taxqh=| e)n tw=| pole/mw| as each one of you would be ashamed to leave the post to which he may be appointed in war
Aes. 3.7.
N. 2.—A relative clause depending on an infinitive rarely takes the optative:

a)lla\ tou= me\n au)to\n le/gein a(\ mh\ safw=s ei)dei/h ei(/rgesqai dei= one should abstain from saying oneself what one does not know for certain
X. C. 1.6.19. (See 2573.)
b. Temporal clauses (regularly): teqnai/hn, o(/te moi mhke/ti tau=ta me/loi may I die when these things no longer delight me Mimnermus 1. 2,

o( me\n e(kw\n peinw=n fa/goi a)\n o(po/te bou/loito he who starves of his own free will can eat whenever he wishes
X. M. 2.1.18, ei) de\ pa/nu spouda/zoi fagei=n, ei)/poim' a)\n o(/ti para\ tai=s gunaici/n e)stin, e(/ws paratei/naimi tou=ton ktl. but if he was very desirous of eating, I would tell him that “he was with the women” until I had tortured him, etc.
X. C. 1.3.11,

o)/loio mh/pw, pri\n ma/qoimi perish not yet . . . until I learn
S. Ph. 961. But

ou)k a)\n a)pe/lqoimi pri\n a)\n panta/pa_sin h( a)gora\_ luqh=| I shall not be leaving until the gathering in the market-place is quite dispersed
X. O. 12.1.
c. Final and object clauses (rarely in prose, but occasionally after an optative of wish in poetry): peirw/|mhn (a)\n) mh\ pro/sw u(_mw=n ei)=nai, i(/na, ei)/ pou kairo\s ei)/h, e)pifanei/hn I will try to keep not far away from you, in order that, if the

An optative referring to general past time in a general supposition usually assimilates the mood of a conditional relative or temporal clause depending on that optative.
e)/xairen o(po/te ta/xista tuxo/ntas w(=n de/ointo a)pope/mpoi but he was wont to rejoice whenever he dismissed without delay his petitioners with their requests granted (lit. obtaining what they wanted) X. Ag. 9. 2. But the indicative may remain unassimilated, as

e)ka/lei de\ kai\ e)ti/_ma_ o(po/te tina\s i)/doi toiou=to/n ti poih/santas o(\ au)to\s e)bou/leto poiei=n and he was wont to honour with an invitation any whom he saw practising anything that he himself wished them to do
X. C. 2.1.30.
So when the optative refers to past time through dependence on a verb of past time, as

proskalw=n tou\s fi/lous e)spoudaiologei=to w(s dhloi/h ou(\s ti_ma=| summoning his friends he used to carry on a serious conversation with them in order to show whom he honoured
X. A. 1.9.28 (here ti_mw/|h would be possible).

Potential Optative.—The potential optative with a)/n states a future possibility, propriety, or likelihood, as an opinion of the speaker; and may be translated by may, might, can (especially with a negative), must, would, should (rarely will, shall). So in Latin velim, videas, cognoscas, credas.

gnoi/hs d' a)\n o(/ti tou=q' ou(/tws e)/xei you may see that this is so
X. C. 1.6.21,

a(/pantes a)\n o(mologh/seian all would agree
I. 11.5, h(de/ws a)\n e)roi/mhn I (would gladly ask) should like to ask
D. 18.64,

ou)k a)\n la/bois thou canst not take
S. Ph. 103,

le/goim' a)\n ta/de I will tell this
A. Supp. 928. The second person singular is often indefinite (one), as gnoi/hs a)/n (cognoscas) = gnoi/h tis a)/n.
a. The potential optative ranges from possibility to fixed resolve. The aorist optative with a)/n and a negative is very common.
b. When stress is laid on the idea of possibility and power, necessity and obligation, Greek uses du/namai, dei= or xrh/ with the infinitive (statement of fact).
c. The potential optative with a)/n is also used in dependent sentences; in purpose clauses (2202 b), in object clauses after verbs of effort (2216) and verbs of fearing (2232), in causal clauses (2243), in result clauses (2278), in the apodosis of conditional (see 2356) and conditional relative sentences (2566). In indirect discourse the infinitive with a)/n or the participle with a)/n may represent the optative with a)/n (1845 ff.).

title: Command or Prohibition
definition: Under commands are included requests, entreaties, summons, prescriptions, exhortations, etc. All imperative tenses refer to the future. The negative with the imperative verbs is μή and indicates prohibition. In exhortations ἄγε, φέρε, ἴθι (usually with δή, sometimes with νύν), often precede the imperative.

smyth.text:
The imperative is used in commands and prohibitions (negative mh/). All its tenses refer to the future.
a. Under commands are included requests, entreaties, summons, prescriptions, exhortations, etc.
b. For the tenses of the imperative, see 1840; for the infinitive used as an imperative, see 2013.

## POSITIVE (COMMANDS）

In exhortations a)/ge, fe/re, i)/qi (usually with dh/, sometimes with nu/n), often precede the imperative:

a)/ge dh\ a)kou/sate come listen
X. Ap. 14,

a)/gete deipnh/sate go now, take your supper
X. H. 5.1.18,

a)ll' i)/qi ei)pe/ but come, say
P. G. 489e.

pa=s is sometimes used with the second person in poetry: a)/koue pa=s hear, every one
Ar. Thesm. 372.

The third person may be used in questions: ou)kou=n kei/sqw tau=ta; shall these points be established?
P. L. 820e. Cp. 1842 a.

The imperative may be used in assumptions (hypothetical imperative), to make a concession, or to grant permission:

e)mou= g' e(/nek' e)/stw let it be assumed as far as I am concerned
D. 20.14,

ou(/tws e)xe/tw w(s su\ le/geis assume it to be as you say
P. S. 201c. So even as a protasis:

deica/tw, ka)_gw\ ste/rcw let him set it forth and I will be content
D. 18.112.

## NEGATIVE (PROHIBITIONS）

Prohibitions are expressed by mh/ with the present or aorist subjunctive in the first person plural; by mh/ with the present imperative or the aorist subjunctive in the second and third person singular or plural (cp. 1800). The aorist imperative is rare in prohibitions.
A. I Person.—mh\ gra/fwmen (mh\ gra/ywmen):

mh\ mainw/meqa mhd' ai)sxrw=s a)polw/meqa let us not act like madmen nor perish disgracefully
X. A. 7.1.29.
B. 2 Person.—mh\ gra/fe (mh\ gra/fete):

mh\ qau/maze don't be astonished
P. G. 482a,

mh\ qorubei=te don't raise a disturbance
P. A. 21a,

ta\ me\n poi/ei, ta\ de\ mh\ poi/ei do this and refrain from doing that
P. Pr. 325d,

mh\ me/ga le/ge don't boast so
P. Ph. 95b.—mh\ gra/yh|s (mh\ gra/yhte):

mhde\ qauma/sh|s to/de and do not wonder at this
A. Ag. 879,

mh\ qorubh/shte don't raise a disturbance
P. A. 20e,

mh\ a)/llws poih/sh|s don't do otherwise
P. Lach. 201b, mhdamw=s a)/llws poih/sh|s
Ar. Av. 133.
N.—The type mh\ gra/fh|s is never used. mh\ gra/yon occurs rarely in poetry (
*d 410,
*s 134.—
w 248, S. fr. 453 parodied in
Ar. Thesm. 870).
C. 3 Person.—mh\ grafe/tw (mh\ grafo/ntwn):

mhdei\s didaske/tw let no one tell me
T. 1.86,

mhdei\s tou=t' a)gnoei/tw let no one be ignorant of this fact
Aes. 3.6. mh\ graya/tw (mh\ graya/ntwn):

mhdei\s nomisa/tw let no one think
X. C. 7.5.73,

mh/t' a)pognw/tw mhde\n mh/te katagnw/tw let him neither acquit nor condemn in any way
Aes. 3.60; and in five other passages giving the actual usage of the orators. In the third person the aorist imperative is much less common than the present imperative.
N.—The type mh\ gra/fh| is used only when the third person represents the first person (1800 c). mh\ gra/yh| is much more common than mh\ graya/tw in the orators, e.g.

mhdei\s qauma/sh| let no one be astonished
D. 18.199,

mhdei\s nomi/sh| let no one think
T. 3.13,
D. 23.1.
D. The perfect imperative is rare in prohibitions (mh\ pefo/bhsqe T 6. 17) and is usually poetical. Cp. 698, 712.

a. mh\ gra/fe, like don't write, is ambiguous and may mean, according to the situation, either cease writing or abstain from writing. Commonly mh\ gra/fe means do not go on writing, write no more, and is an order to stop an action already begun. In many cases, however, mh/ with the present imperative does not refer to the interruption of an action already begun, but to an action still in the more or less distant future against which the speaker urges resistance. Sometimes the reference to the future is directly or indirectly indicated by the context.
b. mh\ gra/yh|s usually has the force of (I beg that) you will not write, (take care that you) don't write, and is commonly a complete prohibition against doing something not already begun. Sometimes, and especially in expressions of a colloquial character, mh/ with the aorist subjunctive marks the speaker's interruption, by anticipation, of a mental (less often of a physical) action that is being done by the person he addresses; as mh\ qauma/sh|s (
P. L. 804b) in reply to an exclamation of surprise. Here the type mh\ gra/yh|s often expresses impatience.
c. If mh\ gra/fe elicits a reply, it is (a)ll') ou) gra/fw, while mh\ gra/yh|s is answered by (a)ll') ou) gra/yw. Thus,

mh/ m' e)kdi/daske toi=s fi/lois ei)=nai kakh/n. a)ll' ou' dida/skw do not teach me to be base to my friends. But I do not
S. El. 395, ei) ou)=n e)/xeis e)narge/steron h(mi=n e)pidei=cai w(s didakto/n e)stin h( a)reth/, mh\ fqonh/sh|s a)ll' e)pi/deicon. a)ll' . . . ou) fqonh/sw now if you can show us more clearly that virtue is capable of being taught, don't refuse, but show us. Well, I will not refuse
P. Pr. 320c. So mh\ gra/fe commonly answers gra/fw, as qauma/zw, h)=n d' e)gw/, kai\ au)to/s. a)lla\ mh\ qau/maz', e)/fh I myself am astonished, said I. Cease your astonishment, said she
P. S. 205b, cp.
S. El. 395. So mh\ gra/yh|s answers gra/yw, as in
Hdt. 3.140,
Ar. Lys. 1036.
d. mh\ gra/fe and mh\ gra/yh|s are often found in closely connected clauses, as

mhdamw=s qu/_maine/ moi, mhde/ m' e)pitri/_yh|s don't be angry with me at all, nor ruin me
Ar. Nub. 1478,

mh/t' o)knei=te mh/t' a)fh=t' e)/pos kako/n do not shrink from me nor utter any harsh words
S. O. C. 731. The second prohibition may be more specific than the first, as

siw/pa_: mhde\n ei)/ph|s nh/pion be silent, don't say anything childish
Ar. Nub. 105. Less often mh\ gra/yh|s is followed by mh\ gra/fe, as mh\ bohqh/sate tw=| peponqo/ti deina/: mh\ eu)orkei=te (they will say) ‘do no

The imperative may be used in subordinate clauses: kra_th=re/s ei)sin . . . w(=n kra=t' e)/reyon there are mixing-bowls, the brims of which thou must crown
S. O. C. 473.
a. Especially after oi)=sqa interrogative in dramatic poetry: oi)=sq' o(\ dra=son; do you know what you are to do?
E. Hec. 225, oi)=sq' w(s poi/hson; do you know how I bid you act?
S. O. T. 543. oi)=sq' o(/ has become a partially fossilized expression, and can be used as subject or be governed by a verb: oi)=sqa/ nun a(/ moi gene/sqw; do you know what I must have done for me?
E. I. T. 1203.

definition: The imperative may be used in many different expressions, including assumptions (hypothetical imperative), to make a concession, or to grant permission. The imperative is commonly used in greetings and curses.

title: Dynamic infinitive
definition:
The dynamic infinitive expresses an action, and complements verbs with meaning of want, desire, force, ask, command, try, teach, etc. The dynamic infinitive indicates a potential action, which may or may not be realized. The prolative infinitive which complement verbs that take an infinitive as the object are dynamic infinitives. Dynamic infinitives, among other uses, can indicate purpose, result, or limit the meaning of an adjective or a noun.
The tenses of this infinitive are purely aspectual, and denote only the stage of action. The negative of dynamic infinitive is μή, while the negative of declarative infinitive is οὐ.

smyth.text:
Infinitive of Purpose.—The infinitive may express purpose (usually only with verbs taking the accusative).

tau/thn th\n xw/ra_n e)pe/treye diarpa/sai toi=s *(/ellhsin he gave this land over to the Greeks to plunder
X. A. 1.2.19, to\ h(/misu (tou= strateu/matos) kate/lipe fula/ttein to\ strato/pedon he left half (of the army) behind to guard the camp 5. 2. 1, i)e/nai e)pi\ basile/a_ ou)k e)gi/gneto ta\ i(era/ the sacrifices did not turn out (favourable) for going against the king 2. 2. 3,

*)arista/rxw| . . . e)/dote h(me/ra_n a)pologh/sasqai you granted a day to Aristarchus to make his defence
X. H. 1.7.28, h( qu/ra_ h( e)mh\ a)ne/w|kto . . . ei)sie/nai tw=| deome/nw| ti e)mou= my door stood open for any petitioner of mine to enter 5. 1. 14,

pare/xw e)mauto\n e)rwta=n I offer myself to be questioned
P. A. 33b, ta\_s gunai=kas piei=n ferou/sa_s the women bringing (something) to drink
X. H. 7.2.9. Cp. also 2032 e.

The infinitive of purpose is used in prose especially after verbs meaning to give, entrust, choose, appoint, take, receive. Verbs signifying to send, go, come usually take the future active participle (2065); but
T. 6.50 has de/ka tw=n new=n prou/pemyan e)s to\n me/gan lime/na pleu=sai they sent ahead ten ships to sail into the great harbour; and in poetry the infinitive often denotes purpose after these verbs, and after ei)=nai in Homer (
*l 20) and Hdt. (5. 25).

After verbs meaning to have (or be) at one's disposition:

oi( stratiw=tai a)rgu/rion ou)k ei)=xon e)pisi_ti/zesqai the soldiers did not have money by means of which they could provision themselves
X. A. 7.1.7,

e)kei= skia/_ t' e)sti\ kai\ po/a_ kaqi/zesqai there is shade and grass to sit down in
P. Phae. 229b.

Infinitive of Result.—The infinitive may be used with w(/ste (sometimes with w(s) to denote a result, often an intended result. See 2260 ff.
a. Several verbs, substantives, and adjectives usually taking the infinitive also admit w(/ste with the infinitive (2271); and the infinitive is found where w(/ste with the infinitive might be expected: mnhmoneu/ousin a)feqe/nta tou=ton e)leu/qeron ei)=nai they recall that he was emancipated (lit. released so as to be free)
D. 29.25. Here the redundant infinitive expresses an intended result.
N.—This redundant use of ei)=nai is common in Hom. and Hdt.

## E. Absolute Infinitive

title: Declarative infinitive
definition:
The declarative infinitive expresses a belief, idea, or speech about an action in indirect discourse. Common verbs that take a declarative infinitive are φημί, λέγω, νομίζω, δοκέω, ἀγγέλλω, etc.
Unlike dynamic infinitives, declarative infinitives are considered to have relative temporal value. The present tense often indicates that the action is simultanious with the main verb, the future tense indicates posteriority, while the aorist tense is used for expressing anteriority. The perfect tense often indicates a state that is simultaneous with the verb of speech or opinion.
The declarative infinitive modified by ἄν has a potential meaning similar to potential optative (Note that the dynamic infinitive never takes ἄν).
The negative of declarative infinitive is οὐ, however, in some cases an emphatic μή is used.

smyth.text:
The infinitive is used as the object of verbs of saying and thinking. Such infinitives denote both time and stage of action (cp. 1866).
a. The finite verb of a sentence placed in dependence on a verb of saying or thinking that requires the infinitive, becomes infinitive, which infinitive stands in the relation of a substantive as subject or object of the leading verb. Commonly as object: thus, *ku=ros ni_ka=| Cyrus is victorious, when made the object of fhsi/ he says, becomes a part of a new sentence fhsi\ *ku=ron ni_ka=n, in which *ku=ron nika=n is the object of fhsi/. As subject, when the verb of saying is passive: thus, in le/getai *ku=ron ni_ka=n, the last two words form the subject of le/getai.

Verbs of saying are e.g.: say fhmi/, fa/skw, le/gw; confess o(mologw=; promise u(pisxnou=mai, u(pode/xomai, e)pagge/llomai, u(fi/stamai; pretend prospoiou=mai; swear o)/mnu_mi; deny a)parnou=mai; gainsay a)ntile/gw; dispute a)mfisbhtw=, etc.
Some verbs of saying admit other constructions than the infinitive, and especially o(/ti or w(s (2579). le/gw, ei)=pon, fra/zw, fwnw= with o(/ti or w(s mean say, with the infinitive command (1997).
a. fhmi/ say, assert, express the opinion that in classical Greek is almost always followed by the infinitive, but by o(/ti very often in the later language. fhmi\ o(/ti occurs in
X. A. 7.1.5 (fhmi\ w(s in
L. 7.19,
X. H. 6.3.7;
D. 4.48, 27. 19 by anacoluthon).
b. le/gw state (impart a fact) takes either the infinitive or o(/ti or w(s. The infinitive occurs usually with the passive (le/getai, etc.) either in the personal or impersonal construction (1982 a). The active forms of le/gw with the infinitive mean command (1997).
c. ei)=pon said usually takes o(/ti or w(s; with the infinitive, it commonly means commanded (1997). Cp. the double use of told.
N.—ei)=pon meaning said with the infinitive is rare, but occurs in good Attic prose:
And. 1.57, 80; Thuc. 7. 35; Lys. 10. 6, 10. 9, 10. 12; Xen. H. 1. 6. 7, 2. 2. 15, C. 5. 5. 24, S. 2. 13;
Is. 2.29; Lyc. 50;
Aes. 3.37, 3. 59; Dem. 15. 18; Plato, G. 473 a, 503 d, Lach. 192 b, Charm. 174 a, Hipp. Maj. 291 b, Pol. 263 c, 290 b, L. 654 a, Clitoph. 409 a, 410 b. In poetry this use is frequent.

Verbs of thinking almost always take the infinitive. Such are: think h(gou=mai, oi)/omai, dokw=, nomi/zw; hope e)lpi/zw; suppose u(polamba/nw; suspect u(popteu/w; guess ei)ka/zw; feel confident pisteu/w; disbelieve a)pistw=. The use of w(s is rare, while o(/ti is very rare (2580).
a. Verbs of perceiving sometimes take the infinitive by analogy to verbs of thinking; as a)kou/w, ai)sqa/nomai, punqa/nomai (2144).

Each tense of direct discourse is retained (with its proper meaning as regards stage of action) when it becomes infinitive in indirect discourse; but an imperfect is represented by the present infinitive; a pluperfect, by the perfect infinitive. See 1866, 1867.
An original ou) of direct discourse is generally, an original mh/ is always, retained in indirect discourse. But in some cases ou) becomes mh/ (2723 ff.).
The infinitive is the subject of the passive of verbs of saying and thinking (1982 a). So with dokei= it seems, fai/netai it is plain, etc.

The infinitive represents a finite verb after verbs of saying and thinking.
a.

eu)=noi/ fa_sin ei)=nai they assert that they are loyal
L. 12.49, ou)dei\s e)/fasken gignw/skein au)to/n nobody said that he knew him 23. 3, oi( h(gemo/nes ou)/ fa_sin (2692)

ei)=nai a)/llhn o(do/n the guides say there is no other road
X. A. 4.1.21,

pa/ntes e)rou=si to\ loipo\n mhde\n ei)=nai kerdalew/teron th=s a)reth=s everybody in time to come will say that there is nothing more profitable than bravery
X. C. 7.1.18. Other examples 1867.
b. basileu\s ni_ka=n h(gei=tai the king thinks he is victorious ( = ni_kw=, cp. 1887)
X. A. 2.1.11, oi)/omai be/ltiston ei)=nai I think it is best 5. 1. 8, u(pw/pteuon e)pi\ basile/a_ i)e/nai they suspected that they were to go against the king 1. 3. 1, (*swkra/ths)

to\ a)gnoei=n e(auto\n e)gguta/tw . . . mani/a_s e)logi/zeto ei)=nai Socrates was of the opinion that for a man not to know himself was very near to madness
X. M. 3.9.6.
c. When a word of saying is expressed or implied in what precedes, several infinitives may be used where the indicative is employed in translation. So in the narration in
X. C. 1.3.5-6.
The infinitive with a)/n represents an indicative with a)/n or a potential optative with a)/n. See 1846, 1848, 1849, 2270.

title: Idiomatic expressions
definition:
Certain idiomatic infinitives are used in parenthetical phrases to limit the application of a single expression or of the entire sentence. This is common with verbs of saying. In these constructions, the infinitive is used absolutely and is not dependant on any other words in the sentence.
Especially common is the absolute εἶναι in ἑκὼν willingly, intentionally, if you can help it, usually in negative or quasi-negative statements (ἑκών may be inflected). Some other expressions are ἐμοὶ δοκεῖν, ὡς ἐμοὶ κρῖναι, (ὡς) εἰκάσαι, (ὡς) ἀκοῦσαι, ὀλίγου δεῖν, μικροῦ δεῖν, etc.

smyth.text:
Certain idiomatic infinitives are used absolutely in parenthetical phrases to limit the application of a single expression or of the entire sentence.
a. Verbs of Saying.—w(s e)/pos ei)pei=n, w(s ei)pei=n so to speak, almost; (w(s) a(plw=s ei)pei=n, w(s sunelo/nti (1497) ei)pei=n, w(s (e)n braxei= or) sunto/mws ei)pei=n to speak briefly, concisely; w(s e)pi\ pa=n ei)pei=n, to\ su/mpan ei)pei=n speaking generally; sxedo\n ei)pei=n so to say, almost (paene dixerim); su\n qew=| ei)pei=n in God's name; and so w(s with le/gein, fra/zein, ei)rh=sqai, as w(s e)n tu/pw| ei)rh=sqai in general. Examples: a)lhqe/s ge w(s e)/pos ei)pei=n ou)de\n ei)rh/ka_sin not one word of truth, I may say, did they utter
P. A. 17a, a)gaqo\n me\n a(plw=s ei)pei=n ou)de\n ge/gone th=| po/lei in a word the State gained no advantage Dinarchus 1.33.
b. w(s (e)/pos) ei)pei=n is often used to limit too strict an application of a general statement, especially pa=s or ou)dei/s. Thus, pa/ntes w(s e)/pos ei)pei=n nearly every one, ou)dei\s w(s e)/pos ei)pei=n almost no one. It is thus used like paene dixerim; rarely, like ut ita dicam, to soften the strength of a metaphor.
c. Especially common is the absolute ei)=nai in e(kw\n willingly, intentionally, if you can help it, usually in negative or quasi-negative statements (e(kw/n may be inflected). Also in to\ kata\ tou=ton (e)pi\ tou/tw|) ei)=nai as far as he is concerned, w(s . . . ei)=nai as far as . . . is concerned, to\ nu=n ei)=nai at present. Examples:

ou)de\ ce/nois e(kw\n ei)=nai ge/lwta pare/xeis nor do you intentionally cause strangers to laugh
X. C. 2.2.15,

e(kou=sa ei)=nai ou)k a)polei/petai it is not willingly separated
P. Phae. 252a, to/ ge e)p' e)kei=non ei)=nai e)sw/qhs (a)/n) so far, at least, as it depended on him you would have been saved
L. 13.58.
d. Other expressions: e)moi\ dokei=n, w(s e)moi\ dokei=n, w(s e)moi\ kri=nai as it seems to me, in my opinion, (w(s) ei)ka/sai to make a guess, (w(s) sumba/llein to compare, (w(s) a)kou=sai to the ear, w(s u(momnh=sai to recall the matter, o(/son ge/ m' ei)de/nai as far as I know, etc.; o)li/gou dei=n, mi_krou= dei=n almost, all but (dei=n may be omitted, 1399). Examples: o( ga\r *kth/sippos e)/tuxe po/rrw kaqezo/menos tou= *kleini/ou, e)moi\ dokei=n for Ctesippus, it seems to me, happened to be sitting at a distance from Clinias
P. Eu. 274b,

mi_krou= dei=n tri/a ta/lanta almost three talents
D. 27.29.
e. Some of these absolute infinitives may be explained by reference to the ide
