title: Infinitive of Commands, Wishes, and Exclamations
definition:
A dynamic infinitive can be used for commands, instead of the second person of the imperative. The person addressed is regarded as the subject. This infinitive is more common in poetry than in prose.
The infinitive with a subject accusative may be used in the sense of the optative of wish.
The infinitive is often used in exclamations of surprise or indignation. The subject stands in the accusative.

smyth.text:
Infinitive in Commands.—The infinitive may be used for the second person of the imperative. The person addressed is regarded as the subject. This infinitive is commoner in poetry than in prose (where it has a solemn or formal force).
qarsw=n nu=n, *dio/mhdes, e)pi\ *trw/essi ma/xesqai with good courage now, Diomed, fight against the Trojans E 124, su\ de/, *kleari/da_ . . . ta\_s pu/la_s a)noi/ca_s e)pekqei=n but do you, Clearidas, open the gates and sally forth
T. 5.9.
a. This infinitive may be used in conjunction with an imperative:

a)kou/ete lew/|: kata\ ta\ pa/tria tou\s xo/as pi/_nein hear ye, good people! drink the Pitchers as our sires drank!
Ar. Ach. 1000.
b. The infinitive for the third person of the imperative often occurs in legal language (laws, treaties, etc.), and does not necessarily depend on the principal verb. Thus,

e)/th de\ ei)=nai ta\_s sponda\_s penth/konta and the treaty shall continue for fifty years
T. 5.18. In this construction the infinitive has the force of an infinitive dependent on e)/doce (it was voted that) or the like. So in medical language, as pi/_nein de\ u(/dwr it is well for the patient to drink water Hippocrates 1. 151.
c. The infinitive (with subject accusative) is rarely used for the third person of the imperative when there is an unconscious ellipsis of a word like do/s grant, or eu)/xomai I pray. Thus, teu/xea su_lh/sa_s fere/tw koi/la_s e)pi\ nh=as, sw=ma de\ oi)/kad' e)mo\n do/menai pa/lin let him strip off my arms and carry them to the hollow ships, but let him give back my body to my home H 78.
d. In negative commands (prohibitions) mh/ with the infinitive is poetic and Ionic: oi(=s mh\ pela/zein do not approach these ( = mh\ pe/laze)
A. Pr. 712,

mhde\ kalei=n pw o)/lbion and do not call him happy yet
Hdt. 1.32.

Infinitive in Wishes.—The infinitive with a subject accusative may be used in the sense of the optative of wish, usually with the same ellipsis as in 2013 c.

qeoi\ poli=tai, mh/ me doulei/a_s tuxei=n ye gods of my country, may bondage not be my lot!
A. Sept. 253, w)= *zeu=, e)kgene/sqai moi *)aqhnai/ous tei/sasqai oh Zeus, that it be granted to me to punish the Athenians!
Hdt. 5.105 (cp. w)= *zeu=, do/s me tei/sasqai mo/ron patro/s oh Zeus, grant that I may avenge my father's murder!
A. Ch. 18). This construction is very rare in Attic prose:

to\n kunhge/thn e)/xonta e)cie/nai . . . e)lafra\_n e)sqh=ta the hunter should go forth in a light dress
X. Ven. 6.11. Here no definite verb can be supplied.
a. The nominative with the infinitive (instead of the optative) after ai' ga/r occurs in Homer (
h 311,
w 376).

Infinitive in Exclamations.—The infinitive is often used in exclamations of surprise or indignation. The subject stands in the accusative.

e)me\ paqei=n ta/de that I should suffer this!
A. Eum. 837,

toioutoni\_ tre/fein ku/na to keep a dog like that!
Ar. Vesp. 835.
On the infinitive with e)f' w(=| (e)f' w(=|te) see 2279; with pri/n, see 2453.

title: Articular Infinitive
definition:
The infinitive in combination with a neuter singular article can function as a noun phrase. The articular infinitive, while having the character of a noun, retains the functions of a verb. The articular infinitive can be used similar to any other noun phrase and admits the constructions of an ordinary noun. It may indicate time (after verbs of saying or thinking), or may be timeless. The case is indicated by the article:
Nom. **τὸ** **ποιεῖν** making or to make, **τὸ** **ποιήσειν, τὸ ποιῆσαι, τὸ πεποιηκέναι**
Gen. **τοῦ** **ποιεῖν** of making, **τοῦ** **ποιήσειν, τοῦ ποιῆσαι**, etc.
Dat. **τῷ** **ποιεῖν** for making, by making, **τῷ** **ποιήσειν, τῷ ποιῆσαι**, etc.
Acc. **τὸ** **ποιεῖν, τὸ ποιήσειν, τὸ ποιῆσαι**, etc.
The negative of the articular infinitive is μή.

smyth.text:
The articular infinitive, while having the character of a substantive, retains the functions of a verb. In its older use the articular infinitive is a subject or object; the nearest approach to this use in Homer is

a)ni/_h kai\ to\ fula/ssein to watch is also trouble
u 52. In the tragic poets the genitive and dative are rarely used; in the speeches in Thucydides and in Demosthenes all of its four cases appear with great frequency. The articular infinitive may take dependent clauses.

The articular infinitive admits the constructions of an ordinary substantive.
Nom. to\ poiei=n making or to make, to\ poih/sein, to\ poih=sai, to\ pepoihke/nai
Gen. tou= poiei=n of making, tou= poih/sein, tou= poih=sai, etc.
Dat. tw=| poiei=n for making, by making, tw=| poih/sein, tw=| poih=sai, etc.
Acc. to\ poiei=n, to\ poih/sein, to\ poih=sai, etc.
The articular infinitive is treated as subject, predicate noun, and object like the simple infinitive (1984-1986).
The negative of the articular infinitive is mh/.
The articular infinitive may indicate time (after verbs of saying or thinking, 2034 g), or may be timeless.

The articular infinitive is in general used like the infinitive without the article, and may take a)/n; as regards its constructions it has the value of a substantive. The article is regularly used when the connection uniting the infinitive to another word has to be expressed by the genitive, the dative, or a preposition.
a. The articular infinitive is rarely used, like a true substantive, with the subjective genitive:

to/ g' eu)= fronei=n au)tw=n mi_mei=sqe imitate at least their wisdom
D. 19.269.

NOMINATIVE OF THE ARTICULAR INFINITIVE
Subject (1984):

ne/ois to\ si_ga=n krei=tto/n e)sti tou= lalei=n in the young silence is better than speech
Men. Sent. 387,

to\ *peloponnhsi/ous au)toi=s mh\ bohqh=sai pare/sxen u(_mi=n . . . *sami/wn ko/lasin the fact that the Peloponnesians did not come to their assistance enabled you to punish the Samians
T. 1.41.

GENITIVE OF THE ARTICULAR INFINITIVE
a. The genitive of the articular infinitive is used to limit the meaning of substantives, adjectives, and verbs.
b. Adnominal (1290):

tou= piei=n e)piqu_mi/a| from desire to drink
T. 7.84, pro\s th\n po/lin prosbalo/ntes e)s e)lpi/da h)=lqon tou= e(lei=n they attacked the city and entertained hopes of taking it 2.56.
c. Partitive (1306):

tou= qarsei=n to\ plei=ston ei)lhfo/tes having gained the greatest amount of courage
T. 4.34. After comparatives (1431): ti/ ou)=n e)stin . . . tou= toi=s fi/lois a)rh/gein ka/lli_on; what then is nobler than to help one's friends?
X. C. 1.5.13.
d. After verbs:

e)pe/sxomen tou= dakru/_ein we desisted from weeping
P. Ph. 117e (cp. 1392).
e. Purpose (cp. 1408), often a negative purpose:

tou= mh\ ta\ di/kaia poiei=n in order not to do what was just
D. 18.107,

e)teixi/sqh *)atala/nth . . . tou= mh\ lh|sta\_s . . . kakourgei=n th\n *eu)/boian Atalante was fortified to prevent pirates from ravaging Euboea
T. 2.32. More common is the use with u(pe/r (2032 g) or e(/neka.
f. Genitive Absolute (2070): e)p' e)kei/nois de\ o)/ntos ai)ei\ tou= e)pixeirei=n kai\ e)f' h(mi=n ei)=nai dei= to\ proamu/_nasqai since the power of attack is always in their hands, so in our hands should lie the power of repelling it in advance
T. 3.12.
g. After prepositions, e.g. a)nti\ tou= e)pi\ *ka_ri/a_n i)e/nai . . . e)pi\ *frugi/a_s e)poreu/eto instead of going against Caria, he marched toward Phrygia
X. H. 3.4.12,

a)/neu tou= swfronei=n without exercising self-control
X. M. 4.3.1. To express purpose the genitive with u(pe/r is very common:

u(pe\r tou= tou/twn gene/sqai ku/_rios . . . pa/nta pra_gmateu/etai he devotes his every effort that he may become master of these
D. 8.45, u(pe\r tou= mh\ to\ keleuo/menon poih=sai in order not to do what was commanded 18. 204. Furthermore, after a)po/, pro/, dia/, meta/, peri/, u(po/, e(/neka, xa/rin, xwri/s, plh/n, me/xri; and after adverbs. In Hdt. tou= may be omitted after a)nti/.

title: Attributive and Substantival Participle
definition: The attributive participle (with any modifier), with or without the article, modifies a noun like any other adjective. The noun with which the attributive participle (with the article) agrees directly, may be omitted, and as a result, the participle becomes a noun. Such participial nouns appear in active, middle, and passive forms, and admit the distinctions of tense. A participle noun may be modified by adjectives or take a genitive when its verbal nature has ceased to be felt. Neuter participles are often substantival, as τὰ δέοντα duties.

smyth.text:
The attributive participle (with any modifier), with or without the article, modifies a substantive like any other adjective.

o( e)festhkw\s ki/ndu_nos th=| po/lei the danger impending over the State
D. 18.176, oi( o)/ntes e)xqroi/ the existing enemies 6. 15, o( parw\n kairo/s the present crisis 3. 3,

to\ *kotu/laion o)nomazo/menon o)/ros the mountain called Cotylaeum
Aes. 3.86,

ai( *ai)o/lou nh=soi kalou/menai the so-called islands of Aeolus
T. 3.88 (cp. 1170). For the position of an attributive participle with its modifiers, see 1166.

The substantive with which the attributive participle (with the article) agrees directly, may be omitted, the participle thus becoming a substantive (1153 b, and N. 1); as,

o( oi)/kade boulo/menos a)pie/nai whoever wants to go home
X. A. 1.7.4. Neuter participles are often substantival, as ta\ de/onta duties.
a. Substantives or relative clauses must often be used to translate such par ticiples, as o( feu/gwn the exile or the defendant, to\ me/llon the future, oi( ni_kw=ntes the victors, o( kle/ptwn the thief, oi( qano/ntes the dead, o( swqei/s the man who has been saved, oi( dedio/tes those who are afraid, oi( a)dikou/menoi those who are (being) wronged,

o( th\n gnw/mhn tau/thn ei)pw/n the one who gave this opinion
T. 8.68,

o( e)ntau=q' e(auto\n ta/ca_s th=s poli_tei/a_s ei)/m' e)gw/ the man who took this position in the State was I
D. 18.62. The participle with the article may represent a relative clause of purpose or result, as
X. A. 2.4.5 cited in 2044.

A participle may be modified by adjectives or take a genitive, when its verbal nature has ceased to be felt:

ta\ mi_kra\ sumfe/ronta th=s po/lews the petty interests of the State
D. 18.28. Cp. sumfe/ron h)=n th=| po/lei it was advantageous to the State 19. 75 (here the participle is used like a predicate). Thucydides often uses in an abstract sense a substantival neuter participle where the infinitive would be more common, e.g., to\ dedio/s fear, to\ qarsou=n courage (for to\ dedie/nai, to\ qarsei=n) 1. 36. See 1153 b, N. 2. In poetry many participles are used substantively, as o( tekw/n father, h( tekou=sa mother, oi( teko/ntes parents.

The article with the participle is either generic or particular (1124). Thus, o( le/gwn the definite speaker on a particular occasion, or orator in general. So o( ou) dra/_sa_s the definite person who did not do something, o( mh\ dra/_sa_s any one who did not do something (a supposed case),

o( mh\ gamw=n a)/nqrwpos ou)k e)/xei kaka/ the unmarried man has no troubles
Men. Sent. 437. Generic are o( tuxw/n, o( boulo/menos, 2050 a.
a. Participles having an indefinite force may, especially in the plural number, be used without the article. Thus,

kataskeyome/nous e)/pempe he sent men to reconnoitre
X. C. 3.1.2,

a)dikou=nta peira_so/meqa . . . a)mu/_nasqai we shall endeavour to avenge ourselves on any one who injures us
X. A. 2.3.23.

A participle and its substantive often correspond to a verbal noun with the genitive or to an articular infinitive. Cp. post urbem conditam and Milton's “Since created man.”
tw=| si/_tw| e)pilei/ponti e)pie/zonto they suffered from the failure of the crops ( = th=| tou= si/_tou e)pilei/yei)
T. 3.20, di' u(_ma=s mh\ cummaxh/santas by reason of your not joining the alliance ( = dia\ to\ u(_ma=s mh\ cummaxh=sai) 6. 80, meta\ *sura_kou/sa_s oi)kisqei/sa_s after the foundation of Syracuse 6. 3,

e)lu/_pei au)to\n h( xw/ra_ porqoume/nh the ravaging of the country grieved him
X. A. 7.7.12,

h( o)rgh\ su\n tw=| fo/bw| lh/gonti a)/peisi his wrath will disappear with the cessation of his fear
X. C. 4.5.21.
a. Except in expressions of time, such as

a(/ma h)=ri a)rxome/nw| at the beginning of spring
T. 2.2, e)pi\ *ko/drou basileu/ontos in the reign of Codrus Lyc. 84 (cp. 1689 b), this construction is in place only when the part. is necessary to the sense. In poetry:

*zeu\s geloi=os o)mnu/menos swearing by Zeus is ridiculous
Ar. Nub. 1241; in Hom. A 601, I 682.

## THE CIRCUMSTANTIAL PARTICIPLE

Position of an attributive participle with its modifiers (A = article, N = noun, P = participle, D = word or words dependent on P): (1) APND:

to\n e)festhko/ta ki/ndu_non th=| po/lei the danger impending over the State
D. 18.176. (2) APDN: tou\s periesthko/tas th=| po/lei kindu/_nous
D. 18.179. (3) ADPN: to\n to/te th=| po/lei perista/nta ki/ndu_non
D. 18.188. (4) NADP:

e(/toimon e)/xei du/namin th\n . . . katadoulwsoue/nhn a)/pantas he has in readiness a force to enslave all
D. 8.46.

The article has the power to make substantival any word or words to which it is prefixed.
a. Adjectives: o( sofo/s the wise man, to\ di/kaion justice.
b. Participles (with indefinite force): o( boulo/menos whoever wills, the first that offers. Cp. 1124.
N. 1.—Such participial nouns appear in active, middle, and passive forms, and admit the distinctions of tense:

oi( e)qelh/sontes me/nein those who shall be willing to remain
X. H. 7.5.24.
N. 2.—Thucydides often substantivizes the neuter participle to form abstract expressions: th=s po/lews to\ ti_mw/menon the dignity of the State 2. 63. Such participial nouns denote an action regulated by time and circumstance. Contrast to\ dedio/s fear (in actual operation) 1. 36 with to\ de/os (simply fear in the abstract).
c. Preposition and case:

oi( e)pi\ tw=n pra_gma/twn those in power, the government
D. 18.247,

oi( e)n th=| h(liki/a| those in the prime of life
T. 6.24.
d. With the genitive, forming a noun-phrase (1299):

ta\ tw=n stratiwtw=n the condition of the soldiers
X. A. 3.1.20,

ta\ th=s o)rgh=s the outbursts of wrath
T. 2.60.
e. Adverbs:

oi(/ t' e)/ndon sunelamba/nonto kai\ oi( e)kto\s kateko/phsan those who were inside were arrested and those outside were cut down
X. A. 2.5.32. Similarly oi( to/te the men of that time, oi( e)kei= the dead, oi( pa/lai the ancients.
N.—An adverb preceded by the article may be used like an adjective:

o( o)rqw=s kubernh/ths the good pilot
P. R. 341c. The article is rarely omitted.
f. Infinitives:

kalou=si/ ge a)kolasi/a_n to\ u(po\ tw=n h(donw=n a)/rxesqai they call intemperance being ruled by one's pleasures
P. Ph. 68e.
g. Any single word or clause: to\ u(_mei=s o(/tan le/gw, th\n po/lin le/gw when I say You, I mean the State
D. 18.88, u(perba\_s to\ di/ka_s u(pexe/tw tou= fo/nou omitting (the words) ‘let him submit to judgment for the murder’
D. 23.220.

title: Circumstantial Participle
definition:
The circumstantial participle is added, without the article, to a noun or pronoun to set forth some circumstance under which an action, generally the main action, takes place. The circumstantial participle thus qualifies the principal verb of the sentence like an adverbial clause or supplementary predicate. The circumstantial participle expresses simply circumstance or manner in general. It may imply various other relations, such as time, manner, means, cause, purpose, concession, condition, etc. It is often impossible to assign a participle exclusively to any one of these relations (which are purely logical), nor can all the delicate relations of the participle be set forth in systematic form.
If the subject of the participle is not identical with the noun or pronoun subject or object of the leading verb, it forms an absolute participle clause of either genitive or accusative absolute (Explained under PartGen. and PartAcc.)

smyth.text:
The circumstantial participle is added, without the article, to a noun or pronoun to set forth some circumstance under which an action, generally the main action, takes place.
a. The circumstantial participle thus qualifies the principal verb of the sentence like an adverbial clause or supplementary predicate. Cp. meta\ tau=ta ei)=pe afterwards he said with gelw=n ei)=pe he said laughingly. Such participles usually have the force of subordinate clauses added to the main verb by conjunctions denoting time, condition, cause, etc.; but may often be rendered by adverbial phrases or even by a separate finite verb, which brings out distinctly the idea latent in the participle.
b. The circumstantial participle has no article. In agreement with a noun and its article, it stands before the article or after the noun (i.e. in the predicate position). By the agreement of the participle with a noun or pronoun, the predicate of the sentence is more exactly defined.
The circumstantial participle has two main constructions each equivalent in meaning to a clause of time, condition, cause, etc.

(I) The subject of the participle is identical with the noun or pronoun subject or object of the leading verb, and agrees with it in gender, number, and case.
（oi( a)/nqrwpoi) lipo/ntes th\n o(do\n feu/gontes o)li/goi a)pe/qnh|skon by leaving the road and making off only a few were killed
X. A. 4.2.7,

prope/myantes kh/ru_ka po/lemon proerou=nta having sent a herald in advance to proclaim war
T. 1.29.
(II) Absolute participial clauses, in which a participle, and not a finite verb, forms the predicate. These are of two kinds.

A. Genitive Absolute.—A participle agreeing in the genitive with its own subject, which is not identical with the subject of the leading verb, is said to stand in the genitive absolute. Cp. 2070.

*ku=ros a)ne/bh e)pi\ ta\ o)/rh ou)deno\s kwlu/_ontos Cyrus ascended the mountains without any one preventing him
X. A. 1.2.22.
N.—The English nominative absolute is represented by the Greek genitive absolute. Cp. Tennyson: “we sitting, as I said, the cock crew loud” = h(mw=n kaqhme/nwn, o(/per e)/legon, me/ga h)=|sen o( a)lektruw/n.

B. Accusative Absolute.—When the participle has no definite subject (i.e. with impersonal verbs), the accusative absolute is used instead of the genitive absolute. Cp. 2076.
sundo/can tw=| patri\ kai\ th=| mhtri\ gamei= th\n *kuaca/rou qugate/ra on the approval of (lit. it seeming good to) his father and mother he married the daughter of Cyaxares
X. C. 8.5.28.

The circumstantial participle expresses simply circumstance or manner in general. It may imply various other relations, such as time, manner, means, cause, purpose, concession, condition, etc. But it is often impossible to assign a participle exclusively to any one of these relations (which are purely logical), nor can all the delicate relations of the participle be set forth in systematic form.

Time.—The time denoted by the participle is only relative to that of the governing verb, and is to be inferred from the context. Each participial form in itself expresses only stage of action (1850).
a)kou/sa_si toi=s strathgoi=s tau=ta e)/doce to\ stra/teuma sunagagei=n on hearing this i<*> seemed best to the generals to collect the troops
X. A. 4.4.19.
a. Several temporal participles have an adverbial force: a)rxo/menos in the beginning, at first, teleutw=n at last, finally, dialipw\n (or e)pisxw\n) xro/non after a while, dialei/pwn xro/non at intervals, xroni/zwn for a long time. Thus,

a(/per kai\ a)rxo/menos ei)=pon as I said at the outset
T. 4.64,

teleutw=n e)xale/painen at last he became angry
X. A. 4.5.16. Note a)rca/menos a)po/ tinos beginning with or especially.

title: Circumstantial Participle \- Genitive Absolute
definition: A circumstantial participle agreeing with a genitive noun or pronoun which is not in the main construction of the sentence, stands in the genitive absolute. The subject of the participle in the genitive absolute construction is different than the subject of the main verb and it should be expressed separately, therefore, both the participle and its subject stand in the genitive, forming a genitive absolute construction. Like other circumstantial participles, the genitive absolute expresses time, cause, condition, concession, or simply any attendant circumstance.

smyth.text:
Any Attendant Circumstance.—

sulle/ca_s stra/teuma e)polio/rkei *mi/_lhton having collected an army he laid siege to Miletus
X. A. 1.1.7, paragge/llei tw=| *klea/rxw| labo/nti h(/kein o(/son h)=n au)tw=| stra/teuma he gave orders to Clearchus to come with all the force he had 1. 2. 1.
a. e)/xwn having, a)/gwn leading, fe/rwn carrying (mostly of inanimate objects), xrw/menos using, labw/n taking are used where English employs with. Thus,

e)/xwn stratia\_n a)fiknei=tai he arrives with an army
T. 4.30, boh=| xrw/menoi with a shout 2. 84, e)ke/leuse labo/nta a)/ndras e)lqei=n o(/ti plei/stous he ordered him to come with all the men he could (or to take . . . and come)
X. A. 1.1.11.
b. In poetry participles (especially) of verbs denoting motion are often added to verbs of giving, setting to make the action more picturesque (H. 304,
S. Aj. 854).

The force of these circumstantial participles does not lie in the participle itself, but is derived from the context. Unless attended by some modifying adverb, the context often does not decide whether the participle has a temporal, a causal, a conditional, a concessive force, etc.; and some participles may be referred to more than one of the above classes. Thus, path\r d' a)peilw=n ou)k e)/xei me/gan fo/bon (Men. fr. 454) may mean: a father by threatening ( = when or because or if or though, he threatens) does not excite much fear.

## GENITIVE ABSOLUTE. ACCUSATIVE ABSOLUTE

Genitive Absolute.—A circumstantial participle agreeing with a genitive noun or pronoun which is not in the main construction of the sentence, stands in the genitive absolute. Like other circumstantial participles, the genitive absolute expresses time, cause, condition, concession, or simply any attendant circumstance.
a. Time:

tau=t' e)pra/_xqh *ko/nwnos strathgou=ntos these things were effected while Conon was in command
I. 9.56,

tou/twn lexqe/ntwn a)ne/sthsan this said, they rose
X. A. 3.3.1,

*)hi+o/na . . . *mh/dwn e)xo/ntwn poliorki/a| ei(=lon they blockaded and captured Eïon which was held by the Medes
T. 1.98.
b. Cause:

tw=n swma/twn qhlu_nome/nwn kai\ ai( yu_xai\ a)rrwsto/terai gi/gnontai by the enfeebling of the body, the spirit too is made weaker
X. O. 4.2.
c. Opposition or Concession: kai\ metapempome/nou au)tou= ou)k e)qe/lw e)lqei=n even though he is sending for me, I am unwilling to go
X. A. 1.3.10. kai/per is usually added (2083).
d. Condition: oi)/omai kai\ nu=n e)/ti e)panorqwqh=nai a)\n ta\ pra/_gmata tou/twn gignome/- nwn if these measures should be taken, I am of the opinion that even now our situation might be rectified
D. 9.76.
e. Attendant Circumstance: *ku=ros a)ne/bh e)pi\ ta\ o)/rh ou)deno\s kwlu/_ontos Cyrus ascended the mountains without opposition (lit. no one hindering)
X. A. 1.2.22 (or since no one opposed him).

e(kw/n willing, a)/_kwn unwilling are properly participles and are treated as such (cp. 2117 c). Thus,

e)mou= ou)x e(ko/ntos without my consent
S. Aj. 455.
a. a)/_kwn, a)ekaco/menos, a)frone/wn, a)elpte/wn, a)na/rmenos, a)nomologou/menos, a)ti/cwn are the only cases in Greek showing the earlier method of negativing the participle with alpha privative. Elsewhere ou) or mh/ is used.

The genitive of the participle may stand without its noun or pronoun
a. When the noun or pronoun may easily be supplied from the context. Thus, oi( de\ pole/mioi, prosio/ntwn (tw=n *(ellh/nwn, previously mentioned),

te/ws me\n h(suxi/azon the enemy, as they were approaching, for a while remained quiet
X. A. 5.4.16, e)rw/ta_, e)/fh, w)= *ku=re, . . . w(s (e)mou=) ta)_lhqh= e)rou=ntos put your question (said he), Cyrus, on the supposition that I will speak the truth
X. C. 3.1.9.
b. When the noun or pronoun may easily be supplied otherwise; here, e.g., a)nqrw/pwn or pra_gma/twn is said to be supplied grammatically. Thus, i)o/ntwn ei)s ma/xhn when (men) are going into battle
X. C. 3.3.54, tou=ton to\n tro/pon pra_xqe/ntwn th=s po/lews gi/gnetai ta\ xrh/mata when (things) have happened in this way, the property belongs to the State
D. 24.12; and in u(/_ontos (*dio/s, 934 a)

pollw=| when it was raining hard
X. H. 1.1.16. Quasi-impersonal verbs (933) thus take the genitive rather than the accusative absolute:

ou(/tws e)/xontos in this state of things
P. R. 381c, influenced by ou(/tws e)xo/ntwn
X. A. 3.1.40.
c. When a subordinate clause with o(/ti follows upon the participle in the passive. Thus,

e)saggelqe/ntwn o(/ti *foi/nissai nh=es e)p' au)tou\s ple/ousin it having been announced that Phoenician ships were sailing against them
T. 1.116, dhlwqe/ntos o(/ti e)n tai=s nausi\ tw=n *(ellh/nwn ta\ pra/_gmata e)ge/neto it having been shown that the salvation of the Greeks depended on their navy 1. 74. The plural is used when the subject of the subordinate clause is plural, or when several circumstances are mentioned.

Exceptionally, the subject of the genitive absolute is the same as that of the main clause. The effect of this irregular construction is to emphasize the idea contained in the genitive absolute. Thus,

bohqhsa/ntwn u(_mw=n proqu/_mws po/lin proslh/yesqe nautiko\n e)/xousan me/ga if you assist us heartily, you will gain to your cause a State having a large navy
T. 3.13. The genitive absolute usually precedes the main verb.
a. The genitive absolute may be used where the grammatical construction demands the dative. Thus,

diabebhko/tos *perikle/ous . . . h)gge/lqh au)tw=| o(/ti *me/gara a)fe/sthke when Pericles had already crossed over, news was brought to him that Megara had revolted
T. 1.114 (in Latin: Pericli iam transgresso nuntiatum est).
b. The subject of the genitive absolute may be identical with the object of the leading verb:

h(=lqon e)pi\ th\n *)epi/dauron w(s e)rh/mou ou)/shs . . . ai(rh/sontes they came against Epidaurus expecting to capture it undefended
T. 5.56.

Observe that the genitive absolute differs from the Latin ablative abso lute herein: 1. The subject need not be expressed (2072). 2. The subject may appear in the leading clause (2073 a). 3. With a substantive the participle w)/n is always added in prose, whereas Latin has to omit the participle. Thus,

pai/dwn o)/ntwn h(mw=n nobis pueris
P. S. 173a. On e)mou= a)/_kontos me invito, see 2071. 4. Because it has a present participle passive and an aorist and perfect participle active, Greek can use the genitive absolute where Latin, through lack of a past participle active, has to use a clause with dum, cum, etc. Thus,

o(/lhs th=s po/lews e)n toi=s polemikoi=s kindu/_nois e)pitrepome/nhs tw=| strathgw=| cum bellicis in periculis universa respublica imperatori committatur
X. M. 3.1.3, tou= paido\s gela/santos cum puer risisset. Latin uses the absolute case more frequently than Greek because it employs the perfect participle passive where Greek uses the aorist participle active. Thus, *ku=ros sugkale/sa_s tou\s strathgou\s ei)=pen Cyrus, convocatis ducibus, dixit
X. A. 1.4.8.

The genitive absolute took its rise from such cases as *sarph/donti d' a)/xos ge/neto *glau/kou a)pio/ntos but sorrow came on Sarpedon for Glaucus—departing M 392. The genitive, here properly dependent on a)/xos ge/neto, ceased to be felt as dependent on the governing expression, and was extended, as a distinct construction, to cases in which the governing expression did not take the genitive. Cp. the development of the accusative with the infinitive (1981).

title: Circumstantial Participle \- Accusative Absolute
definition:
The accusative absolute is an impersonal participe in accusative singular neuter form that does not agree with a subject. When the participle is impersonal, or has an infinitive as its subject, it stands in the accusative absolute, instead of the genitive. Such participles have no apparent grammatical connection with the rest of the sentence.
The participle of a *personal* verb may be used absolutely if it is preceded by ὡς or ὥσπερ. Examples:

smyth.text:
Accusative Absolute.—A participle stands in the accusative absolute, instead of the genitive, when it is impersonal, or has an infinitive as its subject (as under C). When impersonal, such participles have no apparent grammatical connection with the rest of the sentence.
A. Impersonal verbs: de/on, e)co/n, meto/n, paro/n, prosh=kon, me/lon, metame/lon, pare/xon, parasxo/n, tuxo/n, dokou=n, do/can, or do/canta (tau=ta), geno/menon e)p' e)moi/ as it was in my power.
ou)dei\s to\ mei=zon kako\n ai(rh/setai e)co\n to\ e)/la_tton (ai(rei=sqai) no one will choose the greater evil when it is possible to choose the less
P. Pr. 358d, h(=s (boulh=s)

nu=n a)cioi= tuxei=n ou) meto\n au)tw=| to which he now claims admission though he has no right
L. 31.32,

dh=lon ga\r o(/ti oi)=sqa me/lon ge/ soi for of course you know because it concerns you
P. A. 24d, meteme/lonto o(/ti meta\ ta\ e)n *pu/lw|, kalw=s parasxo/n, ou) cune/bhsan they repented that after what had occurred at Pylos, although a favourable occasion had presented itself, they had not come to terms
T. 5.14. Cp. 2086 d, 2087.
N.—Apart from do/can, tuxo/n, the accusative absolute of the aorist participle of impersonal verbs is very rare.
B. Passive participles used impersonally: gegramme/non, dedogme/non, ei)rhme/non, prostaxqe/n, prostetagme/non. Cp. Eng. granted this is so, this done, which said.

ei)rhme/non d' au)tai=s a)panta=n e)nqa/de . . . eu(/dousi kou)x h(/kousin though it was told them to meet here, they sleep and have not come
Ar. Lys. 13, prostaxqe/n moi u(po\ tou= dh/mou *me/nwna a)/gein ei)s *(ellh/sponton a command having been given (it having been commanded) me by the people to convey Menon to the Hellespont
D. 50.12.
N.—The aorist participle passive is rarely used absolutely: a)melhqe/n, a)porrhqe/n, kataxeirotonhqe/n, ku_rwqe/n, o(risqe/n, peranqe/n, prostaxqe/n, xrhsqe/n.
C. Adjectives with o)/n: a)/dhlon o)/n, dunato\n o)/n, a)du/naton o)/n, ai)sxro\n o)/n, kalo\n o)/n, xrew/n (xrew/ + o)/n), etc.

se\ ou)xi\ e)sw/samen . . . oi(=o/n te o)\n kai\ dunato/n we did not rescue you although it was both feasible and possible
P. Cr. 46a, w(s ou)k a)nagkai=on (o)/n)

to\ kle/ptein, ai)tia=| to\n kle/ptonta on the ground that stealing is not necessary you accuse the thief
X. C. 5.1.13.

The impersonal character of the above expressions would not be shown by the genitive since the participle in that case marks a distinction between masculine (neuter) and feminine. The accusative absolute, which occurs first in Herodotus and the Attic prose writers of the fifth century, is probably in its origin an internal accusative, developed, at least in part, by way of apposition (991-994), the neuter of a participle or of an adjective standing in apposition to an idea in the leading clause. Thus, prostaxqe\n au)toi=s ou)k e)to/lmhsan ei)sagagei=n (
Is. 1.22) they did not dare to bring him in—a duty that was enjoined (although it was enjoined) upon them. Cp. pei/qei d' *)ore/sthn mhte/ra . . . ktei=nai, pro\s ou)x a(/pantas eu)/kleian fe/ron he persuaded Orestes to slay his mother, a deed that brings not glory in the eyes of all
E. Or. 30.

The participle of a personal verb may be used absolutely if it is preceded by w(s or w(/sper. Thus, hu)/xeto pro\s tou\s qeou\s ta)_gaqa\ dido/nai, w(s tou\s qeou\s ka/llista ei)do/tas o(poi=a a)gaqa/ e)sti (Socrates) prayed to the gods that they would give him good things, in the belief that the gods know best what sort of things are good
X. M. 1.3.2,

siwph=| e)dei/pnoun, w)/sper tou=to prostetagme/non au)toi=s they were supping in silence just as if this had been enjoined upon them
X. S. 1. 11.
a. Cases without w(s or w(/sper are rare. Thus,

do/canta u(_mi=n tau=ta ei(/lesqe a)/ndras ei)/kosi on reaching this conclusion you chose twenty men
And. 1.81; cp. do/can tau=ta
X. A. 4.1.13 (by analogy to e)/doce tau=ta) and doca/ntwn tou/twn
X. H. 1.7.30. Neuter participles so used come chiefly from impersonal verbs, but
T. 4.125 has ku_rwqe\n ou)de\n oi( *makedo/nes e)xw/roun e)p' oi)/kou the Macedonians proceeded homewards, nothing having been accomplished. The neuter subject is a pronoun, very rarely a substantive (
I. 5.12).

## ADVERBS USED IN CONNECTION WITH CIRCUMSTANTIAL PARTICIPLES

examples.translation: for of course you know because it concerns you

title: Supplementary Participle
definition:
The supplementary participle completes the idea of the verb by showing that to which its action relates. The supplementary participle agrees either with the subject or with the object of the main verb; with the subject when the verb is intransitive or passive, with the object when the verb is transitive.
With verbs of emotion (rejoicing and grieving) the participle often denotes cause.

smyth.text: The supplementary participle completes the idea of the verb by showing that to which its action relates.

The supplementary participle agrees either with the subject or with the object of the main verb; with the subject when the verb is intransitive or passive, with the object when the verb is transitive.

ou)/pot' e)pauo/mhn h(ma=s oi)kti/_rwn I never ceased pitying ourselves
X. A. 3.1.19,

tou\s pe/nhtas e)/paus' a)dikoume/nous I put a stop to the poor being wronged
D. 18.102, e(w/rwn ou) katorqou=ntes kai\ tou\s stratiw/ta_s a)xqome/nous they saw that they (themselves) were not succeeding and that the soldiers were indignant
T. 7.47,

a)dikou=nta fi/lippon e)ch/legca I proved that Philip was acting unjustly
D. 18.136,

eu)qu\s e)legxqh/setai geloi=os w)/n he will straightway be proved to be ridiculous
X. M. 1.7.2.
a. When the object is the same as the subject, it is commonly suppressed, and the participle agrees with the subject. Thus,

o(rw= e)camarta/nwn I see that I err
E. Med. 350,

i)/sqi a)no/htos w)/n know that you are a fool
X. A. 2.1.13, ou)k ai)sqa/nesqe e)capatw/menoi; do you not perceive that you are being deceived?
X. H. 7.1.12,

e)dh/lwse tw=n no/mwn katafronw=n he showed that he despised the laws
And. 4.14.
b. For the sake of emphasis or contrast (and to secure greater symmetry) the object may be expressed by the reflexive pronoun. Thus,

oi)=da e)mauto\n dikai/ws kexrhme/non au)toi=s I know that I have presented my case honestly
I. 15.321,

dei=con ou) pepoihko/ta tau=ta sauto/n show that you did not do this yourself
D. 22.29,

a)mfo/ter' ou)=n oi)=de, kai\ au(to\n u(_mi=n e)pibouleu/onta, kai\ u(_ma=s ai)sqanome/nous now he knows both—that he is himself plotting against you and that you are aware of it
D. 6.18. Observe e)la/nqanon au(tou\s e)pi\ tw=| lo/fw| geno/menoi (agreeing with the subject) without knowing it they found themselves on the hill
X. A. 6.3.22. On the use with su/noida, see 2108.
c. e)/oika (the personal use for the impersonal e)/oike, 1983) usually takes the participle in the dative; as,

e)/oikas o)knou=nti le/gein you seem reluctant to speak
P. R. 414c; but also in the nominative (see 2133).

Many verbs supplementing their meaning by the participle admit of the construction with the infinitive (often with a difference of meaning; see 2123 ff.) or with a substantive clause with o(/ti or w(s.

The present or perfect participle is often used as a simple predicate adjective, especially with ei)mi/ and gi/gnomai. The aorist participle is chiefly poetic.

h)=san a)pistou=nte/s tines fili/ppw| there were some who distrusted Philip
D. 19.53, (*kle/arxos) filoki/ndu_no/s t' h)=n kai\ h(me/ra_s kai\ nukto\s a)/gwn e)pi\ tou\s polemi/ous Clearchus was both fond of danger and by day and by night led his men against the enemy
X. A. 2.6.7, e)gw\ to\ pra=gm' ei)mi\ tou=q' o( dedra_kw/s I am the one who has done this deed
D. 21.104, h)\ tou=to ou)k e)/sti gigno/menon par' h(mi=n; or is not this something that takes place in us?
P. Phil. 39c. So with adjectivized participles (1857), as

sumfe/ron h)=n th=| po/lei it was advantageous to the State
D. 19.75. So with u(pa/rxw am, am assumed (
D. 18.228).
a. Here the participle has the article when it designates the subject itself (third example; cp. 1152). But the article is not used when the participle marks a class in which the subject is included.

The supplementary participle after certain verbs represents a dependent statement.
In h)/kouse *ku=ron e)n *kiliki/a| o)/nta he heard that Cyrus was in Cilicia o)/nta stands for e)sti/, what was heard being “*ku=ros e)n *kiliki/a| e)sti/.” This is shown by the fact that the sentence might have been, according to the principles of indirect discourse, h)/kousen o(/ti *ku=ros e)n *kiliki/a| ei)/h (or e)sti/, 2615). With verbs not introducing indirect discourse, however, there is no such indirect statement; as in

e)pau/santo maxo/menoi they ceased fighting
L. 23.9.

Accordingly, from this point of view, the uses of the supplementary participle are two: (1) not in indirect discourse, and (2) in indirect discourse.
a. Some verbs take the participle either in indirect discourse or not in indirect discourse (2112). It is sometimes impossible to decide whether a participle stands in indirect discourse or not (2113); and the difference, especially after verbs of perceiving (2112 a, b), may be of no great importance to the sense.

## THE SUPPLEMENTARY PARTICIPLE NOT IN INDIRECT DISCOURSE

The supplementary participle not in indirect discourse is often like an object infinitive, the tenses denoting only stage of action and not difference of time (cp. 1850). Thus, compare pau/ome/n se le/gonta we stop you from speaking (of continued action) with kwlu/_ome/n se le/gein we prevent you from speaking (also of continued action).
With verbs denoting being in some modified way (2096-2097).

title: Particular article
definition:
The article ὁ, ἣ, τό marks something or someone as identifiable and known. The particular article denotes individual persons or things as distinguished from others of the same kind, and is used with someone or something that is well known, are already mentioned or in the mind of the speaker or writer, is particularized by an attributive or by the following description, or marked as usual or proper under the circumstances. In Greek, there is no indefinite article; therefore, lack of a definite article functions as an indefinite article.
The article is used when reference is made to a person or thing that is considered to be well known, and therefore is identifiable.

smyth.text:
The article o(, h(\, to/ marks objects as definite and known, whether individuals (the particular article) or classes (the generic article). The context must determine the presence of the generic article.
a. There is no indefinite article in Greek, but a, an is often represented by ti\s (1267).

## THE PARTICULAR ARTICLE

The particular article denotes individual persons or things as distinguished from others of the same kind. Thus, mai/netai a(/_nqrwpos the man is mad (a definite person, distinguished from other men)
P. Phae. 268c.

Special uses of the particular article. The particular article defines
a. Objects well known: o( tw=n e(pta\ sofw/tatos *so/lwn Solon the wisest of the Seven (Sages)
P. Tim. 20d.
b Objects already mentioned or in the mind of the speaker or writer (the anaphoric article): ei)=pon o(/ti ta/lanton a)rguri/ou e(/toimos ei)/hn dou=nai . . . o( de\ labw\n to\ ta/lanton k.t.l. I said that I was ready to give him a talent of silver . . . and he taking the talent, etc.
L. 12.9-10.
c. Objects specially present to the senses or mind (the deictic article):

labe to\ bibli/on take the book
P. Th. 143c,

boulo/menos th\n ma/xhn poih=sai wishing to fight the battle
T. 4.91. Hence the article is regularly used with demonstrative pronouns (1176).
N.—The foregoing (a - c) uses recall the old demonstrative force of the article. Words that ordinarily have no article may receive the article when this older force is present.
d. Objects particularized by an attributive or by a following description:

o( dh=mos o( *)aqhnai/wn the people of the Athenians
Aes. 3.116,

le/ge th\n e)pistolh/n, h(\n e)/pemyen read the letter that he sent
D. 18.39. Cp. 1178 d.
e. Objects marked as usual or proper under the circumstances: to\ me/ros tw=n yh/fwn o( diw/kwn ou)k e)/laben the prosecutor did not get the (requisite) part of the votes
D. 18.103.
f. Objects representative of their class (the distributive article, which resembles the generic use; often translated by a, each):

u(pisxnei=tai dw/sein tri/a h(mida_reika\ tou= mhno\s tw=| stratiw/th| he promises to give each soldier three half-darics a month
X. A. 1.3.21. But the article may be omitted: kai\ ei(/lonto de/ka, e(/na a)po\ fu_lh=s and they chose ten, one from (each) tribe
X. H. 2.4.23.

title: As Substantivizer
definition: When the article is added to a word or word group other than a noun, it is substantivised. The article has the power to make a noun of any word or words to which it is prefixed. It can be used with adjectives, participles, prepositional phrases, adverbs, attributive genitives, and whole word groups, sentences and clauses.

smyth.text:
The article has the power to make substantival any word or words to which it is prefixed.
a. Adjectives: o( sofo/s the wise man, to\ di/kaion justice.
b. Participles (with indefinite force): o( boulo/menos whoever wills, the first that offers. Cp. 1124.
N. 1.—Such participial nouns appear in active, middle, and passive forms, and admit the distinctions of tense:

oi( e)qelh/sontes me/nein those who shall be willing to remain
X. H. 7.5.24.
N. 2.—Thucydides often substantivizes the neuter participle to form abstract expressions: th=s po/lews to\ ti_mw/menon the dignity of the State 2. 63. Such participial nouns denote an action regulated by time and circumstance. Contrast to\ dedio/s fear (in actual operation) 1. 36 with to\ de/os (simply fear in the abstract).
c. Preposition and case:

oi( e)pi\ tw=n pra_gma/twn those in power, the government
D. 18.247,

oi( e)n th=| h(liki/a| those in the prime of life
T. 6.24.
d. With the genitive, forming a noun-phrase (1299):

ta\ tw=n stratiwtw=n the condition of the soldiers
X. A. 3.1.20,

ta\ th=s o)rgh=s the outbursts of wrath
T. 2.60.
e. Adverbs:

oi(/ t' e)/ndon sunelamba/nonto kai\ oi( e)kto\s kateko/phsan those who were inside were arrested and those outside were cut down
X. A. 2.5.32. Similarly oi( to/te the men of that time, oi( e)kei= the dead, oi( pa/lai the ancients.
N.—An adverb preceded by the article may be used like an adjective:

o( o)rqw=s kubernh/ths the good pilot
P. R. 341c. The article is rarely omitted.
f. Infinitives:

kalou=si/ ge a)kolasi/a_n to\ u(po\ tw=n h(donw=n a)/rxesqai they call intemperance being ruled by one's pleasures
P. Ph. 68e.
g. Any single word or clause: to\ u(_mei=s o(/tan le/gw, th\n po/lin le/gw when I say You, I mean the State
D. 18.88, u(perba\_s to\ di/ka_s u(pexe/tw tou= fo/nou omitting (the words) ‘let him submit to judgment for the murder’
D. 23.220.

## POSITION OF THE ARTICLE

## Attributive Position of the Article

The Article with Participles.—A participle with the article may denote an entire class: o( boulo/menos any one who wishes. Cp. 2050, 2052.
o( tuxw/n any chance comer, o( h(ghso/menos a guide,

ou)k a)porh/sete tw=n e)qelhso/ntwn u(pe\r u(_mw=n kindu_neu/ein you will not be in want of those who will be willing to encounter danger for you
D. 20.166, oi( logopoiou=ntes newsmongers 4. 49. The same sense is expressed by pa=s o( with a participle or adjective. On the article with a participle in the predicate, see 1152.
a. When the reference is to a particular occasion, the article may be particular (2052); as o( le/gwn the speaker on a definite occasion.

## THE ARTICLE WITH NUMERALS

The article with the participle is either generic or particular (1124). Thus, o( le/gwn the definite speaker on a particular occasion, or orator in general. So o( ou) dra/_sa_s the definite person who did not do something, o( mh\ dra/_sa_s any one who did not do something (a supposed case),

o( mh\ gamw=n a)/nqrwpos ou)k e)/xei kaka/ the unmarried man has no troubles
Men. Sent. 437. Generic are o( tuxw/n, o( boulo/menos, 2050 a.
a. Participles having an indefinite force may, especially in the plural number, be used without the article. Thus,

kataskeyome/nous e)/pempe he sent men to reconnoitre
X. C. 3.1.2,

a)dikou=nta peira_so/meqa . . . a)mu/_nasqai we shall endeavour to avenge ourselves on any one who injures us
X. A. 2.3.23.

title: Pronominal
definition: Greek articles originally were demonstrative pronouns and the transition from the demonstrative to the article is so gradual that it is often impossible to distinguish between the two in earlier texts. In Homer ὁ, ἡ, τό is usually a demonstrative pronoun and is used substantively or adjectively; it also serves as the personal pronoun of the third person; however, the pronominal use of article is not common in classical Greek and survives mainly in connection with particles (μέν, δέ, γέ, τοί; and with καί preceding ὁ).

smyth.text:
In Homer o(, h(, to/ is usually a demonstrative pronoun and is used substantively or adjectively; it also serves as the personal pronoun of the third person:

a)lla\ to\ qauma/zw but I marvel at this
d 655, to\n lwbhth=ra e)pesbo/lon this prating brawler B 275, th\n d' e)gw\ ou) lu/_sw but her I will not release A 29.

In its substantival use o( either marks a contrast or recalls the subject (the anaphoric use). But with a)lla/, de/, au)ta/r the subject is generally changed. It often precedes an explanatory relative clause: tw=n oi(\ nu=n brotoi/ ei)si of those who are now mortal men A 272.

o(, h(, to/ often approaches to its later use as the definite article or is actually so used: to\n me/n . . . to\n d' e(/teron E 145 (cp. 1107). a. The substantive often stands in apposition, and is added, as an afterthought, to the demonstrative (especially o( de/) which is still an independent pronoun:

au)ta\r o( toi=si ge/rwn o(do\n h(gemo/neuen but he, the old man, was leading the way for them
w 225. In some cases the appositive is needed to complete the sense:

e)pei\ to/ ge kalo\n a)koue/men e)sti\n a)oidou= since this—to listen to a minstrel—is a good thing
a 370. b. Often with adjectives and participles used substantively, with pronouns, and adverbs; especially when a contrast or distinction is implied:

oi( a)/lloi the others
*f 371, ta\ e)sso/mena the things that are to be A 70, to\ pa/ros formerly N 228. The attributive adj. before the noun:

tou\s sou/s thy
*y 572,

ta\ me/gista a)/eqla the greatest prizes
*y 640; and in apposition: *)=iron to\n a)lh/thn Irus, the beggar
s 333. Hom. has path\r ou(mo/s *q 360 (but does not use o( path\r o( e)mo/s).
In Hom. o( contrasts two objects, indicates a change of person, or a change of action on the part of the same person. Attic o( defines.

The transition from the demonstrative to the article is so gradual that it is often impossible to distinguish between the two. Ordinarily Homer does not use the article where it is required in Attic prose. The Epic use is adopted in general by the lyric poets and in the lyric parts of tragedy. Even in tragic dialogue the article is less common than in prose. Hdt. has o( de/ and he, o( ga/r for he.

## o(, h(, to/ AS A RELATIVE

The demonstrative o(, h(, to/ is used as a relative pronoun in Homer only when the antecedent is definite (cp. that): teu/xea d' e)cena/rice, ta/ oi( po/re xa/lkeos *)/arhs he stripped off the arms that brazen Ares had given him H 146. The tragic poets use only the forms in t-, and chiefly to avoid hiatus or to produce position:

ktei/nousa tou\s ou) xrh\ ktanei=n slaying those whom it is not right to slay
E. And. 810. (o(/ = o(/s
E. Hipp. 525.) On the use in Herodotus, see 338 D. 3.

## o(, h(, to/ AS A DEMONSTRATIVE IN ATTIC PROSE
The demonstrative force of o(, h(, to/ survives chiefly in connection with particles (me/n, de/, ge/, toi/; and with kai/ preceding o().

o( is a demonstrative commonly before me/n, de/, and especially in contrasted expressions: o( me/n . . . o( de/ the one, this . . . the other, that, as in

oi( me\n e)poreu/onto, oi( d' ei(/ponto the one party proceeded, the other followed
X. A. 3.4.16.

title: Generic
definition:
The generic article denotes an entire class as distinguished from other classes. Thus, ὁ ἄνθρωπος man (as distinguished from other beings), οἱ γέροντες the aged.
In the singular the generic article makes a single object the representative of the entire class; in the plural it denotes all the objects belonging to a class. The generic article is especially common, in the plural, with adjectives used substantively. A participle with the article may also denote an entire class.

smyth.text:
The generic article denotes an entire class as distinguished from other classes. Thus, o( a)/nqrwpos man (as distinguished from other beings), oi( ge/rontes the aged; dei= to\n stratiw/thn fobei=sqai ma=llon to\n a)/rxonta h)\ tou\s polemi/ous the (a) soldier should fear his commander rather than the enemy
X. A. 2.6.10,

ponhro\n o( su_kofa/nths the informer is a vile thing
D. 18.242.

In the singular the generic article makes a single object the representative of the entire class; in the plural it denotes all the objects belonging to a class. The generic article is especially common, in the plural, with adjectives used substantively:

ou)k a)/n tis ei)/poi w(s tou\s kakou/rgous kai\ a)di/kous ei)/a_ katagela=n no one could say that he permitted the malefactor and the wrongdoer to deride him
X. A. 1.9.13.

The Article with Participles.—A participle with the article may denote an entire class: o( boulo/menos any one who wishes. Cp. 2050, 2052.
o( tuxw/n any chance comer, o( h(ghso/menos a guide,

ou)k a)porh/sete tw=n e)qelhso/ntwn u(pe\r u(_mw=n kindu_neu/ein you will not be in want of those who will be willing to encounter danger for you
D. 20.166, oi( logopoiou=ntes newsmongers 4. 49. The same sense is expressed by pa=s o( with a participle or adjective. On the article with a participle in the predicate, see 1152.
a. When the reference is to a particular occasion, the article may be particular (2052); as o( le/gwn the speaker on a definite occasion.

## THE ARTICLE WITH NUMERALS

title: Abstract Concept
definition:
Abstract nouns generally have the article:
However, the names of the *virtues*, *vices*, *arts*, *sciences*, *occupations* often omit the article.

smyth.text:
Abstract substantives generally have the article:

h( a)reth\ ma=llon h)\ h( fugh\ sw/|zei ta\_s yu_xa/_s valour rather than flight saves men's lives
X. C. 4.1.5.

The names of the virtues, vices, arts, sciences, occupations often omit the article: ti/ swfrosu/nh, ti/ mani/a_; what is temperance, what is madness?
X. M. 1.1.16, a)rxh\ fili/a_s me\n e)/painos, e)/xqra_s de\ yo/gos praise is the beginning of friendship, blame of enmity
I. 1.33. Similarly mousikh/ music, gewrgi/a_ agriculture. So also with do/ca opinion, nou=s mind, te/xnh art, no/mos law.

The article must be used when reference is made to a definite person or thing or to an object well known:

h( tw=n *(ellh/nwn eu)/noia the goodwill of the Greeks
Aes. 3.70, (u(_mi=n)

h( sxolh/ your usual idleness
D. 8.53.

The article may be omitted in designations of space; as ba/qos depth, u(/yos height; also me/geqos size, plh=qos size, amount. ge/nos and o)/noma, used as accusatives of respect (1600), may omit the article.

The article may be omitted with some concrete words conveying a general idea, as yu_xh/ soul, sw=ma body (but the parts of the body regularly have the article).

## THE ARTICLE WITH PROPER NAMES

title: Proper Names
definition: Proper names may take the article if they are previously mentioned or specially marked as well known. However, the use of articles with proper names depends on the style of the author.

smyth.text:
Names of persons and places are individual and therefore omit the article unless previously mentioned (1120 b) or specially marked as well known:

*qouku_di/dhs *)aqhnai=os Thucydides an Athenian
T. 1.1, tou\s stratiw/ta_s au)tw=n, tou\s para\ *kle/arxon a)pelqo/ntas, ei)/a_ *ku=ros to\n *kle/arxon e)/xein their soldiers who seceded to Clearchus, Cyrus allowed Clearchus to retain
X. A. 1.4.7, o( *so/lwn
D. 20.90, oi( *(hra_<*>le/es the Heracleses
P. Th. 169b.

Names of deities omit the article, except when emphatic (nh\ to\n *di/a by Zeus) or when definite cults are referred to: to\ th=s *)aqhna=s e(/dos the sanctuary of Athena (at Athens)
I. 15.2. Names of festivals vary in prose writers (no article in inscriptions): *panaqh/naia the Panathenaea (but

*panaqhnai/ois toi=s mi_kroi=s at the Lesser Panathenaea
L. 21.4). Names of shrines have the article.

Names of nations may omit the article, but oi( *(/ellhnes is usual when opposed to oi( ba/rbaroi the barbarians. When nations are opposed, the article is usually absent: o( po/lemos *)aqhnai/wn kai\ *peloponnhsi/wn
T. 2.1 (but o( po/lemos tw=n *peloponnhsi/wn kai\ *)aqhnai/wn 1. 1). The name of a nation without the article denotes the entire people. Names of families may omit the article: *)asklhpia/dai
P. R. 406a.

Continents: h( *eu)rw/ph Europe, h( *)asi/a_ Asia. Other names of countries, except those originally adjectives (as h( *)attikh/ Attica), omit the article (*libu/h Libya). gh= and xw/ra_ may be added only to such names as are treated as adjectives: h( *boiwti/a_ (gh=) Boeotia. The names of countries standing in the genitive of the divided whole (1311) usually omit the article only when the genitive precedes the governing noun:

*sikeli/a_s to\ plei=ston the most of Sicily
T. 1.12. The article is generally used with names of mountains and rivers; but is often omitted with names of islands, seas (but o( *po/ntos the Pontus), and winds. Names of cities usually omit the article. Names of cities, rivers, and mountains often add po/lis, potamo/s, o)/ros (1142 c). The article is omitted with proper names joined with au)to/s used predicatively (1206 b):

au)tou\s *)aqhnai/ous the Athenians themselves
T. 4.73.

Several appellatives, treated like proper names, may omit the article: basileu/s the king of Persia (o( basileu/s is anaphoric (1120 b) or refers expressly to a definite person). Titles of official persons: pruta/neis the Prytans, strathgoi/ the Generals. Names of relationship, etc.: path/r father, a)nh/r husband, gunh/ wife (but the article is needed when a definite individual is spoken of). Thus:

h)=kon de\ tw=| me\n mh/thr, tw=| de\ gunh\ kai\ pai=des to one there came his mother, to another his wife and children
And. 1.48. So also patri/s fatherland.

Similarly in the case of words forming a class by themselves, and some others used definitely: h(/lios sun, ou)rano/s heaven, w(=rai seasons, kerauno/s thunder, qa/natos death; a)/stu, po/lis city, a)kro/polis citadel, a)gora/_ market-place, tei=xos city-wall, prutanei=on prytaneum, nh=sos island (all used of definite places), qa/latta sea as opposed to the mainland, but h( qa/latta of a definite sea; similarly gh= earth, land.

When the name of a person or place is defined by an appositive (916) or attributive, the following distinctions are to be noted:
a. Persons: *perdi/kka_s *)aleca/ndrou Perdiccas, son of Alexander
T. 2.99: the official designation merely stating the parentage. *dhmosqe/nhs o( *)alkisqe/nous (the popular designation) distinguishes Demosthenes, the son of Alcisthenes (
T. 3.91) from other persons named Demosthenes. (Similarly with names of nations.)
b. Deities: the article is used with the name and with the epithet or (less often) with neither:

tw=| *dii\ tw=| *)olumpi/w| to Olympian Zeus
T. 5.31, *dii\ e)leuqeri/w| to Zeus guardian of freedom 2. 71.
c. Geographical Names are usually treated as attributives, as

o( *eu)fra/_ths potamo/s the river Euphrates
X. A. 1.4.11,

h( *bo/lbh li/mnh lake Bolbe
T. 4.103. In a very few cases (six times in Thuc.) o( is omitted with the name of a river when potamo/s is inserted; but Hdt. often omits o(. With the names of mountains the order is

to\ *ph/lion o)/ros Mt. Pelion
Hdt. 7.129 when the gender agrees, but otherwise

e)s to\ o)/ros th\n *)istw/nhn to Mt. Istone
T. 3.85 (rarely as

u(po\ th=| *ai)/tnh| tw=| o)/rei at the foot of Mt. Aetna
T. 3.116). With names of islands, towns, etc., the order varies:

to\ *parqe/nion po/lisma the town of Parthenium
X. A. 7.8.21;

h( *yutta/leia nh=sos the island of Psyttalea
Hdt. 8.95;

*tragi/a_ h( nh=sos the island of Tragia
T. 1.116;

tou= *peiraiw=s tou= lime/nos of the harbour of Peiraeus
T. 2.93; to\ frou/rion to\ *la/bdalon fort Labdalon 7. 3. The city of Mende would be *me/ndh po/lis, h( *me/ndh h( po/lis, *me/ndh h( po/lis.

title: Emphatic
definition:
The pronoun αὐτός is intensive when it is standing alone in the *nominative* case, or in the predicate position with a noun, or in agreement with a pronoun, in any case. For instance, αὐτὸς ὁ ἀνήρ, ὁ ἀνὴρ αὐτός the man himself, αὐτοῦ τοῦ ἀνδρός, τοῦ ἀνδρὸς αὐτοῦ, etc.
In Homer αὐτός denotes the principal person or thing, in opposition to what is subordinate, and is intensive by contrast:

smyth.text: au)to/s is used as an adjective and as a pronoun. It has three distinct uses: (1) as an intensive adjective pronoun it means self (ipse). (2) As an adjective pronoun, when preceded by the article, it means same (idem). (3) In oblique cases as the personal pronoun of the third person, him, her, it, them (eum, eam, id, eos, eas, ea).

Only the first two uses are Homeric. In Hom. au)to/s denotes the principal person or thing, in opposition to what is subordinate, and is intensive by contrast: au)to\n kai\ qera/ponta the man himself and his attendant Z 18 (cp. sw/sa_s' au)to\n kai\ pai=das
P. G. 511e and see 1208 d). On au)to/s as a reflexive, see 1228 a; on au)to/s emphatic with other pronouns, see 1233 ff.

au)to/s is intensive (self)
a. In the nominative case, when standing alone: au)toi\ th\n gh=n e)/sxon they (the Athenians) seized the land themselves
T. 1.114. Here au)to/s emphasizes the word understood and is not a personal pronoun.
b. In any case, when in the predicate position (1168) with a substantive, or in agreement with a pronoun: au)to\s o( a)nh/r, o( a)nh\r au)to/s the man himself, au)tou= tou= a)ndro/s, tou= a)ndro\s au)tou=, etc.

With a proper name or a word denoting an individual, the article is omitted:

au)to\s *me/nwn Menon himself
X. A. 2.1.5, pro\ au)tou= basile/ws in front of the Great King himself 1. 7. 11.

The word emphasized may be an oblique case which must be supplied: e)/lege de\ kai\ au)to\s o( *bra_si/da_s th=| *qessalw=n gh=| kai\ au)toi=s (scil. toi=s *qessaloi=s) fi/los w)\n i)e/nai and Brasidas himself also said that he came as a friend to the country of the Thessalians and to the Thessalians themselves
T. 4.78, dei= toi/nun tou=t' h)/dh skopei=n (scil. h(ma=s)

au)tou/s we must forthwith consider this matter ourselves
D. 2.2.

examples.translation: the naked truth

examples.greek: τὸ πλέον τοῦ χωρίου αὐτὸ καρτερὸν ὑπῆρχε
examples.translation: the greater part of the place was strong in itself (without artificial fortification)
merely this

the man himself and his attendant

title: Personal Pronoun
definition: When αὐτός is unemphatic and standing alone in the cases other than nominative, it has the meaning of the personal pronoun of the third person (him, her, it, them). This use of αὐτός as a personal pronoun always refers to someone or something that is already introduced.

smyth.text:
au)to/s when unemphatic and standing alone in the oblique cases means him, her, it, them.

e)ke/leuon au)th\n a)pie/nai they ordered her to depart
L. 1.12.

examples.translation: they ordered her to depart

examples.greek: ἄρχει τις αὐτῶν ἢ 'πὶ τῷ πλήθει λόγος;
examples.translation: Does someone govern them, or does authority rest with the masses?

title: Identicalness
definition:
After the article, in the attributive position, αὐτός in any case means same. Thus, ὁ αὐτὸς ἀνήρ, rarely (ὁ) ἀνὴρ ὁ αὐτός the same man.
With a proper name or a word denoting an individual, the article is omitted

smyth.text:
After the article, in the attributive position (1154), au)to/s in any case means same.
Thus o( au)to\s a)nh/r, rarely (o() a)nh\r o( au)to/s the same man;

tou= au)tou= qe/rous in the same summer
T. 4.58,

ta\ au)ta\ tau=ta these same things
X. A. 1.1.7,

oi( tou\s au)tou\s ai)ei\ peri\ tw=n au)tw=n lo/gous le/gontes the people who are continually making the same speeches about the same things
Ant. 5.50.
a. So as a predicate: e)gw\ me\n o( au)to/s ei)mi, i(_mei=s de\ metaba/llete I am the same, it is you who change
T. 2.61.

examples.translation: in the same summer
these same things

examples.greek: οἱ τοὺς αὐτοὺς αἰεὶ περὶ τῶν αὐτῶν λόγους λέγοντες
examples.translation: the people who are continually making the same speeches about the same things

examples.greek: ἐγὼ μὲν ὁ αὐτός εἰμι, ἱμεῖς δὲ μεταβάλλετε
examples.translation: I am the same, it is you who change
Menon himself
in front of the Great King himself

title: Reflexive
definition:
Instead of the indirect ἑαυτοῦ, etc., the oblique cases of αὐτός may be used as a reflexive pronoun:
When ἑαυτοῦ, etc. precede, αὐτοῦ, etc. are usual instead of the direct reflexive:

smyth.text:
Instead of the indirect e(autou=, etc., there may be used
a. The oblique cases of au)to/s:

e)peira=to tou\s *)aqhnai/ous th=s e)s au)to\n o)rgh=s paralu/_ein he tried to divert the Athenians from their anger against himself
T. 2.65. When e(autou=, etc. precede, au)tou=, etc. are usual instead of the direct reflexive:

th\n e(autou= gnw/mhn a)pefai/neto *swkra/ths pro\s tou\s o(mi_lou=ntas au)tw=| Socrates was wont to set forth his opinion to those who conversed with him
X. M. 4.7.1.
b. Of the forms of the third personal pronoun, oi(= and sfi/si (rarely ou(=, sfei=s, sfw=n, and sfa=s). Thus,

h)rw/ta_ au)th\n ei) e)qelh/soi dia_konh=sai/ oi( he asked her if she would be willing to do him a service
Ant. 1.16,

tou\s pai=das e)ke/leuon tou= *ku/_rou dei=sqai diapra/_casqai sfi/sin they ordered their boys to ask Cyrus to get it done for them
X. C. 1.4.1,

keleu/ousi ga\r h(ma=s koinh=| meta\ sfw=n polemei=n for they urge us to make war in common with them
And. 3.27, e)/fh de/, e)peidh\ ou(= e)kbh=nai th\n yu_xh\n . . . . . . a)fiknei=sqai sfa=s ei)s to/pon tina\ daimo/nion he said that when his soul had departed out of him, they (he and others) came to a mysterious place
P. R. 614b. See 1195.
N. 1.—sfei=s may be employed in a dependent sentence if the pronoun is itself the subject of a subordinate statement, and when the reference to the subject of the leading verb is demanded by way of contrast or emphasis:

ei)sagagw\n tou\s a)/llous strathgou\s . . . le/gein e)ke/leuen au)tou\s o(/ti ou)de\n a)\n h(=tton sfei=s a)ga/goien th\n stratia\_n h)\ *cenofw=n after bringing in the rest of the generals he urged them to say that they could lead the army just as well as Xenophon
X. A. 7.5.9. Here au)toi/ (ipsi) is possible. In the singular au)to/s is necessary.
N. 2.—Thucydides often uses the plural forms in reference to the nearest subject: tou\s cumma/xous e)de/disan sfw=n they were afraid of their own allies ( = sfw=n au)tw=n) 5. 14.
N. 3.—e(autou=, etc., are either direct or indirect reflexives, oi(= and sfi/si are only indirect reflexives.

Of the plural forms, h(mw=n au)tw=n, etc. may be either emphatic or reflexive; au)tw=n h(mw=n, etc. are emphatic only; but sfw=n au)tw=n is only reflexive (au)tw=n sfw=n is not used). In Hom. au)to/n may mean myself, thyself , or himself, and e(\ au)to/n, oi(= au)tw=|, etc. are either emphatic or reflexive.
